title: Chinese HSK 3
description: The third step in Mandarin Chinese, from HSK 2 to the new HSK 3 (HSK 3.0). Grammar lessons cover the 把 and 被 sentences, potential complements (听得懂, 看不见), compound direction complements, comparisons with 更, 越…越 and 跟…一样, the modal verbs 应该, 得 and 需要, and the complex sentences of the level: 不但…而且, 如果…就, 只要…就, 只有…才, 除了…以外, 为了, 一边…一边 and 先…然后. The 500 new words (1,000 in all) are learned through typed review cards and the 284 new characters (655 in all) through notecards, words and tracing, with pinyin you can turn off and a switch to traditional characters. The last lessons practise reading, listening, writing sentences, the speaking test and the exam format. Requires Chinese HSK 2.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Neighbours and the people around us: 老-, -员, 咱们
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Welcome to HSK 3. HSK 1 and HSK 2 gave you 500 words and 371 **[[characters]]**: enough to talk about
yourself, your day, travel, school and the weather, to compare things and to say what happened.
This course adds 500 words and 284 characters, for 1,000 words and 655 characters in all, and the
grammar of the level: the {把|bǎ} and {被|bèi} sentences, "can you finish it?" ({吃得完|chī de wán}), comparisons
with {跟|gēn}…{一样|yí yàng} and {越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}, and the linked sentences of real conversation ({不但|bú dàn}…{而且|ér qiě}, {只要|zhǐ yào}…{就|jiù}, {为了|wèi le}).

This first lesson is about the people who live around you: neighbours, the "aunties" and "uncles"
of the building, couples, old people and children. Along the way you'll see how Chinese builds
words from small pieces ({老|lǎo}-, -{员|yuán}, -{子|zi}, -{家|jiā}), when to say {咱们|zán men} instead of {我们|wǒ men}, how to talk about
other people with {别人|bié ren}, and how to put several descriptions in front of one noun.

## How this course works

The lessons have the same parts as in HSK 1 and HSK 2: words in context, a character section with
tracing pads, a dialogue, speaking practice and a quiz, with **[[pinyin]]** over every character (the
Pinyin switch hides it) and an optional colour for each **[[tone]]**. What's new:

- **Longer reading.** Every lesson has an original text of 150 to 250 characters in modules 1–3,
  and 250 to 300 later: notices, emails, messages and short stories, with questions and a
  translation to open when you've tried it yourself.
- **Writing in characters.** Every quiz has questions you answer in characters (type them with
  your device's Chinese keyboard, or with pinyin where the question allows it) and sentence
  builders. From module 4 on, lessons also ask you to write one or two sentences of your own.
- **Speaking.** The new HSK 3 comes with a speaking test, so every module practises answering
  questions and describing things out loud.
- **Handwriting.** 150 more characters (✎) to write from memory, 250 in all by the end of the
  course. Each lesson has a "Write it" line for its ✎ characters, and each module reviews some of
  the 100 from HSK 1 and HSK 2.
- **Sound parts.** Few new radicals are left, so the character sections now show the part of a
  character that gives its sound: the {令|lìng} in {冷|lěng}, {零|líng} and this lesson's {={邻居|lín jū}=}.
- **Tone questions.** Quizzes include items where you hear a word and pick its tones.
- **Traditional characters.** As before, the Traditional switch shows the course in traditional
  characters. Character sections stay in simplified and give the traditional form in brackets where
  it differs: {=邻=} (traditional {+邻+}).

## The people around you

| Word | Meaning | When people use it |
|---|---|---|
| {邻居|lín jū} | neighbour | {我|wǒ}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}, {邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā} (the neighbours' home) |
| {叔叔|shū shu} | uncle (father's younger brother) | also any man of your parents' age: {王叔叔|Wáng shū shu} |
| {阿姨|ā yí} | aunt (mother's sister) | also any woman of your parents' age: {张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí} |
| {大人|dà ren} | adult, grown-up | the opposite of {孩子|hái zi} / {小孩儿|xiǎo háir} |
| {老人|lǎo rén} | old person | {老人|lǎo rén} and {孩子|hái zi}, the old and the young |
| {男人|nán rén} / {女人|nǚ rén} | man / woman | general words for men and women |
| {爱人|ài ren} | husband or wife, spouse | {这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爱人|ài ren} |
| {夫妻|fū qī} | husband and wife, a couple | {他们|tā men}{是|shì}{夫妻|fū qī} |
| {姐妹|jiě mèi} | sisters | {我们|wǒ men}{是|shì}{姐妹|jiě mèi} |
| {名人|míng rén} | famous person | {他|tā}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{名人|míng rén} |

### {叔叔|shū shu} and {阿姨|ā yí}: family words for people outside the family

You met these two in HSK 2 with a gloss. In the family, {叔叔|shū shu} is your father's younger brother and
{阿姨|ā yí} your mother's sister. Outside the family they're the friendly way to address an adult of your
parents' generation: a neighbour, a friend's parent, a shop owner, a driver. Children say them to
almost any adult; adults use them too, especially with neighbours. With a family name in front they
become a name: {王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}, {张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí}.

{阿姨|ā yí}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！ — Hello! (to a woman of your parents' age)

{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{是|shì}{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}。 — Uncle Wang is our neighbour.

For people of your grandparents' age, use the words you know from HSK 2: {爷爷|yé ye} and {奶奶|nǎi nai} ({王|Wáng}{爷爷|yé ye},
{张|Zhāng}{奶奶|nǎi nai}). In many families {阿姨|ā yí} is also the word for a woman who helps at home, cleans or looks after
the children.

### {大人|dà ren} and {老人|lǎo rén}

{大人|dà ren} is an adult, said mostly when children are part of the picture; {老人|lǎo rén} is an old person.
Both are {人|rén} with a word in front, like {家人|jiā rén} from HSK 1:

{这个|zhè ge}{电影|diàn yǐng}{大人|dà ren}{和|hé}{孩子|hái zi}{都|dōu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{看|kàn}。 — Adults and children both like this film.

{我们|wǒ men}{小区|xiǎo qū}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{老人|lǎo rén}，{他们|tā men}{每天|měi tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{一起|yì qǐ}{跑步|pǎo bù}。 — There are lots of old people in our compound; they go
running together every morning.

### {男人|nán rén} and {女人|nǚ rén}

These are the general words for men and women: {男人|nán rén}{和|hé}{女人|nǚ rén} (men and women), {一|yí}{个|gè}{女人|nǚ rén} (a woman). To
point someone out in speech, people often say {那个|nà ge}{男|nán}{的|de} / {那个|nà ge}{女|nǚ}{的|de} (that man / that woman: the {的|de}
phrase from HSK 2). To address a stranger, use {先生|xiān sheng}, {女士|nǚ shì}, {叔叔|shū shu} or {阿姨|ā yí}, never {男人|nán rén} or {女人|nǚ rén}.

### {爱人|ài ren} and {夫妻|fū qī}

{爱人|ài ren} is "the person you love": in mainland usage, your husband or wife. It was the everyday
word for "spouse" for much of the 20th century, and many people, especially older ones, still use
it; younger people often say {丈夫|zhàng fu} and {妻子|qī zi} (HSK 2), or the informal {老公|lǎo gōng} (hubby) and {老婆|lǎo po}
(wife). {夫妻|fū qī} is a husband and wife together, a married couple:

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爱人|ài ren}，{他|tā}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{工作|gōng zuò}。 — This is my husband; he works at a hospital.

{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{和|hé}{张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí}{是|shì}{夫妻|fū qī}。 — Uncle Wang and Auntie Zhang are husband and wife.

### {姐妹|jiě mèi} and {名人|míng rén}

{姐妹|jiě mèi} is "sisters" ({姐姐|jiě jie} + {妹妹|mèi mei}); brothers are {兄弟|xiōng dì} (not a course word). {名人|míng rén} is {名|míng} (name,
fame) + {人|rén}: someone with a name, a famous person.

{她们|tā men}{是|shì}{姐妹|jiě mèi}，{姐姐|jiě jie}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}，{妹妹|mèi mei}{是|shì}{老师|lǎo shī}。 — They're sisters: the older one is a doctor, the younger one a
teacher.

## {咱们|zán men}: "we", and you're included

{咱们|zán men} is "we" when the person you're talking to is part of it: you and me, us and you.
{我们|wǒ men} can include the listener or leave them out. So:

{咱们|zán men}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}！ — Let's go! (you and I)

{咱们|zán men}{是|shì}{邻居|lín jū}，{有|yǒu}{事|shì}{就|jiù}{找|zhǎo}{我|wǒ}。 — We're neighbours: if you need anything, come to me.

{我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}，{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？ — We're going to Beijing tomorrow; are you coming?

In the last sentence the listener isn't (yet) part of the group, so {咱们|zán men} would be wrong. When in
doubt, {我们|wǒ men} is always possible. {咱们|zán men} is a spoken word, used most in northern speech; many speakers
from the south say {我们|wǒ men} for both. It sounds warm and inclusive, which is why a neighbour says
{咱们|zán men}{小区|xiǎo qū} (our compound, yours and mine).

## {别人|bié ren}: other people

{别人|bié ren} means "other people, someone else". It works as a subject or an object, and with {的|de}
for "someone else's":

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{别人|bié ren}{的|de}{书|shū}，{不|bú}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}。 — This is someone else's book, not mine.

{别人|bié ren}{都|dōu}{走|zǒu}{了|le}，{他|tā}{还|hái}{在|zài}。 — Everyone else has left; he's still here.

{别|bié}{听|tīng}{别人|bié ren}{的|de}，{你|nǐ}{自己|zì jǐ}{想想|xiǎng xiang}。 — Don't listen to what other people say; think it over yourself.

The last sentence has both {别|bié}: {别|bié} "don't" (HSK 2) and {别人|bié ren}. In {别人|bié ren} the second
syllable is light. For "other (things)" Chinese says {别的|bié de} (lesson 27's word): {别人|bié ren} is only
for people.

## Building words: prefixes and suffixes

Chinese has a small number of syllables and builds most of its words from them. This **[[word formation]]**
is something you can use: once you know what the pieces mean, you can often guess a
new word, and remember it more easily. Most words are two pieces side by side ({名|míng} + {人|rén}, {大|dà} + {人|rén}). A
few pieces attach in a fixed place: a **[[prefix]]** comes before the main part, a **[[suffix]]** after it.

### The prefix {老|lǎo}-: Lao Wang, Lao Zhang

{老|lǎo} + family name is how adults address and talk about people they know well, of about their own age
or older: colleagues, neighbours, old friends. It's friendly, not rude, and it doesn't mean the
person is old:

{老王|Lǎo Wáng}，{你|nǐ}{今天|jīn tiān}{去|qù}{公司|gōng sī}{吗|ma}？ — Lao Wang, are you going to the office today?

{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{老张|Lǎo Zhāng}。 — This is my classmate Lao Zhang.

For someone younger, people say {小|xiǎo} + family name ({小王|Xiǎo Wáng}, {小李|Xiǎo Lǐ}). Neither is used for strangers, or for
your teacher or boss: for them, family name + title ({王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}, {王|Wáng}{先生|xiān sheng}).

{老|lǎo} has its ordinary meaning "old" too. For people and relationships it means old in years or of
long standing:

{老人|lǎo rén} — an old person

{老朋友|lǎo péng you} — an old friend (a friend for a long time; not necessarily old in years)

{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{老|lǎo}{了|le}。 — My dad has got old.

For things, "old, not new" is usually {旧|jiù} (next lesson). And in {老师|lǎo shī} (teacher), {老|lǎo} is only a prefix,
with no meaning of its own.

### The suffix -{员|yuán}: a person with a role

{员|yuán} after a word makes a person who does that job or belongs to that group. {员|yuán} isn't a
word on its own: you can't say "a {员|yuán}".

| Word | Parts | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {服务员|fú wù yuán} | {服务|fú wù} (to serve, lesson 19) + {员|yuán} | waiter, waitress; attendant |
| {运动员|yùn dòng yuán} | {运动|yùn dòng} (sport, HSK 2) + {员|yuán} | athlete (lesson 21) |
| {店员|diàn yuán} | {店|diàn} (shop) + {员|yuán} | shop assistant |
| {学员|xué yuán} | {学|xué} (to learn) + {员|yuán} | student (on a course), trainee |

{服务员|fú wù yuán}，{请|qǐng}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{一|yì}{杯|bēi}{水|shuǐ}。 — Excuse me (waiter), a glass of water, please.

### The suffix -{子|zi}: a noun maker

-{子|zi}, said with a light tone, turns a syllable into a noun. Most of the time it adds no
meaning at all; it just makes a word out of a syllable. You know many: {桌子|zhuō zi}, {椅子|yǐ zi}, {杯子|bēi zi}, {裤子|kù zi}, {本子|běn zi},
{个子|gè zi}, {孩子|hái zi}, {儿子|ér zi}, {妻子|qī zi}. This module adds {房子|fáng zi} (house, lesson 02) and {箱子|xiāng zi} (box,
suitcase, lesson 03), {盘子|pán zi} (plate) and {瓶子|píng zi} (bottle).

In {儿子|ér zi} and {孩子|hái zi} the {子|zi} keeps its old meaning, "child". In a few words it has a full tone,
{子|zǐ}, and a meaning of its own, as in the names of ancient thinkers ({孔子|Kǒng zǐ}, Confucius:
honors lesson 20h1).

### The suffix -{家|jiā}: an expert

After a field of work, {家|jiā} means a person known for it: {画家|huà jiā} (painter: {画|huà}, to paint, is HSK 2; the
word is lesson 22's), {作家|zuò jiā} (writer). This is the same {家|jiā} as "home, family" in {家人|jiā rén} and
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}, used in another way. Don't confuse it with {大家|dà jiā} (everyone, HSK 1).

## Several descriptions before one noun

In Chinese, everything that describes a noun comes before it. When there are several of these
**[[multiple attributives]]**, they follow a fixed order:

| 1. Whose | 2. Which (this / that + number + measure) | 3. What it's like + {的|de} | 4. The noun |
|---|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de} | {那个|nà ge} | {可爱|kě ài}{的|de} | {孩子|hái zi} |
| {王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{家|jiā}{的|de} | {那|nà}{两|liǎng}{个|gè} | {很|hěn}{大|dà}{的|de} | {房间|fáng jiān} |
| {我|wǒ}{的|de} | {这|zhè}{本|běn} | {新|xīn} | {书|shū} |

{我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de}{那个|nà ge}{可爱|kě ài}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi} — that cute child of my neighbours' ({可爱|kě ài}, cute, lesson 04)

{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{家|jiā}{的|de}{那|nà}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{很|hěn}{大|dà}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān} — those two big rooms in Uncle Wang's home

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{这|zhè}{本|běn}{新|xīn}{书|shū} — this new book of mine

The rule of thumb: whose it is, then which one, then what it's like, then the noun. English often
puts the owner at the end ("of my neighbours'"); Chinese puts it first. A one-syllable adjective
such as {新|xīn}, {小|xiǎo} or {大|dà} joins the noun without {的|de} and stays right next to it ({新|xīn}{书|shū}, {小孩儿|xiǎo háir}).

Two more points. Don't stack {的|de} after every word: close relations drop it, as in HSK 1 ({我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū},
{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}), so {我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi} is natural and ~~{我|wǒ}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}{的|de}{家|jiā}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}~~ is not. And you'll sometimes hear the
description before {这|zhè} / {那|nà} ({可爱|kě ài}{的|de}{那个|nà ge}{孩子|hái zi}, "the cute one"): that picks one out from others. The order
in the table is the everyday one.

## Life in a {小区|xiǎo qū}

Many city people in mainland China live in a {小区|xiǎo qū}, a housing estate or residential compound: a
group of apartment buildings with its own gate and paths, often a small shop, a playground and a
place for older people to sit and talk. Neighbours meet there every day.

{我们|wǒ men}{小区|xiǎo qū}{很|hěn}{大|dà}，{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{楼|lóu}。 — Our compound is big; there are lots of buildings.

{小区|xiǎo qū}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}，{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi}{很|hěn}{方便|fāng biàn}。 — There's a supermarket in the compound, so shopping is convenient.
({方便|fāng biàn}, convenient: next lesson)

{我|wǒ}{在|zài}{小区|xiǎo qū}{门口|mén kǒu}{等|děng}{你|nǐ}。 — I'll wait for you at the compound gate.

Honors lesson 05h1 compares this way of living with the older courtyard houses.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 阿 | (a prefix in address and names) | ā (and others) | 阝 | 7 | {阿姨|ā yí} |
| 姨 | aunt (mother's sister) | yí | 女 | 9 | {阿姨|ā yí} |
| 叔 | uncle (father's younger brother) | shū | 又 | 8 | {叔叔|shū shu} |
| 邻 (traditional 鄰) | neighbour; nearby | lín | 阝 | 7 | {邻居|lín jū} |
| 居 | to live, reside | jū | 户 | 8 | {邻居|lín jū} |
| 咱 ✎ | we (including you) | zán | 口 | 9 | {咱们|zán men} |
| 区 (traditional 區) ✎ | area, district | qū | 匸 | 4 | {小区|xiǎo qū} |
| 员 (traditional 員) | member, staff | yuán | 口 | 7 | {员|yuán}, {服务员|fú wù yuán}, {运动员|yùn dòng yuán} |

- 阿 is 阝 + {可|kě}, which gave the sound long ago. Today it's read *ā* in {阿姨|ā yí} and in
  friendly names such as {阿明|Ā Míng} (used in the south); in a few other words it has other
  readings.
- 姨 is {女|nǚ} (woman) + 夷 *yí*, the sound part: here the sound still matches exactly.
- 叔 is {又|yòu} (a hand) + the left part 尗 *shū*, which gives the sound. "Uncle" is a borrowed
  meaning: the character is traditionally explained as "to pick up" (with the hand).
- 邻 is 令 *lìng* + 阝. 令 gives the sound, as it does in {冷|lěng} (cold) and {零|líng} (zero): three
  characters you can now read as a family. The traditional form 鄰 has a different sound part,
  粦 *lín*.
- 居 is 古 *gǔ* (old), which once gave the sound, under a roof-like top. The readings no longer
  match. Make Me a Hanzi files it under 户 (door); most dictionaries file it under 尸, the radical of
  next lesson's 屋 and {层|céng}.
- 咱 is {口|kǒu} (mouth: a word of speech) + 自 ({自|zì}, self). A memory aid: "myself and yourself, said
  out loud". Some dictionaries call 自 the sound part, but *zì* and *zán* are far apart.
- 区 is an enclosure open on the right (匸) around a cross, 乂. In the traditional form 區 the
  inside is 品 (three mouths: many things); the cross is a shorthand that simplified characters use
  for several shapes.
- {员|yuán} is {口|kǒu} over 贝 (a cowrie shell, once used as money; traditional 貝). It's the sound part of
  {圆|yuán} (round), which isn't a course word.

### The two 阝

阝 is the radical of 阿 and 邻, but they aren't the same 阝. **On the left** (阿, and 院 from
{医院|yī yuàn}, 阴 from {阴|yīn}, cloudy, HSK 2) it's a hill or mound. **On the right** (邻, and {都|dōu} from HSK
1) it was once 邑, a town: fitting for 邻, the people in the next house. Both are written with the
same two strokes.

### Stroke order

- **阿, 邻**: 阝 is two strokes: first the bent stroke that looks like a "3" (across, down and
  round, ending with a hook), then the vertical. In 阿 it comes first; in 邻 it comes last, after
  令.
- **区**: the top horizontal, then the cross (left-falling stroke, then the dot), and last the
  stroke that goes down the left side and along the bottom. The enclosure closes last.
- **叔**: the left part first (a short vertical, a short horizontal, the long horizontal, then the
  vertical hook and its two small strokes), then {又|yòu}.
- **居**: 尸 first (the top in two strokes, then the long left-falling stroke), then 古 inside:
  horizontal, vertical, then {口|kǒu}.
- **咱**: {口|kǒu} first, small and high on the left, then 自: the short left-falling stroke on top,
  then the box with its two inner horizontals.

```trace
阿姨叔邻居咱区员
```

Write it: 咱 and 区 are on the handwriting list. Write each three times from memory, on paper or on
the pad: in 区 the bottom-left stroke goes last.
=}

## Dialogue: a new neighbour

{大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫) has just moved into a flat in Beijing. In the compound he meets {张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí} (张阿姨) and
her husband {王叔叔|Wáng shū shu} (王叔叔).

```dialogue
# A new neighbour
张阿姨: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{新|xīn}{来|lái}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}{吧|ba}？
= Hello! You must be the new neighbour?
大卫: {对|duì}，{我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{大卫|Dà wèi}，{住|zhù}{在|zài}{三|sān}{号|hào}{楼|lóu}。{阿姨|ā yí}，{您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？
= That's right, I'm David. I live in Building 3. And your name, please?
张阿姨: {我|wǒ}{姓|xìng}{张|Zhāng}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{叫|jiào}{我|wǒ}{张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí}。{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爱人|ài ren}，{老王|Lǎo Wáng}。
= My family name is Zhang; everyone calls me Auntie Zhang. This is my husband, Lao Wang.
王叔叔: {你好|nǐ hǎo}！{你|nǐ}{就|jiù}{叫|jiào}{我|wǒ}{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{吧|ba}。{你|nǐ}{是|shì}{哪|nǎ}{国|guó}{人|rén}？
= Hello! Just call me Uncle Wang. Where are you from?
大卫: {我|wǒ}{是|shì}{英国人|Yīng guó rén}，{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}{的|de}{一|yì}{家|jiā}{公司|gōng sī}{工作|gōng zuò}。
= I'm British. I work for a company here.
王叔叔: {咱们|zán men}{小区|xiǎo qū}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{外国人|wài guó rén}，{也|yě}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{孩子|hái zi}，{你|nǐ}{会|huì}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{这儿|zhèr}{的|de}。
= There are lots of foreigners in our compound, and lots of children too. You'll like it here.
张阿姨: {有|yǒu}{问题|wèn tí}{就|jiù}{来|lái}{找|zhǎo}{我们|wǒ men}。{老王|Lǎo Wáng}{在|zài}{这个|zhè ge}{小区|xiǎo qū}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三十|sān shí}{年|nián}{了|le}，{谁|shéi}{都|dōu}{认识|rèn shi}{他|tā}。
= If you have any problems, just come to us. Lao Wang has lived in this compound for thirty years; everyone knows him.
大卫: {太|tài}{好|hǎo}{了|le}，{谢谢|xiè xie}{叔叔|shū shu}{阿姨|ā yí}！
= That's great, thank you!
王叔叔: {不客气|bú kè qi}，{咱们|zán men}{是|shì}{邻居|lín jū}。
= Not at all, we're neighbours.
张阿姨: {明天|míng tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{我们|wǒ men}{家|jiā}{包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{你|nǐ}{也|yě}{来|lái}{吧|ba}！
= We're making dumplings at home tomorrow evening. Come along!
大卫: {好|hǎo}{啊|a}，{谢谢|xiè xie}{您|nín}！
= I'd love to, thank you!
```

- {新|xīn}{来|lái}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū} is "the newly arrived neighbour": {新|xīn} + verb + {的|de} describes the person.
- {英国人|Yīng guó rén} (a British person) and {外国人|wài guó rén} (foreigner, HSK 2).
- {谁|shéi}{都|dōu}{认识|rèn shi}{他|tā} is "everyone knows him": a question word with {都|dōu} that doesn't ask anything. Lesson 11
  explains the pattern.
- {包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi} is "to make (wrap) dumplings", with {包|bāo} "to wrap" from HSK 2.
- {谢谢|xiè xie}{叔叔|shū shu}{阿姨|ā yí} thanks both of them at once, by their forms of address.

## Reading: my neighbours

> {我|wǒ}{叫|jiào}{赵军|Zhào Jūn}，{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{的|de}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小区|xiǎo qū}{里|lǐ}。{我|wǒ}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}{是|shì}{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{和|hé}{张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí}，{他们|tā men}{是|shì}{夫妻|fū qī}，{都|dōu}{六十|liù shí}{多|duō}{岁|suì}{了|le}。{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{每天|měi tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{在|zài}{小区|xiǎo qū}{里|lǐ}{跑步|pǎo bù}，{张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{跟|gēn}{小区|xiǎo qū}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{老人|lǎo rén}{一起|yì qǐ}{唱|chàng}{歌|gē}。{他们|tā men}{的|de}{女儿|nǚ ér}{是|shì}{医生|yī shēng}，{在|zài}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{工作|gōng zuò}，{不常|bù cháng}{回来|huí lái}。{所以|suǒ yǐ}{叔叔|shū shu}{阿姨|ā yí}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}。{我|wǒ}{儿子|ér zi}{今年|jīn nián}{五|wǔ}{岁|suì}，{他|tā}{不|bú}{叫|jiào}{他们|tā men}“{叔叔|shū shu}”“{阿姨|ā yí}”，{叫|jiào}{他们|tā men}“{王|Wáng}{爷爷|yé ye}”“{张|Zhāng}{奶奶|nǎi nai}”。{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{爱人|ài ren}{工作|gōng zuò}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}，{有时候|yǒu shí hou}{很|hěn}{晚|wǎn}{才|cái}{下班|xià bān}，{张阿姨|Zhāng ā yí}{就|jiù}{给|gěi}{孩子|hái zi}{做饭|zuò fàn}，{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{给|gěi}{他|tā}{讲|jiǎng}{故事|gù shi}。{王叔叔|Wáng shū shu}{常|cháng}{说|shuō}：“{咱们|zán men}{是|shì}{邻居|lín jū}，{邻居|lín jū}{就|jiù}{是|shì}{家人|jiā rén}。”{我|wǒ}{觉得|jué de}{有|yǒu}{这样|zhè yàng}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}{真|zhēn}{好|hǎo}。

- {不常|bù cháng} is "not often" ({常|cháng} is lesson 27's word, short for HSK 2's {经常|jīng cháng}).
- {很|hěn}{晚|wǎn}{才|cái}{下班|xià bān} is "don't finish work until late": {才|cái} (only then) is lesson 25's.
- {讲|jiǎng}{故事|gù shi} is "to tell stories" (both words come later in the course).

1. How old are Uncle Wang and Auntie Zhang?
2. What does Zhao Jun's son call them, and why not {叔叔|shū shu} and {阿姨|ā yí}?
3. What do the neighbours do when Zhao Jun and his wife work late?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. They're both over sixty ({都|dōu}{六十|liù shí}{多|duō}{岁|suì}{了|le}).
2. {王|Wáng}{爷爷|yé ye} and {张|Zhāng}{奶奶|nǎi nai} (Grandpa Wang and Granny Zhang). For a five-year-old they're the age of
   grandparents; Zhao Jun, an adult, calls them {叔叔|shū shu} and {阿姨|ā yí}.
3. Auntie Zhang cooks for the boy and Uncle Wang tells him stories.

"My name is Zhao Jun and I live in a residential compound in Beijing. My neighbours are Uncle Wang
and Auntie Zhang; they're husband and wife, and both over sixty. Uncle Wang goes running in the
compound every morning, and Auntie Zhang likes singing with the other old people of the compound.
Their daughter is a doctor in Shanghai and doesn't come home often, so they're very fond of my
child. My son is five this year. He doesn't call them 'uncle' and 'auntie': he calls them 'Grandpa
Wang' and 'Granny Zhang'. My wife and I are very busy at work, and sometimes we don't finish until
late; then Auntie Zhang cooks for our son and Uncle Wang tells him stories. Uncle Wang often says:
'We're neighbours, and neighbours are family.' I think it's really good to have neighbours like
that."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Meeting your neighbours
{您|nín}{好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{新|xīn}{来|lái}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}。
= Hello, I'm the new neighbour.
{阿姨|ā yí}，{您|nín}{贵姓|guì xìng}？
= Excuse me, what's your family name? (to an older woman)
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{爱人|ài ren}。
= This is my husband / my wife.
{咱们|zán men}{一起|yì qǐ}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}！
= Let's go together!
{我们|wǒ men}{小区|xiǎo qū}{很|hěn}{大|dà}，{邻居|lín jū}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。
= Our compound is big, and the neighbours are all very nice.
{那个|nà ge}{孩子|hái zi}{是|shì}{谁|shéi}{家|jiā}{的|de}？
= Whose child is that?
```

Practise describing too. Say two or three sentences about a neighbour or a friend's family: who
they are ({他们|tā men}{是|shì}{夫妻|fū qī}), how old they are, and what they like doing. Then record yourself and compare.

## Pronunciation

- {阿姨|ā yí}: a high level *ā*, then a rising *yí*.
- {叔叔|shū shu}: *sh* with the tongue curled back; the second syllable is light.
- {咱们|zán men}: *z* is "dz", with no puff of air. Don't say *zǎn*.
- {邻居|lín jū}: after *j* the *u* is ü (lips rounded as for "oo", tongue as for "ee").
- {大人|dà ren}, {爱人|ài ren} and {别人|bié ren} have a light {人|rén}; {老人|lǎo rén}, {男人|nán rén},
  {女人|nǚ rén} and {名人|míng rén} keep its rising tone. Listen to the dialogue for both.
- {女人|nǚ rén}: the ü of *nǚ* again, and a dipping third tone.

## Common mistakes

- {咱们|zán men} when the listener isn't included: ~~{咱们|zán men}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}，{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？~~ Say {我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}，{你|nǐ}{去|qù}{吗|ma}？
- English order for descriptions: ~~{那个|nà ge}{孩子|hái zi}{我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de}~~ or ~~{那个|nà ge}{可爱|kě ài}{的|de}{我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}~~. Say
  {我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de}{那个|nà ge}{可爱|kě ài}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}: whose, which, what it's like, then the noun.
- Too many {的|de}: ~~{我|wǒ}{的|de}{邻居|lín jū}{的|de}{家|jiā}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}.
- {员|yuán} on its own: ~~{他|tā}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{员|yuán}~~. {员|yuán} is a suffix: {他|tā}{是|shì}{服务员|fú wù yuán}.
- {老王|Lǎo Wáng} to a stranger or your boss: {老|lǎo} + family name is for people you know well. Use a title:
  {王|Wáng}{先生|xiān sheng}, {王|Wáng}{老师|lǎo shī}.
- {男人|nán rén} / {女人|nǚ rén} to call someone: ~~{女人|nǚ rén}，{请问|qǐng wèn}…~~ Say {阿姨|ā yí}, {请问|qǐng wèn}… or {女士|nǚ shì}, {请问|qǐng wèn}…
- {别人|bié ren} for things: ~~{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{要|yào}{别人|bié ren}{的|de}~~ (for "I want a different one") means "I want someone else's".
  "Another one, a different one" is {别的|bié de} (lesson 27).

## Key points

- People: {邻居|lín jū}, {叔叔|shū shu} / {阿姨|ā yí} (relatives, and any adult of your parents' age), {大人|dà ren}, {老人|lǎo rén}, {男人|nán rén}, {女人|nǚ rén},
  {爱人|ài ren} (spouse), {夫妻|fū qī} (a couple), {姐妹|jiě mèi}, {名人|míng rén}.
- {咱们|zán men} includes the listener; {我们|wǒ men} can include or leave out the listener.
- {别人|bié ren}: other people, someone else; {别人|bié ren}{的|de} someone else's.
- Word formation: prefix {老|lǎo}- ({老王|Lǎo Wáng}: friendly, for people you know; {老|lǎo} also "old", {老人|lǎo rén}, {老朋友|lǎo péng you}),
  suffixes -{员|yuán} ({服务员|fú wù yuán}, {店员|diàn yuán}), -{子|zi} ({房子|fáng zi}, {箱子|xiāng zi}: a noun maker), -{家|jiā} ({画家|huà jiā}, {作家|zuò jiā}).
- Multiple attributives: whose + which ({这|zhè} / {那|nà} + measure) + what it's like + {的|de} + noun:
  {我|wǒ}{邻居|lín jū}{家|jiā}{的|de}{那个|nà ge}{可爱|kě ài}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}.
- {小区|xiǎo qū}: a residential compound, where neighbours meet.
- {=Sound parts: 令 in 邻, {冷|lěng}, {零|líng}; 夷 in 姨. The two 阝: hill on the left, town on the right.=}

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Moving house: 搬进去, 搬上来, 层
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In HSK 2 you described a flat with {上面|shàng miàn} and {里面|lǐ miàn}, counted floors with {楼|lóu} ({五|wǔ}{楼|lóu}) and carried things
{上来|shàng lái} and {下去|xià qù}. This lesson moves house. You'll learn:

- {房子|fáng zi}, {屋子|wū zi} and {房间|fáng jiān}: a house, a room, a room;
- {层|céng} for floors and layers ({住|zhù}{在|zài}{十二|shí èr}{层|céng}), {电梯|diàn tī} and {楼梯|lóu tī};
- {搬|bān} and {搬家|bān jiā}, and the **[[direction complement]]** with a place or a thing in it: {搬|bān}{进|jìn}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}{去|qù},
  {搬|bān}{上|shàng}{五|wǔ}{楼|lóu}, {搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}{一|yí}{个|gè}{沙发|shā fā};
- the things in a home: {沙发|shā fā}, {冰箱|bīng xiāng}, {洗衣机|xǐ yī jī}, {空调|kōng tiáo}, {灯|dēng}, {卫生间|wèi shēng jiān};
- three words for describing it: {方便|fāng biàn}, {安静|ān jìng} and {旧|jiù}.

At the end you can read a flat-to-let notice and say what your own home is like.

## A house, a room: {房子|fáng zi}, {屋子|wū zi}, {房间|fáng jiān}

| Word | Meaning | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| {房子|fáng zi} | a house; a flat (as a home or property) | {买|mǎi}{房子|fáng zi} (to buy a home), {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{的|de}{房子|fáng zi} |
| {房间|fáng jiān} | a room (HSK 1) | {我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}, {宾馆|bīn guǎn}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān} (a hotel room: {宾馆|bīn guǎn} is lesson 14's) |
| {屋子|wū zi} | a room; indoors (spoken, especially in the north) | {屋子|wū zi}{里|lǐ}{很|hěn}{热|rè} |

{房子|fáng zi} is the home as a whole: in a city that's usually a flat (apartment), not a separate house. It's
also the word for property: {买|mǎi}{房子|fáng zi} is "to buy a flat (or a house)". {房间|fáng jiān} is the standard word for a
room, and the only one for hotels and offices. {屋子|wū zi} is a room too, or "inside, indoors", and is
heard most in northern speech:

{他们|tā men}{去年|qù nián}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{房子|fáng zi}。 — They bought a flat last year.

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{可是|kě shì}{很|hěn}{舒服|shū fu}。 — My room isn't big, but it's comfortable.

{屋子|wū zi}{里|lǐ}{很|hěn}{热|rè}，{咱们|zán men}{出去|chū qù}{走走|zǒu zou}{吧|ba}。 — It's hot indoors; let's go out for a walk.

{可是|kě shì} (but) is lesson 27's word, a spoken twin of {但是|dàn shì}. Flats are often described by their rooms:
in a {两室一厅|liǎng shì yì tīng} there are two bedrooms ({室|shì}) and one living room ({厅|tīng}). You'll see it
in every flat advert.

## Floors: {层|céng}, {楼|lóu}, {电梯|diàn tī} and {楼梯|lóu tī}

In HSK 2 you said which floor with {楼|lóu}: {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{五|wǔ}{楼|lóu}. **{层|céng}** is the measure word for floors and layers.
It counts them:

{这个|zhè ge}{楼|lóu}{有|yǒu}{二十|èr shí}{层|céng}。 — This building has twenty floors.

and, like {楼|lóu}, it says which one:

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{十二|shí èr}{层|céng}。 = {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{十二|shí èr}{楼|lóu}。 — We live on the twelfth floor.

{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{几|jǐ}{层|céng}？ — Which floor do you live on?

In mainland China the ground floor is {一楼|yī lóu} or {一|yī}{层|céng}, the first floor counted, so {二|èr}{楼|lóu} is the floor
above it. {层|céng} is also any layer: {两|liǎng}{层|céng}{衣服|yī fu} (two layers of clothes), and the "storey" of a building in
{这|zhè}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{两|liǎng}{层|céng}{的|de}{房子|fáng zi} (this is a two-storey house).

Getting up there: {电梯|diàn tī} (a lift, elevator: an "electric ladder") or {楼梯|lóu tī} (the stairs: the building's
ladder). With them you {坐|zuò}{电梯|diàn tī} (take the lift) or {走|zǒu}{楼梯|lóu tī} (walk up or down the stairs):

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{十二|shí èr}{层|céng}，{我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{坐|zuò}{电梯|diàn tī}{上去|shàng qù}。 — We're on the twelfth floor; I go up in the lift every day.

{电梯|diàn tī}{坏|huài}{了|le}，{咱们|zán men}{走|zǒu}{楼梯|lóu tī}{吧|ba}。 — The lift's broken; let's take the stairs.

{坏|huài}{了|le} is "broken, out of order" from HSK 2.

## Moving: {搬|bān} and {搬家|bān jiā}

{搬|bān} is to move something heavy or big: furniture, boxes, a fridge. {搬家|bān jiā} is "to move house": {搬|bān} + {家|jiā}.
It's a verb with its own object, a **[[separable verb]]** like {睡觉|shuì jiào} or {帮忙|bāng máng}, so other words can go
inside: {搬|bān}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{次|cì}{家|jiā} (moved twice). To say where to, use {搬|bān}{到|dào} + place:

{我们|wǒ men}{下个月|xià gè yuè}{搬家|bān jiā}。 — We're moving next month.

{请|qǐng}{帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{搬|bān}{一下|yí xià}{这个|zhè ge}{桌子|zhuō zi}。 — Please help me move this table.

{他们|tā men}{从|cóng}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{搬|bān}{到|dào}{北京|Běi jīng}{了|le}。 — They've moved from Shanghai to Beijing.

{我|wǒ}{搬|bān}{了|le}{三|sān}{次|cì}{家|jiā}，{现在|xiàn zài}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{这个|zhè ge}{小区|xiǎo qū}。 — I've moved three times; now I live in this compound.

## Moving things in, up and down: direction complements with objects

You know the **[[direction complement]]** from HSK 2: a verb followed by {上|shàng}, {下|xià}, {进|jìn}, {出|chū}, {回|huí}, {过|guò} or {起|qǐ},
often with {来|lái} (towards the speaker) or {去|qù} (away from the speaker):

{搬|bān}{上去|shàng qù} (carry up there), {搬|bān}{下来|xià lái} (carry down here), {搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái} (move in here), {搬|bān}{出去|chū qù} (move out of here).

Moving house is full of these. The new point is where the object goes.

### A place goes before {来|lái} / {去|qù}

When the object is a place, it goes between {上|shàng} / {进|jìn} / {回|huí}… and {来|lái} / {去|qù}. It never comes after {来|lái} or {去|qù}:

{我们|wǒ men}{下个月|xià gè yuè}{搬|bān}{进|jìn}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}{去|qù}。 — We're moving into the new flat next month.

{他|tā}{走|zǒu}{上|shàng}{楼|lóu}{来|lái}{了|le}。 — He's come up the stairs (up here).

{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{跑|pǎo}{出|chū}{房间|fáng jiān}{去|qù}{了|le}。 — The children ran out of the room.

You can also stop after the place, without {来|lái} or {去|qù}. Then nothing is said about the speaker's
position; this is common when the place is the point:

{他们|tā men}{搬|bān}{进|jìn}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}{了|le}。 — They've moved into the new flat.

{沙发|shā fā}{要|yào}{搬|bān}{上|shàng}{五|wǔ}{楼|lóu}。 — The sofa has to go up to the fifth floor.

### A thing can go either side

When the object is a thing, it can go before {来|lái} / {去|qù} or after them:

{他|tā}{搬|bān}{进|jìn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{沙发|shā fā}{来|lái}。 = {他|tā}{搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}{一|yí}{个|gè}{沙发|shā fā}。 — He carried a sofa in.

{我|wǒ}{从|cóng}{楼上|lóu shàng}{拿|ná}{下来|xià lái}{一|yí}{个|gè}{箱子|xiāng zi}。 — I brought a box down from upstairs.

The second order, with the thing at the end, is the more common one for something new to the
story ("a sofa", "a box"). {箱子|xiāng zi} (box, suitcase) is lesson 03's word.

| a place | before {来|lái} / {去|qù} only | {搬|bān}{进|jìn}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}{去|qù}, {走|zǒu}{上|shàng}{楼|lóu}{来|lái} |
| a thing | before {来|lái} / {去|qù}, or after them | {搬|bān}{进|jìn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{沙发|shā fā}{来|lái} / {搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}{一|yí}{个|gè}{沙发|shā fā} |
| no object | | {搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}, {搬|bān}{上去|shàng qù} |

~~{搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}~~ is the typical mistake: a place can't follow {来|lái}.

## What it's like: {方便|fāng biàn}, {安静|ān jìng}, {旧|jiù}

**{方便|fāng biàn}** means convenient, easy to get to or to use:

{这儿|zhèr}{离|lí}{地铁站|dì tiě zhàn}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}，{坐|zuò}{车|chē}{很|hěn}{方便|fāng biàn}。 — It's close to the metro station here, so getting about is easy.

shopping.

It's also how you ask whether a time suits someone:

{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{下午|xià wǔ}{方便|fāng biàn}{吗|ma}？ — Are you free tomorrow afternoon? (Is tomorrow afternoon convenient?)

**{安静|ān jìng}** is quiet, calm, peaceful, for places and people:

{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{小区|xiǎo qū}{很|hěn}{安静|ān jìng}。 — Our compound is very quiet.

{请|qǐng}{大家|dà jiā}{安静|ān jìng}{一下|yí xià}！ — Quiet please, everyone!

**{旧|jiù}** is old in the sense "not new, used, worn": things, clothes, buildings. Its opposite is {新|xīn}:

For people (and friendships) "old" is {老|lǎo} (lesson 01): {老人|lǎo rén}, {老朋友|lǎo péng you}. ~~{旧|jiù}{人|rén}~~ and ~~{旧|jiù}{朋友|péng you}~~ don't mean

### Sound parts

Many of these characters are a meaning part plus a sound part, and in several the sound still
works:

- {搬|bān} is 扌 (hand: moving things by hand) + 般 *bān*, the 般 of {一般|yì bān} (usually: lesson 10). Same
  sound, exactly.
- 梯 *tī* is 木 (wood: a ladder) + 弟 *dì*, the 弟 of {弟弟|dì di}. The vowel still matches.
- 箱 *xiāng* is ⺮ (bamboo: boxes were woven) + 相 *xiāng*, as in {相信|xiāng xìn} (to believe, lesson 24).
- 空 *kōng* is 穴 (a cave, a hollow) + 工 *gōng*. 工 is the sound part of {红|hóng} and {江|jiāng} (river)
  too: the vowel *-ong* / *-ang* is what's left of the old sound.
- {灯|dēng} is 火 (fire: early lamps burned oil) + 丁 *dīng*. Traditional 燈 has 登 *dēng* instead:
  an exact match.
- 调 *tiáo* is 讠 (speech) + {周|zhōu}, which once gave the sound and no longer does.
- 方 *fāng* gives its sound to {房|fáng} ({房间|fáng jiān}) and {放|fàng} (to put, next lesson).
- 静 *jìng*: the old dictionaries count 争 *zhēng* (on the right) as its sound part and 青 as its
  meaning ("clear, still"). But 静 rhymes with the 青 *qīng* family you already know: {请|qǐng},
  {晴|qíng}, {情|qíng} ({事情|shì qing}) and {睛|jīng} ({眼睛|yǎn jing}). 清 *qīng* (clear) comes in
  lesson 18.

### The other characters

- 屋 is 尸 + 至 (to arrive): coming in under a roof. {层|céng} is 尸 + 云; its traditional form 層 has 曾
  *céng* as the sound part.
- 沙 is 氵 (water) + {少|shǎo} (little): traditionally explained as what you see when the water is low,
  sand.
- {冰|bīng} is 冫 (ice, the radical of {冷|lěng}) + {水|shuǐ}: frozen water.
- 安 is 宀 (a roof) + {女|nǚ} (a woman), traditionally explained as "safe at home": peace, safety.
- {旧|jiù}, 卫 and {发|fā} are new simplified shapes. Traditional 舊 has 臼 *jiù* as its sound part, and 衛
  has {行|xíng} (to go) around 韋.
- {发|fā} stands for two traditional characters: 發 (to send out, emit, start) and 髮 (hair). So {沙发|shā fā}
  is 沙發, {发烧|fā shāo} (fever, lesson 05) is 發燒, and {头发|tóu fa} (hair, lesson 04) is 頭髮. With the Traditional
  switch on, the course shows the right one in each word. In {头发|tóu fa} it's read with a light *fa*.

### New radical: 尸

尸 (尸字头 *shī zì tóu*, "the 尸 top") is the character for a body, but as a radical it usually
stands for a roof or a building shape. Three characters in this track have it: 屋 and {层|céng} here,
and 展 (in {发展|fā zhǎn}, to develop: lesson 23). Many dictionaries also file 居 (lesson 01) under it.

Radical review: 扌 (hand) in {搬|bān}; 氵 (water) and 冫 (ice) in 沙 and {冰|bīng}, which differ by one dot;
火 (fire) in {灯|dēng}; 宀 (roof) in 安, as in {家|jiā}.

### Stroke order

- **方**: the dot, the horizontal, then the stroke that turns down and hooks, and the left-falling
  stroke last. It's easy to write the left-falling stroke too early: it comes after the hook.
- **发**: the short stroke at the top left that goes down and turns right, the long left-falling stroke, then the stroke that
  goes across, down and sweeps left, then the long right-falling stroke, and the dot at the top
  right last.
- **冰**: 冫 first (a dot, then a rising stroke), then {水|shuǐ}: the vertical hook in the middle, the
  left part, then the two strokes on the right.
- **层**: 尸 (the top in two strokes, then the long left-falling stroke), then 云 inside: two
  horizontals, the turning stroke and the dot.
- **安**: 宀 (dot, short vertical, the horizontal that hooks), then {女|nǚ}: the turning stroke first, the
  left-falling stroke, and the horizontal last.
- **旧**: the short vertical on the left first, then {日|rì}.
- **卫**: three strokes: the turning stroke with the hook, the vertical inside it, and the long
  horizontal at the bottom.

```speak
= We live on the twelfth floor.
{我们|wǒ men}{下个月|xià gè yuè}{搬家|bān jiā}。
= We're moving next month.
{电梯|diàn tī}{坏|huài}{了|le}，{咱们|zán men}{走|zǒu}{楼梯|lóu tī}{吧|ba}。
= The lift's broken; let's take the stairs.
{请|qǐng}{帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{搬|bān}{一下|yí xià}{这个|zhè ge}{箱子|xiāng zi}。
= Please help me move this box.
{我们|wǒ men}{的|de}{房子|fáng zi}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{可是|kě shì}{很|hěn}{安静|ān jìng}。
= Our flat isn't big, but it's very quiet.
{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{方便|fāng biàn}{吗|ma}？
= Is tomorrow convenient for you?
```

Now describe your own home in three or four sentences: which floor it's on, how you get up there,
what's in it, and what it's like ({方便|fāng biàn}, {安静|ān jìng}, {旧|jiù}, {新|xīn}, {大|dà}, {小|xiǎo}). Record yourself and listen back.

## Pronunciation

- {层|céng}: *c* is "ts" with a puff of air, and *-eng* as in "sung". Don't say *zēng*.
- {冰箱|bīng xiāng}, {沙发|shā fā}, {空调|kōng tiáo}: high, level first tones. Keep them high and flat
  all the way, and let {调|tiáo} rise.
- {搬|bān} and {般|bān} ({一般|yì bān}) sound the same; {班|bān} ({上班|shàng bān}) too. {半|bàn} (half) falls.
- {旧|jiù} and {就|jiù} (then, right away) are the same syllable.
- {卫生间|wèi shēng jiān}: falling, then two level tones.
- {洗衣机|xǐ yī jī}: a low *xǐ*, then two high ones.

## Common mistakes

- A place after {来|lái} / {去|qù}: ~~{搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}~~, ~~{走|zǒu}{上去|shàng qù}{楼|lóu}~~. Say {搬|bān}{进|jìn}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}{来|lái}, {走|zǒu}{上|shàng}{楼|lóu}{去|qù}.
- {旧|jiù} for people: ~~{我|wǒ}{的|de}{旧|jiù}{朋友|péng you}~~ for "my old friend" (a long-time friend). Say {我|wǒ}{的|de}{老朋友|lǎo péng you}. {旧|jiù} is for
  things.
- {十二|shí èr}{层|céng}{楼|lóu} for "the 12th floor": without {第|dì} it usually means a building with twelve floors. Say {十二|shí èr}{层|céng} or {十二|shí èr}{楼|lóu} ({第|dì}{十二|shí èr}{层|céng} and {第|dì}{十二|shí èr}{层|céng}{楼|lóu} are heard too).
- {搬|bān} for moving house without {家|jiā}: ~~{我们|wǒ men}{下个月|xià gè yuè}{搬|bān}~~ sounds unfinished. Say {我们|wǒ men}{下个月|xià gè yuè}{搬家|bān jiā}.
- {房子|fáng zi} for one room: ~~{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房子|fáng zi}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{床|chuáng}~~ for "there's a bed in my room". A room is {房间|fáng jiān} (or {屋子|wū zi}).
- {=Writing {冰|bīng} with 氵: three strokes on the left are water (沙); two are ice ({冰|bīng}, {冷|lěng}).=}

## Key points

- {房子|fáng zi}: a house or flat (the home, property); {房间|fáng jiān}: a room; {屋子|wū zi}: a room, indoors (spoken).
- {层|céng}: floors and layers: {二十|èr shí}{层|céng} (twenty floors), {住|zhù}{在|zài}{十二|shí èr}{层|céng} (on the twelfth floor), {几|jǐ}{层|céng}？
- {电梯|diàn tī} (lift) / {楼梯|lóu tī} (stairs): {坐|zuò}{电梯|diàn tī}, {走|zǒu}{楼梯|lóu tī}.
- {搬|bān}: to move (heavy things); {搬家|bān jiā}: to move house ({搬|bān}{了|le}{三|sān}{次|cì}{家|jiā}); {搬|bān}{到|dào} + place.
- Direction complements: a place goes before {来|lái} / {去|qù} ({搬|bān}{进|jìn}{新|xīn}{房子|fáng zi}{去|qù}); a thing can go either side
  ({搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}{一|yí}{个|gè}{沙发|shā fā} / {搬|bān}{进|jìn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{沙发|shā fā}{来|lái}).
- In the home: {沙发|shā fā}, {冰箱|bīng xiāng}, {洗衣机|xǐ yī jī}, {空调|kōng tiáo}, {灯|dēng}, {卫生间|wèi shēng jiān}.
- {方便|fāng biàn} (convenient; {你|nǐ}{方便|fāng biàn}{吗|ma}？), {安静|ān jìng} (quiet), {旧|jiù} (old, worn: things) vs {老|lǎo} (people).
- {=Sound parts: 般 in {搬|bān}, 弟 in 梯, 相 in 箱, 工 in 空, 方 in 房. {发|fā} is both 發 and 髮. New radical
  尸.=}

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Housework: the 把 sentence
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about keeping a home clean: sweeping, washing up, putting things away, switching
things off, and finding what's gone missing. It teaches the most famous pattern of HSK 3, the
**[[把 sentence]]**:

{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le}。 — I've washed the bowls clean.

{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{书|shū}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。 — Please put the books on the table.

You'll learn what {把|bǎ} does, when Chinese reaches for it, and the one rule that catches every
learner: something must come after the verb. You'll also learn {不见|bú jiàn}{了|le} (to have gone missing), {丢|diū} (to
lose), and {把|bǎ} as a measure word for things with a handle.

## Housework words

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {打扫|dǎ sǎo} | to clean (a room, a flat) | {打扫|dǎ sǎo}{房间|fáng jiān} |
| {扫|sǎo} | to sweep | {扫|sǎo}{地|dì} (sweep the floor) |
| {干净|gān jìng} | clean | {很|hěn}{干净|gān jìng} |
| {脏|zāng} | dirty | {很|hěn}{脏|zāng}, {脏|zāng}{衣服|yī fu} (dirty clothes) |
| {洗澡|xǐ zǎo} | to have a bath or shower | {晚上|wǎn shang}{洗澡|xǐ zǎo} |
| {刷|shuā} | to brush; to swipe (a card) | {刷牙|shuā yá} (brush your teeth) |
| {牙刷|yá shuā} | toothbrush | {一|yí}{个|gè}{新|xīn}{牙刷|yá shuā} |
| {碗|wǎn} | bowl | {洗碗|xǐ wǎn} (wash up) |
| {盘子|pán zi} | plate, dish | {一|yí}{个|gè}{盘子|pán zi} |
| {瓶子|píng zi} | bottle | {空瓶子|kōng píng zi} (an empty bottle) |
| {箱子|xiāng zi} | box, case, suitcase | {一|yí}{个|gè}{大|dà}{箱子|xiāng zi} |
| {放|fàng} | to put, place | {放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} |
| {关|guān} | to close; to switch off | {关|guān}{门|mén}, {关|guān}{灯|dēng} |

{打扫|dǎ sǎo} is the general word for cleaning a place; {扫|sǎo} is sweeping, with a broom. In {扫|sǎo}{地|dì} the {地|dì} is *dì*,
the ground or floor (lesson 11's word). {干净|gān jìng} and {脏|zāng} are adjectives: {房间|fáng jiān}{很|hěn}{干净|gān jìng}, {衣服|yī fu}{很|hěn}{脏|zāng}. Neither is
a verb: "to clean" is {打扫|dǎ sǎo} (a room) or {洗|xǐ} (clothes, dishes, hands).

{我|wǒ}{每|měi}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{一|yí}{次|cì}{房间|fáng jiān}。 — I clean my room once a week.

{洗碗|xǐ wǎn} is literally "wash the bowls", the everyday word for washing up. {洗澡|xǐ zǎo} is a separable verb, like
{睡觉|shuì jiào}: {洗|xǐ}{个|gè}{澡|zǎo} (have a quick shower), {洗|xǐ}{了|le}{澡|zǎo} (had a shower).

{吃|chī}{完|wán}{饭|fàn}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{我|wǒ}{洗碗|xǐ wǎn}，{他|tā}{扫|sǎo}{地|dì}。 — After dinner I wash up and he sweeps the floor. ({以后|yǐ hòu}, after, is
lesson 25's.)

{刷|shuā} is to brush or scrub. {刷牙|shuā yá} is brushing your teeth; {刷卡|shuā kǎ} is swiping (or tapping) a card to pay, a
word you'll meet again in lesson 09.

{关|guān} is the opposite of {开|kāi}: {关|guān}{门|mén} (close the door), {关|guān}{灯|dēng} (switch off the light), {关|guān}{空调|kōng tiáo}. {放|fàng} is to put
something somewhere, almost always with {在|zài} + place after it: {放|fàng}{在|zài}{冰箱|bīng xiāng}{里|lǐ}, {放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}.

## The {把|bǎ} sentence

### What it looks like

In an ordinary sentence the object follows the verb: {我|wǒ}{洗|xǐ}{了|le}{碗|wǎn}. In a {把|bǎ} sentence, {把|bǎ} brings the object
forward, before the verb:

| Subject | {把|bǎ} + object | Verb | What happens to the object |
|---|---|---|---|
| {我|wǒ} | {把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn} | {洗|xǐ} | {干净|gān jìng}{了|le} |
| {请|qǐng} (you) | {把|bǎ}{书|shū} | {放|fàng} | {在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng} |
| {你|nǐ} | {把|bǎ}{灯|dēng} | {关|guān} | {了|le} |
| {他|tā} | {把|bǎ}{箱子|xiāng zi} | {搬|bān} | {进来|jìn lái}{了|le} |
| {我|wǒ} | {把|bǎ}{手机|shǒu jī} | {给|gěi} | {他|tā}{了|le} |

{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le}。 — I've washed the bowls (and they're clean).

{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{书|shū}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。 — Please put the books on the table.

{你|nǐ}{把|bǎ}{灯|dēng}{关|guān}{了|le}{吧|ba}。 — Switch the light off, would you.

{他|tā}{把|bǎ}{箱子|xiāng zi}{搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}{了|le}。 — He's carried the box in.

{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{手机|shǒu jī}{给|gěi}{他|tā}{了|le}。 — I gave him the phone.

### What it means: doing something to a thing

{把|bǎ} sentences are about **[[disposal]]**: what the subject does to a particular thing, and what becomes
of it. The thing is moved ({放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}, {搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}), changed ({洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}, {打扫|dǎ sǎo}{干净|gān jìng}), switched off or used up
({关|guān}{了|le}, {吃|chī}{完|wán}{了|le}), or handed over ({给|gěi}{他|tā}). That's why {把|bǎ} is everywhere in housework, instructions and
requests: they're all about doing something to things.

Two conditions make a {把|bǎ} sentence natural:

1. **The object is particular**: this one, that one, or one both speakers know about. {把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn} means
   "the bowls" (the ones in the sink), not "some bowls". With a new, unknown object, use the
   ordinary order: {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{碗|wǎn} (I bought a bowl), not ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{碗|wǎn}{买|mǎi}{了|le}~~.
2. **The verb acts on it, with a result.** {把|bǎ} goes with verbs that do something to the object:
   {放|fàng}, {洗|xǐ}, {关|guān}, {打扫|dǎ sǎo}, {搬|bān}, {给|gěi}, {吃|chī}, {写|xiě}. Verbs of feeling, knowing, being or perceiving don't do anything to
   their object, so they never take {把|bǎ}: ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{他|tā}{喜欢|xǐ huan}~~, ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}{知道|zhī dào}{了|le}~~, ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{电影|diàn yǐng}{看见|kàn jiàn}{了|le}~~.

### The rule: something must follow the verb

The verb in a {把|bǎ} sentence can't stand alone at the end. Something has to say what happened to the
object:

| ✗ | ✓ | What follows the verb |
|---|---|---|
| ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{饭|fàn}{吃|chī}~~ | {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{饭|fàn}{吃|chī}{了|le}。 | {了|le} (it's done) |
| ~~{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{书|shū}{放|fàng}~~ | {请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{书|shū}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。 | {在|zài} + place |
| ~~{他|tā}{把|bǎ}{房间|fáng jiān}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}~~ | {他|tā}{把|bǎ}{房间|fáng jiān}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le}。 | a result complement ({干净|gān jìng}) |
| ~~{你|nǐ}{把|bǎ}{箱子|xiāng zi}{搬|bān}~~ | {你|nǐ}{把|bǎ}{箱子|xiāng zi}{搬|bān}{上去|shàng qù}。 | a direction complement ({上去|shàng qù}) |
| ~~{把|bǎ}{门|mén}{开|kāi}~~ | {把|bǎ}{门|mén}{开|kāi}{一下|yí xià}。 | {一下|yí xià} (a quick action) |
| ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{钱|qián}{给|gěi}~~ | {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{钱|qián}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}。 | {给|gěi} + person |

These "somethings" are the **[[complements]]** and other endings you know: result complements ({洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng},
{吃|chī}{完|wán}, {做|zuò}{好|hǎo}: HSK 2), direction complements ({搬|bān}{进来|jìn lái}, lesson 02), {在|zài} / {到|dào} + place, {给|gěi} + person, {一下|yí xià} or a
doubled verb, and {了|le}.

### Not, don't, can, want: before {把|bǎ}

Negatives, modal verbs and most adverbs go before {把|bǎ}, not before the verb:

{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}。 — I didn't get the bowls clean.

{别|bié}{把|bǎ}{脏|zāng}{衣服|yī fu}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{沙发|shā fā}{上|shàng}！ — Don't put dirty clothes on the sofa!

{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{把|bǎ}{门|mén}{关|guān}{上|shàng}{吗|ma}？ — Could you close the door?

{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{把|bǎ}{房间|fáng jiān}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{一下|yí xià}。 — I'd like to give my room a quick clean.

{我|wǒ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{把|bǎ}{灯|dēng}{关|guān}{了|le}。 — I've already switched the light off.

~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{没|méi}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}~~ is a typical slip. Use {没|méi} for the past ({没|méi}{把|bǎ}…, no {了|le} at the end)
and {不|bù} / {别|bié} / {不要|bú yào} for intentions and requests. {关|guān}{上|shàng} in the third sentence is {关|guān} + {上|shàng}, "shut, closed":
{上|shàng} as a result complement.

### Why not just say {我|wǒ}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le}{碗|wǎn}?

That order exists, but with a result complement and a particular object it sounds stiff, and with
{在|zài} + place it's impossible: ~~{我|wǒ}{放|fàng}{书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}~~ is wrong. Chinese wants the verb and its result (or
place) close together at the end of the sentence, where the news is, and {把|bǎ} moves the object out
of the way. The other natural option is to make the object the topic: {碗|wǎn}{我|wǒ}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le} (the bowls, I've
washed them).

## {不见|bú jiàn}{了|le} and {丢|diū}: gone missing

{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le} means "has disappeared, can't be found". The missing thing is the subject:

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{牙刷|yá shuā}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}！ — My toothbrush has gone!

{刚才|gāng cái}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{还|hái}{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}，{现在|xiàn zài}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}。 — My phone was here a moment ago; now it's gone. ({刚才|gāng cái}, a moment
ago, is lesson 25's.)

{丢|diū} is to lose something. The person who lost it is the subject, and {丢|diū} often comes with {把|bǎ} or {了|le}:

{我|wǒ}{丢|diū}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{箱子|xiāng zi}。 — I've lost a suitcase.

{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{手机|shǒu jī}{丢|diū}{了|le}。 — I've lost my phone.

{丢|diū} also means to throw away: {把|bǎ}{空瓶子|kōng píng zi}{丢|diū}{了|le} (throw the empty bottles away). The context makes it clear.
{不见|bú jiàn} on its own is also "not see": {好久不见|hǎo jiǔ bú jiàn}！ (Long time no see!, with {好久|hǎo jiǔ} from lesson 23).

## {把|bǎ} as a measure word

The same character is also a measure word for things you hold by a handle or a back:

{一|yì}{把|bǎ}{椅子|yǐ zi} — a chair

{两|liǎng}{把|bǎ}{伞|sǎn} — two umbrellas ({伞|sǎn}, umbrella: lesson 10)

{一|yì}{把|bǎ}{牙刷|yá shuā} — a toothbrush ({一|yí}{个|gè}{牙刷|yá shuā} is also common)

In a sentence the two uses don't get confused: {把|bǎ} + noun + verb is the {把|bǎ} sentence, and number + {把|bǎ} +
noun is counting. You can even have both: {请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{这|zhè}{把|bǎ}{椅子|yǐ zi}{搬|bān}{出去|chū qù} (please carry this chair out).

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 扫 (traditional 掃) | to sweep | sǎo | 扌 | 6 | {扫|sǎo}, {打扫|dǎ sǎo} |
| 干 (traditional 乾, 幹) ✎ | dry; to do | gān (and gàn) | {十|shí} | 3 | {干净|gān jìng}, {干|gàn} (to do, lesson 19) |
| 净 (traditional 淨) ✎ | clean | jìng | 冫 | 8 | {干净|gān jìng} |
| 脏 (traditional 髒) | dirty | zāng | ⺼ | 10 | {脏|zāng} |
| 放 ✎ | to put; to let go | fàng | 攵 | 8 | {放|fàng}, {放学|fàng xué} (lesson 16), {放心|fàng xīn} (lesson 24) |
| 澡 | bath | zǎo | 氵 | 16 | {洗澡|xǐ zǎo} |
| 牙 ✎ | tooth | yá | {牙|yá} | 4 | {牙刷|yá shuā}, {牙|yá} (lesson 04) |
| 刷 | brush; to brush | shuā | 刂 | 8 | {牙刷|yá shuā}, {刷|shuā} |
| 碗 | bowl | wǎn | 石 | 13 | {碗|wǎn} |
| 盘 (traditional 盤) | plate | pán | 皿 | 11 | {盘子|pán zi} |
| 瓶 ✎ | bottle | píng | 瓦 | 10 | {瓶子|píng zi} |
| 丢 (traditional 丟) ✎ | to lose | diū | {一|yī} | 6 | {丢|diū} |
| 把 ✎ | to hold; (the {把|bǎ} sentence) | bǎ | 扌 | 7 | {把|bǎ} |

### Sound parts

- {把|bǎ} is 扌 (hand: holding) + 巴 *bā*. 巴 gives the sound to {爸|bà} ({爸爸|bà ba}) and {吧|ba} too: three
  tones, one sound.
- {放|fàng} is 方 *fāng* (lesson 02) + 攵 (a hand with a stick: action). 方 gives the sound, as in 房.
- 净 *jìng* is 冫 + 争 *zhēng*, the same sound part as 静 *jìng* (lesson 02). {干净|gān jìng} and {安静|ān jìng} end with the
  same syllable, and their second characters share their right-hand side.
- {碗|wǎn} is 石 (stone) + 宛 *wǎn*, an exact match.
- 瓶 *píng* is 并 *bìng* (together) + 瓦 (tile, pottery: old bottles were clay).
- {澡|zǎo} is 氵 (water) + 喿 *zào*, which gives the sound. {澡|zǎo} sounds like {早|zǎo}: a memory aid,
  {早上|zǎo shang}{洗澡|xǐ zǎo}.
- {脏|zāng} is ⺼ (meat moon) + 庄 *zhuāng*, which gives the sound. Simplified {脏|zāng} stands for two
  traditional characters: 髒 (dirty) and 臟 *zàng* (an inner organ). In this course it's always 髒.
- 盘 *pán* is 舟 (a boat) over 皿 (a dish). Its traditional form 盤 has {般|bān} on top, the sound
  part of last lesson's {搬|bān}.

### The other characters

- {扫|sǎo} is 扌 + 彐, a short form of 帚 (a broom): traditional 掃.
- {刷|shuā} is 尸 + 巾 (a cloth) + 刂 (a knife): scraping and scrubbing.
- {牙|yá} is traditionally explained as a drawing of back teeth meeting. It's its own radical, and it
  has 4 strokes.
- {丢|diū} looks like {去|qù} (to go) with a short stroke on top: a memory aid, "it's gone".
- {干|gàn} stands for three traditional characters: 乾 (dry, clean: {干净|gān jìng} → 乾淨), 幹 (to do: {干|gàn}, lesson
  19) and {干|gàn} (shield, in old words). The Traditional switch shows the right one.

### Look-alikes: {干|gàn}, {千|qiān}, 于, 午, {牛|niú}

{干|gàn} is two horizontals and a straight vertical, the top one shorter. {千|qiān} (thousand) starts with a
left-falling stroke instead; 于 (as in {终于|zhōng yú}, lesson 21) has a hook at the bottom; {午|wǔ}
({中午|zhōng wǔ}) and {牛|niú} ({牛奶|niú nǎi}) have a short stroke on top and the vertical
through the middle ({牛|niú} pokes out at the top).

### New radical: 石

石 (石字旁 *shí zì páng*, stone) is in {碗|wǎn} here: a bowl was once stone or earthenware. Two more
characters of this track have it: 矿 (in {矿泉水|kuàng quán shuǐ}, mineral water: lesson 07) and 码 (in {号码|hào mǎ}, number:
lesson 09). On the left, 石 is narrow, with a short top horizontal and a small {口|kǒu}.

Radical review: 扌 in {扫|sǎo} and {把|bǎ} (things done by hand); 氵 in {澡|zǎo} (water) and 冫 in 净 (here it's an
old variant of 氵, not ice); ⺼ in {脏|zāng} (the body: compare {脸|liǎn}, {脚|jiǎo} next lesson).

### Stroke order

- **干**: the short top horizontal, the long horizontal, then the vertical.
- **牙**: the top horizontal, the short stroke that goes down and turns right, the vertical hook,
  and the left-falling stroke last.
- **把**: 扌 (horizontal, vertical hook, rising stroke), then 巴: the box-like turn, the short
  vertical, the horizontal, and the long stroke that goes down, along and hooks up.
- **丢**: the short left-falling stroke on top first, then {去|qù} (horizontal, vertical, long
  horizontal, the turning stroke and the dot).
- **放**: 方 first (narrow on the left), then 攵: short left-falling stroke, horizontal, the long
  left-falling stroke and the right-falling stroke.
- **瓶**: 并 first, then 瓦: horizontal, the stroke that goes down and turns, the turning stroke
  that hooks, and the dot.

```trace trad=掃乾淨髒放澡牙
扫干净脏放澡牙
```


Write it: {干|gàn}, 净, {放|fàng}, {牙|yá}, 瓶, {丢|diū} and {把|bǎ} are on the handwriting list. Write each three times from
memory. Check {牙|yá}: four strokes, the second one short.

## Dialogue: Saturday morning

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) and {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) share the flat Wang Fang moved into in lesson 02. It's cleaning day.

```dialogue
# Saturday morning
王芳: {安娜|Ān nà}，{今天|jīn tiān}{咱们|zán men}{把|bǎ}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{一下|yí xià}{吧|ba}。
= Anna, let's give the flat a clean today.
安娜: {好|hǎo}{啊|a}。{我|wǒ}{先|xiān}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{和|hé}{盘子|pán zi}{洗|xǐ}{了|le}。
= OK. I'll wash the bowls and plates first.
王芳: {好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{扫|sǎo}{地|dì}。{你|nǐ}{的|de}{脏|zāng}{衣服|yī fu}{呢|ne}？{别|bié}{把|bǎ}{它们|tā men}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{沙发|shā fā}{上|shàng}！
= Fine, I'll sweep. And your dirty clothes? Don't leave them on the sofa!
安娜: {对不起|duì bu qǐ}，{我|wǒ}{马上|mǎ shàng}{把|bǎ}{衣服|yī fu}{放|fàng}{进|jìn}{洗衣机|xǐ yī jī}{里|lǐ}。
= Sorry, I'll put them in the washing machine right away.
王芳: {还有|hái yǒu}，{冰箱|bīng xiāng}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{空瓶子|kōng píng zi}，{把|bǎ}{它们|tā men}{丢|diū}{了|le}{吧|ba}。
= And there are lots of empty bottles in the fridge: let's throw them away.
安娜: {好|hǎo}。{哎|āi}，{我|wǒ}{的|de}{牙刷|yá shuā}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}！{你|nǐ}{看见|kàn jiàn}{了|le}{吗|ma}？
= OK. Hey, my toothbrush has gone! Have you seen it?
王芳: {是|shì}{不|bú}{是|shì}{在|zài}{那个|nà ge}{箱子|xiāng zi}{里|lǐ}？{昨天|zuó tiān}{你|nǐ}{把|bǎ}{卫生间|wèi shēng jiān}{的|de}{东西|dōng xi}{都|dōu}{放|fàng}{进去|jìn qù}{了|le}。
= Isn't it in that box? Yesterday you put all the bathroom things in it.
安娜: {对|duì}！{在|zài}{这儿|zhèr}。{谢谢|xiè xie}！
= Yes! Here it is. Thanks!
王芳: {现在|xiàn zài}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{干净|gān jìng}{多|duō}{了|le}。{走|zǒu}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}{把|bǎ}{灯|dēng}{和|hé}{空调|kōng tiáo}{关|guān}{了|le}。
= The flat's much cleaner now. When you go out, don't forget to switch off the lights and the air conditioning.
安娜: {知道|zhī dào}{了|le}。{你|nǐ}{也|yě}{别|bié}{把|bǎ}{钥匙|yào shi}{丢|diū}{了|le}！
= Got it. And don't you lose the keys!
```

- {先|xiān} (first) is lesson 25's word; {马上|mǎ shàng} (right away) lesson 13's.
- {它们|tā men} (them) stands for things here, as in HSK 1: {把|bǎ}{它们|tā men}{丢|diū}{了|le} (throw them away).
- {是|shì}{不|bú}{是|shì}{在|zài}{那个|nà ge}{箱子|xiāng zi}{里|lǐ}？ is "isn't it in that box?": {是|shì}{不|bú}{是|shì} checks a guess.
- {干净|gān jìng}{多|duō}{了|le} (much cleaner) is lesson 04's comparison.
- {钥匙|yào shi} (key) isn't a course word.

## Reading: a note for the helper

Mrs Li leaves a note for the woman who helps her with the housework.

> {阿姨|ā yí}，{您|nín}{好|hǎo}！
>
> {今天|jīn tiān}{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{爱人|ài ren}{去|qù}{上海|Shàng hǎi}，{晚上|wǎn shang}{很|hěn}{晚|wǎn}{回来|huí lái}，{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{在|zài}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{家|jiā}。{请|qǐng}{您|nín}{帮|bāng}{我|wǒ}{做|zuò}{下面|xià miàn}{这些|zhè xiē}{事|shì}：
>
> 1. {把|bǎ}{客厅|kè tīng}{和|hé}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{房间|fáng jiān}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{一下|yí xià}，{地|dì}{很|hěn}{脏|zāng}，{请|qǐng}{扫|sǎo}{一|yi}{扫|sǎo}。
> 2. {把|bǎ}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}{的|de}{碗|wǎn}{和|hé}{盘子|pán zi}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}，{放|fàng}{在|zài}{厨房|chú fáng}{里|lǐ}。
> 3. {孩子|hái zi}{的|de}{脏|zāng}{衣服|yī fu}{在|zài}{卫生间|wèi shēng jiān}，{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{它们|tā men}{放|fàng}{进|jìn}{洗衣机|xǐ yī jī}{里|lǐ}{洗|xǐ}{一下|yí xià}。
> 4. {冰箱|bīng xiāng}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{空瓶子|kōng píng zi}{都|dōu}{不要|bú yào}{了|le}，{您|nín}{把|bǎ}{它们|tā men}{丢|diū}{了|le}{吧|ba}。
> 5. {我|wǒ}{的|de}{书|shū}{和|hé}{本子|běn zi}{请|qǐng}{不要|bú yào}{动|dòng}，{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{要|yào}{用|yòng}。
>
> {您|nín}{走|zǒu}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{灯|dēng}{和|hé}{空调|kōng tiáo}{都|dōu}{关|guān}{了|le}，{把|bǎ}{门|mén}{关|guān}{好|hǎo}。
>
> {谢谢|xiè xie}{您|nín}！
>
> {李太太|Lǐ tài tai}

- {下面|xià miàn}{这些|zhè xiē}{事|shì} is "the following things": {下面|xià miàn} (below) from HSK 2.
- {客厅|kè tīng} (living room) and {厨房|chú fáng} (kitchen) aren't course words.
- {扫|sǎo}{一|yi}{扫|sǎo} is {扫|sǎo} doubled with {一|yī}: "give it a sweep". {动|dòng} (to move, touch) is HSK 2's; {用|yòng} (to use) is
  lesson 09's.
- {关|guān}{好|hǎo} is "close properly": {好|hǎo} as a result complement. {太太|tài tai} (Mrs) is a polite title for a
  married woman.

1. What should the helper do with the children's clothes?
2. What should she do with the empty bottles?
3. What should she not touch, and why?
4. What should she do before she leaves?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Put them in the washing machine and wash them ({把|bǎ}{它们|tā men}{放|fàng}{进|jìn}{洗衣机|xǐ yī jī}{里|lǐ}{洗|xǐ}{一下|yí xià}).
2. Throw them away ({把|bǎ}{它们|tā men}{丢|diū}{了|le}{吧|ba}).
3. The books and notebooks: Mrs Li still needs them ({我|wǒ}{还|hái}{要|yào}{用|yòng}).
4. Switch off the lights and the air conditioning and close the door properly.

"Hello! My husband and I are going to Shanghai today and will be back very late tonight; the children are at their grandma's. Could you
please do these things for me: 1. Give the living room and the two bedrooms a clean; the floor is
very dirty, so please give it a sweep. 2. Wash the bowls and plates on the table and put them in
the kitchen. 3. The children's dirty clothes are in the bathroom: please put them in the washing
machine and wash them. 4. We don't want the empty bottles in the fridge any more; please throw them
away. 5. Please don't move my books and notebooks; I still need them. When you leave, please switch
off the lights and the air conditioning and close the door properly. Thank you! Mrs Li"
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Housework
{我们|wǒ men}{把|bǎ}{房间|fáng jiān}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{一下|yí xià}{吧|ba}。
= Let's give the room a clean.
{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{书|shū}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。
= Please put the books on the table.
{别|bié}{把|bǎ}{脏|zāng}{衣服|yī fu}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{沙发|shā fā}{上|shàng}！
= Don't put dirty clothes on the sofa!
{走|zǒu}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{灯|dēng}{关|guān}{了|le}。
= Please switch off the light when you leave.
{我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}！
= My phone's gone!
{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{钥匙|yào shi}{丢|diū}{了|le}。
= I've lost my keys.
```

Now give three instructions to a flatmate with {把|bǎ} (clean, put, switch off), and answer as if you
were the flatmate: {好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{马上|mǎ shàng}{把|bǎ}…

## Pronunciation

- {把|bǎ} (third tone), {爸|bà} (fourth) and {吧|ba} (neutral): the same syllable three ways.
- {扫|sǎo} and {澡|zǎo} dip; *s* is a hiss and *z* a "dz". {洗澡|xǐ zǎo} is two third tones, said
  *xí zǎo*.
- {打扫|dǎ sǎo} is two third tones too: said *dá sǎo*.
- {脏|zāng} is level and high; don't make it *zhāng* (the surname {张|Zhāng}).
- {碗|wǎn} and {晚|wǎn} (late) sound the same; {万|wàn} (ten thousand) falls.
- {刷|shuā}: *sh* + *ua*, one quick syllable.
- {丢|diū}: *d* + *iou*, written *iu*, high and level.

## Common mistakes

- Nothing after the verb: ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{饭|fàn}{吃|chī}~~, ~~{请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{门|mén}{关|guān}~~. Add the result: {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{饭|fàn}{吃|chī}{了|le}, {请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{门|mén}{关|guān}{上|shàng}.
- {把|bǎ} with feelings or knowledge: ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{他|tā}{喜欢|xǐ huan}~~, ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}{知道|zhī dào}{了|le}~~. Use the plain order: {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{他|tā}.
- {把|bǎ} with a new, unknown thing: ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{碗|wǎn}{买|mǎi}{了|le}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{碗|wǎn}.
- {没|méi} in the wrong place: ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{没|méi}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}~~. Negatives go before {把|bǎ}: {我|wǒ}{没|méi}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}.
- {了|le} after {没|méi}: ~~{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le}~~. {没|méi} already says it didn't happen: no {了|le}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{放|fàng}{书|shū}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}~~: with {在|zài} + place, use {把|bǎ}: {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{书|shū}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}.
- {干净|gān jìng} as a verb: ~~{我|wǒ}{干净|gān jìng}{房间|fáng jiān}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{房间|fáng jiān} or {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{房间|fáng jiān}{打扫|dǎ sǎo}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le}.
- {不见|bú jiàn}{了|le} with a person as subject: ~~{我|wǒ}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}{手机|shǒu jī}~~. The thing disappears ({我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}); the person
  loses it ({我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{手机|shǒu jī}{丢|diū}{了|le}).

## Key points

- Housework: {打扫|dǎ sǎo} (clean a place), {扫|sǎo} (sweep), {洗碗|xǐ wǎn}, {洗澡|xǐ zǎo}, {刷牙|shuā yá}; {干净|gān jìng} / {脏|zāng} (adjectives); {放|fàng} (put), {关|guān}
  (close, switch off); {碗|wǎn}, {盘子|pán zi}, {瓶子|píng zi}, {箱子|xiāng zi}, {牙刷|yá shuā}.
- The {把|bǎ} sentence: subject + {把|bǎ} + object + verb + something ({了|le}, a complement, {在|zài} + place, {给|gěi} +
  person, {一下|yí xià}): {我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{碗|wǎn}{洗|xǐ}{干净|gān jìng}{了|le}, {请|qǐng}{把|bǎ}{书|shū}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}.
- Use it for doing something to a particular thing (disposal): moving, changing, finishing,
  handing over. Not with {喜欢|xǐ huan}, {知道|zhī dào}, {是|shì}, {有|yǒu}, {看见|kàn jiàn}.
- Negatives and modal verbs go before {把|bǎ}: {没|méi}{把|bǎ}…, {别|bié}{把|bǎ}…, {能|néng}{把|bǎ}…, {想|xiǎng}{把|bǎ}….
- {不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}: has gone missing (the thing is the subject); {丢|diū}: to lose (the person is the subject;
  also to throw away).
- {把|bǎ} as a measure word: {一|yì}{把|bǎ}{椅子|yǐ zi}, {两|liǎng}{把|bǎ}{伞|sǎn}.
- {=Sound parts: 巴 in {把|bǎ} (爸, {吧|ba}), 方 in {放|fàng}, 争 in 净 and 静, 宛 in {碗|wǎn}. New radical 石.=}

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Looking alike and different: 比, 没有, 跟…一样
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 2 described people with topic-comment sentences ({她|tā}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà}) and compared them with {比|bǐ} ({他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}).
This lesson gives you the rest of the face and body, words for build and age, and the three
comparisons you need to say who looks like whom:

- A {比|bǐ} B + adjective + {一点儿|yì diǎnr} / {多|duō}{了|le} / {得|de}{多|duō}: a little or a lot more;
- A {没有|méi yǒu} B ({那么|nà me}) + adjective: not as … as;
- A {跟|gēn} B {一样|yí yàng} (+ adjective), and {不|bù}{一样|yí yàng} / {不同|bù tóng}: the same, different;
- {像|xiàng} (to look like) and {好像|hǎo xiàng} (to seem);
- height in numbers: {身高|shēn gāo}{一米七五|yì mǐ qī wǔ}.

## The face and body

| Word | Meaning | You know already |
|---|---|---|
| {脸|liǎn} | face | {头|tóu} (head), {眼睛|yǎn jing} (eyes) |
| {耳朵|ěr duo} | ear | {手|shǒu} (hand), {身体|shēn tǐ} (body) |
| {嘴|zuǐ} | mouth | {口|kǒu} (mouth, in words: {门口|mén kǒu}, {人|rén}{口|kǒu}) |
| {牙|yá} | tooth | {牙刷|yá shuā} (lesson 03) |
| {头发|tóu fa} | hair (on the head) | {个子|gè zi} (build, height) |
| {腿|tuǐ} | leg | {高|gāo} (tall), {长|cháng} (long) |
| {脚|jiǎo} | foot | |

Describe people with the topic-comment sentences of HSK 2: the person, then the feature, then
what it's like.

{她|tā}{脸|liǎn}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{眼睛|yǎn jing}{很|hěn}{大|dà}。 — She has a small face and big eyes.

{他|tā}{腿|tuǐ}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}，{跑|pǎo}{得|de}{很|hěn}{快|kuài}。 — He has long legs and runs fast.

{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{耳朵|ěr duo}{不|bú}{太|tài}{好|hǎo}，{你|nǐ}{说话|shuō huà}{大声|dà shēng}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 — My grandpa's hearing isn't very good; speak up a bit. ({大声|dà shēng},
loudly, is {大|dà} + {声|shēng}, sound: lesson 22.)

{头发|tóu fa} is hair on the head only; it's usually used without a measure word: {她|tā}{的|de}{头发|tóu fa}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}
(her hair is long), and never with {个|gè} (~~{一|yí}{个|gè}{头发|tóu fa}~~). Its second syllable is light, *tóu fa*, and in traditional characters it's
頭髮, with the "hair" character, not the 發 of {沙发|shā fā}.

{嘴|zuǐ} is the mouth you see; {口|kǒu} is "mouth" in fixed words and as a measure word ({几|jǐ}{口|kǒu}{人|rén}). {牙|yá} on its own
is a tooth, or teeth: {刷牙|shuā yá} (brush your teeth), {我|wǒ}{牙疼|yá téng} (I've got toothache: {疼|téng} from HSK 2).

## Build and age

| Word | Meaning | Opposite |
|---|---|---|
| {胖|pàng} | fat, plump, chubby | {瘦|shòu} (thin, slim) |
| {矮|ǎi} | short (in height) | {高|gāo} (tall) |
| {短|duǎn} | short (in length) | {长|cháng} (long) |
| {年轻|nián qīng} | young (of adults) | {老|lǎo} (old) |
| {可爱|kě ài} | cute, lovely | |

Two words for "short": {矮|ǎi} is for height (people, buildings, tables), {短|duǎn} is for length and time
(hair, legs, trousers, a short holiday). {他|tā}{很|hěn}{矮|ǎi} means he's short; ~~{他|tā}{很|hěn}{短|duǎn}~~ doesn't work.

{她|tā}{头发|tóu fa}{很|hěn}{短|duǎn}，{个子|gè zi}{不|bù}{高|gāo}{也|yě}{不|bù}{矮|ǎi}。 — She has short hair and she's neither tall nor short.

{胖|pàng} is blunt when it's about an adult: people say it among family and friends, and it's a compliment
for babies ({胖胖|pàng pàng}{的|de}, nice and chubby). {瘦|shòu} is often meant kindly: {你|nǐ}{瘦|shòu}{了|le}！ (You've lost weight!) is
something people say to friends.

{年轻|nián qīng} is "young" for adults: {一|yí}{个|gè}{年轻人|nián qīng rén} (a young person), {我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{很|hěn}{年轻|nián qīng}. For children, use {小|xiǎo}: {他|tā}{还|hái}{小|xiǎo}
(he's still little).

{可爱|kě ài} is "cute, lovely": children, small animals, and anything sweet. {这个|zhè ge}{孩子|hái zi}{真|zhēn}{可爱|kě ài}！ (What a sweet
child!)

## Height in numbers: {身高|shēn gāo}

In HSK 2 you asked {你|nǐ}{多|duō}{高|gāo}？ and answered with {米|mǐ} (metre: lesson 13's word). {身高|shēn gāo} is a person's height
as a figure, the word used on forms and in descriptions:

{我|wǒ}{身高|shēn gāo}1.75{米|mǐ}。 — I'm 1.75 m tall.

Say it {一米七五|yì mǐ qī wǔ}: one metre, then the centimetres as two digits, each read on its own.
1.80 is {一米八|yì mǐ bā}, 1.62 is {一米六二|yì mǐ liù èr}, 1.58 is {一米五八|yì mǐ wǔ bā}. In everyday speech the {身高|shēn gāo} is often left out:

{他|tā}{一米八|yì mǐ bā}，{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le}。 — He's 1.80 m, much taller than me.

{你|nǐ}{身高|shēn gāo}{多少|duō shao}？ — How tall are you? (on a form, or from a doctor)

{身高|shēn gāo} is the figure; {个子|gè zi} (HSK 2) is your build: {他|tā}{个子|gè zi}{很|hěn}{高|gāo} (he's tall).

## Comparing: more, much more, a little more

You know A {比|bǐ} B + adjective from HSK 2, and that {很|hěn} or {非常|fēi cháng} can't go inside it. To say how big the
difference is, put it **after** the adjective:

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| A {比|bǐ} B + adj | A is more … than B | {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}。 |
| A {比|bǐ} B + adj + {一点儿|yì diǎnr} | a little more | {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 |
| A {比|bǐ} B + adj + {多|duō}{了|le} | much more | {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le}。 |
| A {比|bǐ} B + adj + {得|de}{多|duō} | much more | {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{得|de}{多|duō}。 |
| A {比|bǐ} B + adj + number + measure | by an exact amount | {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{大|dà}{两|liǎng}{岁|suì}。 |

{多|duō}{了|le} and {得|de}{多|duō} mean the same; {多|duō}{了|le} is a little more common in speech. Both go after the adjective,
never before it:

{今天|jīn tiān}{比|bǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{冷|lěng}{多|duō}{了|le}。 — Today's much colder than yesterday.

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{房间|fáng jiān}{比|bǐ}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{大|dà}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 — My room's a bit bigger than yours.

{他|tā}{比|bǐ}{他|tā}{哥哥|gē ge}{小|xiǎo}{三|sān}{岁|suì}。 — He's three years younger than his brother.

## Not as … as: A {没有|méi yǒu} B ({那么|nà me}) + adjective

To say A doesn't reach B's level, use {没有|méi yǒu}:

{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{我|wǒ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{高|gāo}。 — I'm not as tall as my sister.

{这个|zhè ge}{房子|fáng zi}{没有|méi yǒu}{那个|nà ge}{房子|fáng zi}{那么|nà me}{大|dà}。 — This flat isn't as big as that one.

{那么|nà me} (so, that) from HSK 2 is optional; it adds "as … as that". Ask with {吗|ma} or A-not-A on {有|yǒu}:

{他|tā}{有|yǒu}{你|nǐ}{高|gāo}{吗|ma}？ — Is he as tall as you?

The positive, A {有|yǒu} B ({那么|nà me}) + adjective, is mostly used in questions like this one. Two things to
avoid: degree words after the adjective (~~{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{他|tā}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le}~~: {没有|méi yǒu} already says "not as"), and {不|bù}{比|bǐ},
which means something else ("no more … than", often in a contradiction).

## The same: A {跟|gēn} B {一样|yí yàng} (+ adjective)

{一样|yí yàng} means "the same". With {跟|gēn} (or {和|hé}), it compares two things:

{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{我|wǒ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{一样|yí yàng}{高|gāo}。 — I'm as tall as my sister. (my sister and I are the same height)

{他|tā}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{跟|gēn}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{一样|yí yàng}。 — His phone's the same as mine.

{我们|wǒ men}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}{一样|yí yàng}{大|dà}。 — We're the same age. ({两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}, the two of us, as the subject)

Put the adjective after {一样|yí yàng} to say in what way they're the same. No {很|hěn} before it: ~~{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{她|tā}{一样|yí yàng}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}~~.
The negative is {不|bù}{一样|yí yàng}:

{我|wǒ}{的|de}{想法|xiǎng fǎ}{跟|gēn}{你|nǐ}{不|bù}{一样|yí yàng}。 — My view is different from yours. ({想法|xiǎng fǎ}, way of thinking, isn't a course
word)

{这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{字|zì}{不|bù}{一样|yí yàng}。 — These two characters are different.

### {不同|bù tóng}: different

{不同|bù tóng} means "different" too, but it's more formal, and it's most at home before a noun, often with {的|de}:

{不同|bù tóng}{的|de}{人|rén}{有|yǒu}{不同|bù tóng}{的|de}{习惯|xí guàn}。 — Different people have different habits. ({习惯|xí guàn}, habit: lesson 23)

{这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{字|zì}{的|de}{意思|yì si}{不同|bù tóng}。 — These two characters have different meanings.

In speech, for "A and B aren't the same", {不|bù}{一样|yí yàng} is the everyday word; before a noun ("different
colours"), {不同|bù tóng}{的|de} is the natural one: {不同|bù tóng}{的|de}{颜色|yán sè}.

## Looking like: {像|xiàng} and {好像|hǎo xiàng}

**{像|xiàng}** is "to look like, resemble", for people and things:

{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{像|xiàng}{你|nǐ}{妈妈|mā ma}。 — You look a lot like your mum.

{这个|zhè ge}{孩子|hái zi}{的|de}{眼睛|yǎn jing}{像|xiàng}{他|tā}{爸爸|bà ba}。 — This child has his father's eyes.

You'll often hear {长|zhǎng}{得|de}{像|xiàng} (to look like: {长|zhǎng}, to grow, is lesson 28's): {他|tā}{长|zhǎng}{得|de}{像|xiàng}{他|tā}{爸爸|bà ba}. Add {一样|yí yàng}
+ adjective to compare one quality: {她|tā}{像|xiàng}{她|tā}{妈妈|mā ma}{一样|yí yàng}{漂亮|piào liang} (she's as pretty as her mother).

**{好像|hǎo xiàng}** is "to seem, to look as if": what you think from what you see.

{他|tā}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{病|bìng}{了|le}。 — He seems to be ill.

{外面|wài miàn}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。 — It looks as if it's raining outside.

{你|nǐ}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{瘦|shòu}{了|le}。 — You seem to have got thinner.

So {他|tā}{像|xiàng}{他|tā}{爸爸|bà ba} is about resemblance, and {他|tā}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{很|hěn}{累|lèi} (he seems tired) is about an impression.

### Sound parts

- {腿|tuǐ} is ⺼ + 退 *tuì* (to step back): an exact sound except for the tone, and a leg is what you
  step back with.
- {像|xiàng} is 亻 + 象 *xiàng* (elephant; image): exact. {像|xiàng} first meant a likeness of a person.
- {胖|pàng} is ⺼ + {半|bàn} ({半|bàn}, half). The rhyme *-ang* / *-an* has drifted; the shape is a good
  memory aid anyway.
- {脸|liǎn} is ⺼ + 佥 *qiān*. The same right side gives the sound of 检 *jiǎn* (in {检查|jiǎn chá}, to check:
  next lesson): {脸|liǎn} and 检 rhyme.
- {脚|jiǎo} is ⺼ + 却 *què*, which once gave the sound; today it doesn't.
- {嘴|zuǐ} is {口|kǒu} + 觜 *zī*, an old word for a bird's beak, which gives the sound.
- {瘦|shòu} is 疒 (illness: being too thin) + 叟 *sǒu* (an old man), which gives the sound.
- {矮|ǎi} is 矢 (an arrow) + 委 *wěi*, which gives part of the sound.
- 轻 *qīng*: the right side is the same as in {经|jīng} ({经常|jīng cháng}, HSK 2). In traditional
  characters both have 巠 *jīng*: 輕 and 經. {年轻|nián qīng} is "light in years".

### Meaning parts: ⺼ and 矢

⺼, the "meat moon" from HSK 1 ({脑|nǎo} in {电脑|diàn nǎo}), marks parts of the body: {脸|liǎn}, {脚|jiǎo}, {腿|tuǐ}, {胖|pàng},
and {脏|zāng} from last lesson. It looks like {月|yuè} (moon), but on the left of body words it's flesh.

矢 is an arrow. It's on the left of both {矮|ǎi} and {短|duǎn}: short things, measured against an arrow, as the
traditional explanation goes. A memory aid that works: both "short" characters have the arrow.
{短|duǎn} has 豆 *dòu* (a bean, as in {豆腐|dòu fu}) on the right, {矮|ǎi} has 委.

### New radical: 耳

耳 (耳字旁 *ěr zì páng*, ear) began as a drawing of an ear. It's the first character of {耳朵|ěr duo}, and it
marks hearing in two later characters: 聪 (in {聪明|cōng ming}, clever: lesson 18; someone who hears and
understands quickly) and {聊|liáo} (in {聊天儿|liáo tiānr}, to chat: lesson 22). On the left, its bottom stroke rises.

### Stroke order

- **耳**: the top horizontal, then the short vertical on the left, then the long vertical on the
  right, the two short horizontals inside, and the bottom stroke last (on the left of 聪 and {聊|liáo},
  it rises).
- **朵**: {几|jǐ} on top (a left-falling stroke, then the stroke that goes across and curves down), then
  木.
- **{胖|pàng}, {脸|liǎn}, {脚|jiǎo}, {腿|tuǐ}**: ⺼ first, narrow: left-falling stroke, the turning hook, then the two short
  horizontals inside.
- **{短|duǎn}, {矮|ǎi}**: 矢 first, narrow: short left-falling stroke, two horizontals, the left-falling stroke
  and a dot instead of the long right-falling stroke.
- **轻**: {车|chē} first, narrow, its last stroke rising; then the right side: the turning strokes on
  top ({又|yòu}), then 工.
- **{像|xiàng}**: 亻, then 象: the short stroke and the box at the top, then the long body with its
  left-falling strokes, and the right-falling stroke last.
