hers, but my eyes are just as big. People say my sister looks like our mum and I look like our
dad. I think our personalities are different too: my sister likes talking and going out with her
friends, while I'm much quieter and like reading at home. But there's one way we're the same: we
both love eating! So neither of us is thin."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Describing people
{你|nǐ}{很|hěn}{像|xiàng}{你|nǐ}{妈妈|mā ma}。
= You look a lot like your mum.
{我|wǒ}{身高|shēn gāo}{一米七五|yì mǐ qī wǔ}。
= I'm 1.75 m tall.
{他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le}。
= He's much taller than me.
{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}{那么|nà me}{高|gāo}。
= I'm not as tall as my brother.
{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{我|wǒ}{姐姐|jiě jie}{一样|yí yàng}{高|gāo}。
= I'm the same height as my sister.
{你|nǐ}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{瘦|shòu}{了|le}。
= You seem to have lost weight.
```

Now describe someone in your family in four or five sentences: their height ({身高|shēn gāo}), hair, face,
build, and who they look like. Then compare yourself with them using {比|bǐ}, {没有|méi yǒu} and {跟|gēn}…{一样|yí yàng}.

## Pronunciation

- {耳朵|ěr duo}: *er* with the tongue curled back, then a light *duo*.
- {脚|jiǎo} dips; {叫|jiào} (to be called) falls.
- {嘴|zuǐ} dips; {最|zuì} (most) falls.
- {瘦|shòu} falls; {手|shǒu} (hand) dips. {我|wǒ}{手|shǒu}{很|hěn}{瘦|shòu} is a nice tone drill.
- {矮|ǎi} dips; {爱|ài} (love) falls.
- {胖|pàng} falls sharply; {腿|tuǐ} and {短|duǎn} dip.
- {一样|yí yàng}: {一|yī} rises before the fourth tone. {不同|bù tóng}: {不|bù} keeps its fourth tone before a
  second tone.
- {一米七五|yì mǐ qī wǔ}: {一|yī} before a third tone is said *yì*.

## Common mistakes

- {很|hěn} inside a {比|bǐ} sentence: ~~{他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}~~. Say {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}, or {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le} / {高|gāo}{得|de}{多|duō} for "much".
- Degree before the adjective: ~~{他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{多|duō}{了|le}{高|gāo}~~. The amount goes after: {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le}.
- {没有|méi yǒu} with an amount: ~~{我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{他|tā}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{他|tā}{高|gāo} (I'm not as tall as him).
- {很|hěn} with {一样|yí yàng}: ~~{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{她|tā}{一样|yí yàng}{很|hěn}{高|gāo}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{她|tā}{一样|yí yàng}{高|gāo}.
- {短|duǎn} for people: ~~{他|tā}{很|hěn}{短|duǎn}~~. Height is {矮|ǎi}: {他|tā}{很|hěn}{矮|ǎi}. {短|duǎn} is for length: {头发|tóu fa}{很|hěn}{短|duǎn}.
- A measure word with {头发|tóu fa} for "hair": ~~{她|tā}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{长|cháng}{头发|tóu fa}~~. Say {她|tā}{的|de}{头发|tóu fa}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}, or {她|tā}{头发|tóu fa}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}.
- {像|xiàng} for "seem": ~~{他|tā}{像|xiàng}{病|bìng}{了|le}~~. Say {他|tā}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{病|bìng}{了|le}. {像|xiàng} is resemblance: {他|tā}{像|xiàng}{他|tā}{爸爸|bà ba}.

## Key points

- Face and body: {脸|liǎn}, {耳朵|ěr duo}, {嘴|zuǐ}, {牙|yá}, {头发|tóu fa} (頭髮), {腿|tuǐ}, {脚|jiǎo}; topic-comment: {她|tā}{头发|tóu fa}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}.
- Build: {胖|pàng} / {瘦|shòu}, {高|gāo} / {矮|ǎi} (height), {长|cháng} / {短|duǎn} (length); {年轻|nián qīng} (young adults), {可爱|kě ài} (cute).
- {身高|shēn gāo} + figure: 1.75{米|mǐ} is read {一米七五|yì mǐ qī wǔ}.
- A {比|bǐ} B + adj (+ {一点儿|yì diǎnr} / {多|duō}{了|le} / {得|de}{多|duō} / number + measure): {他|tā}{比|bǐ}{我|wǒ}{高|gāo}{多|duō}{了|le}.
- A {没有|méi yǒu} B ({那么|nà me}) + adj: not as … as: {我|wǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{他|tā}{高|gāo}.
- A {跟|gēn} B {一样|yí yàng} (+ adj), {不|bù}{一样|yí yàng}; {不同|bù tóng} (more formal, before nouns: {不同|bù tóng}{的|de}{人|rén}).
- {像|xiàng}: look like ({他|tā}{像|xiàng}{他|tā}{爸爸|bà ba}); {好像|hǎo xiàng}: seem ({他|tā}{好像|hǎo xiàng}{病|bìng}{了|le}).
- {=Sound parts: 退 in {腿|tuǐ}, 象 in {像|xiàng}, {半|bàn} in {胖|pàng}, the right side of {脸|liǎn} and 检. Meaning parts: ⺼ (body), 矢
  (short). New radical 耳.=}

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Staying healthy: 一…就, 小心, 不用
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 1 and HSK 2 gave you {病|bìng}, {生病|shēng bìng}, {看病|kàn bìng}, {医院|yī yuàn}, {休息|xiū xi}, {舒服|shū fu}, {疼|téng} and {药|yào}. This lesson goes further: catching a
cold, running a fever, going into hospital and coming out again, keeping fit, and looking after
someone. You'll learn:

- {感冒|gǎn mào}, {发烧|fā shāo}, {住院|zhù yuàn}, {出院|chū yuàn}, {病人|bìng rén}, {检查|jiǎn chá};
- {健康|jiàn kāng}, {锻炼|duàn liàn}, and {坚持|jiān chí} + verb (to keep on doing something);
- the linked sentence **{一|yī}…{就|jiù}** (as soon as; whenever): {我|wǒ}{一|yí}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{就|jiù}{累|lèi};
- warnings and advice with {小心|xiǎo xīn} and {注意|zhù yì}, and "no need" with {不用|bú yòng};
- {担心|dān xīn} (to worry) and {照顾|zhào gù} (to look after).

The reading tells the story of an illness from start to finish: what caused it, what happened and
how it ended.

## Being ill

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {感冒|gǎn mào} | a cold; to catch a cold | {我|wǒ}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le}。 |
| {发烧|fā shāo} | to have a fever, a temperature | {他|tā}{发烧|fā shāo}{了|le}，{三十八|sān shí bā}{度|dù}。 |
| {病人|bìng rén} | patient, sick person | {医院|yī yuàn}{里|lǐ}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{病人|bìng rén}。 |
| {检查|jiǎn chá} | to examine, check; a check-up | {医生|yī shēng}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{检查|jiǎn chá}{了|le}{一下|yí xià}。 |
| {住院|zhù yuàn} | to be in hospital | {他|tā}{住院|zhù yuàn}{了|le}。 |
| {出院|chū yuàn} | to leave hospital | {她|tā}{明天|míng tiān}{出院|chū yuàn}。 |

{感冒|gǎn mào} is both the illness and the verb: {我|wǒ}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le} (I've caught a cold), {感冒药|gǎn mào yào} (cold medicine). {发烧|fā shāo}
is a verb with its own object, like {睡觉|shuì jiào}: {发烧|fā shāo}{了|le} (has a temperature), {发高烧|fā gāo shāo} (a high fever). The
temperature is in degrees, {度|dù} (not a course word): {三十九|sān shí jiǔ}{度|dù} is 39 °C.

{检查|jiǎn chá} is to check or examine something carefully: a doctor examining a patient, a teacher checking
homework, a mechanic checking a car. {给|gěi} + person + {检查|jiǎn chá} is "examine someone":

{医生|yī shēng}{给|gěi}{他|tā}{检查|jiǎn chá}{了|le}{一下|yí xià}，{说|shuō}{他|tā}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le}。 — The doctor examined him and said he had a cold.

{请|qǐng}{你|nǐ}{再|zài}{检查|jiǎn chá}{一下|yí xià}。 — Please check it again.

{住院|zhù yuàn} and {出院|chū yuàn} are {住|zhù} (to stay) or {出|chū} (to go out) + {院|yuàn}, the {院|yuàn} of {医院|yī yuàn}. Like {搬家|bān jiā}, {住院|zhù yuàn} is separable,
so a length of time can go inside: {他|tā}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}{院|yuàn} (he was in hospital for three days). {他|tā}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}
says the same.

## Staying healthy: {健康|jiàn kāng}, {锻炼|duàn liàn}, {坚持|jiān chí}

**{健康|jiàn kāng}** is "healthy" and "health":

{我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{七十|qī shí}{多|duō}{岁|suì}{了|le}，{身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{健康|jiàn kāng}。 — My grandpa's over seventy and in very good health.

{健康|jiàn kāng}{很|hěn}{重要|zhòng yào}。 — Health is very important. ({重要|zhòng yào}, important, is lesson 28's.)

**{锻炼|duàn liàn}** is to exercise, to work out, usually {锻炼|duàn liàn}{身体|shēn tǐ} (keep fit):

{我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 — I exercise for an hour every morning.

**{坚持|jiān chí}** is to keep at something, not give up. With a verb after it, it means "keep doing":

{他|tā}{坚持|jiān chí}{每天|měi tiān}{跑步|pǎo bù}。 — He keeps up his daily run.

{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{要|yào}{坚持|jiān chí}，{每天|měi tiān}{学|xué}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}。 — With Chinese you have to keep at it: learn a little every day.

## As soon as, whenever: {一|yī}…{就|jiù}

**{一|yī}…{就|jiù}** links two things: as soon as the first happens, the second follows. {一|yī} goes before the
first verb, {就|jiù} before the second, and both come after their subjects:

{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{到|dào}{家|jiā}{就|jiù}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{了|le}。 — As soon as I got home, I went to sleep.

{他|tā}{一|yí}{下课|xià kè}{就|jiù}{去|qù}{锻炼|duàn liàn}。 — He goes to exercise as soon as class is over.

When the two events repeat, it means "whenever, every time":

{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{就|jiù}{累|lèi}。 — Whenever I exercise, I get tired.

{她|tā}{一|yì}{感冒|gǎn mào}{就|jiù}{发烧|fā shāo}。 — Every time she catches a cold, she gets a temperature.

With two different subjects, each one stands before its own part:

{你|nǐ}{一|yì}{说|shuō}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{明白|míng bai}{了|le}。 — The moment you said it, I understood. ({明白|míng bai}, to understand, is lesson 18's.)

This is a **[[compressed sentence]]**: two clauses squeezed into one, with no {如果|rú guǒ} (if) or {以后|yǐ hòu} (after),
just {一|yī} and {就|jiù}. Remember that {一|yī} changes its tone with the next syllable: {一|yí}{到|dào} *yí dào*, {一|yí}{下课|xià kè} *yí
xià kè*, {一|yì}{感冒|gǎn mào} *yì gǎn mào*, {一|yì}{说|shuō} *yì shuō*.

## Be careful, pay attention: {小心|xiǎo xīn} and {注意|zhù yì}

**{小心|xiǎo xīn}** is "careful", and on its own a warning: "Watch out!" It goes before a noun (the danger) or a
verb:

{小心|xiǎo xīn}！{车|chē}{来|lái}{了|le}！ — Look out! There's a car coming!

{天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le}，{小心|xiǎo xīn}{感冒|gǎn mào}。 — It's getting cold; be careful not to catch a cold.

{路上|lù shang}{小心|xiǎo xīn}！ — Take care on the way!

It's an adjective too: {他|tā}{做事|zuò shì}{很|hěn}{小心|xiǎo xīn} (he's very careful in what he does).

**{注意|zhù yì}** is to pay attention to, watch, take care of:

{注意|zhù yì}{身体|shēn tǐ}！ — Look after yourself! (look after your health)

{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{注意|zhù yì}{休息|xiū xi}。 — You must make sure you rest.

{请|qǐng}{大家|dà jiā}{注意|zhù yì}，{飞机|fēi jī}{马上|mǎ shàng}{要|yào}{起飞|qǐ fēi}{了|le}。 — Attention please, everyone: the plane is about to take off. ({马上|mǎ shàng},
{起飞|qǐ fēi}: lessons 13 and 14.)

{小心|xiǎo xīn} warns about a danger; {注意|zhù yì} asks someone to keep something in mind. {小心|xiǎo xīn}{感冒|gǎn mào} and {注意|zhù yì}{身体|shēn tǐ} are two
ways of saying "take care".

## No need: {不用|bú yòng} + verb

**{不用|bú yòng}** means "there's no need to": it's the negative of {要|yào} in the sense "need to".

{你|nǐ}{不用|bú yòng}{担心|dān xīn}。 — You don't need to worry.

{明天|míng tiān}{不用|bú yòng}{上班|shàng bān}。 — There's no need to go to work tomorrow.

{不用谢|bú yòng xiè}！ — No need to thank me! (You're welcome.)

{不用|bú yòng} isn't a command: "don't" is {别|bié} or {不要|bú yào} (HSK 1 and 2). {别|bié}{说话|shuō huà}！ means "Don't talk!"; {不用|bú yòng}{说|shuō} means
"there's no need to say it" (or "it goes without saying"). The {不|bù} changes to *bú* before {用|yòng}.

## Worrying and caring: {担心|dān xīn} and {照顾|zhào gù}

**{担心|dān xīn}** is to worry, or to worry about someone or something. Its object can be a person, a thing, or a
whole clause:

{别|bié}{担心|dān xīn}，{我|wǒ}{没事|méi shì}。 — Don't worry, I'm fine.

{妈妈|mā ma}{很|hěn}{担心|dān xīn}{你|nǐ}。 — Mum is very worried about you.

{我|wǒ}{担心|dān xīn}{明天|míng tiān}{会|huì}{下雨|xià yǔ}。 — I'm worried it'll rain tomorrow.

**{照顾|zhào gù}** is to look after, take care of: patients, children, old people, guests.

{孩子|hái zi}{病|bìng}{了|le}，{她|tā}{在|zài}{家|jiā}{照顾|zhào gù}{孩子|hái zi}。 — The child is ill; she's staying home to look after them.

{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{照顾|zhào gù}{好|hǎo}{自己|zì jǐ}。 — Take good care of yourself. ({好|hǎo} as a result complement: properly)

The character {顾|gù} is taught in the next lesson.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 感 | to feel; to touch | gǎn | 心 | 13 | {感冒|gǎn mào}, {感兴趣|gǎn xìng qù} (lesson 22), {感到|gǎn dào} (lesson 24) |
| 冒 | to give off; to risk | mào | 冂 | 9 | {感冒|gǎn mào} |
| 烧 (traditional 燒) | to burn | shāo | 火 | 10 | {发烧|fā shāo} |
| 健 | strong, healthy | jiàn | 亻 | 10 | {健康|jiàn kāng} |
| 康 | well, healthy | kāng | 广 | 11 | {健康|jiàn kāng} |
| 锻 (traditional 鍛) | to forge (metal) | duàn | 钅 | 14 | {锻炼|duàn liàn} |
| 炼 (traditional 煉; 鍊 in 鍛鍊) | to refine, smelt | liàn | 火 | 9 | {锻炼|duàn liàn} |
| 检 (traditional 檢) | to check | jiǎn | 木 | 11 | {检查|jiǎn chá}, {检票|jiǎn piào} (lesson 14) |
| 查 ✎ | to check, look up | chá | 木 | 9 | {检查|jiǎn chá}, {查|chá} (lesson 09) |
| 坚 (traditional 堅) | firm, hard | jiān | 土 | 7 | {坚持|jiān chí} |
| 持 | to hold | chí | 扌 | 9 | {坚持|jiān chí} |
| 心 ✎ | heart; mind | xīn | 心 | 4 | {小心|xiǎo xīn}, {担心|dān xīn}, {放心|fàng xīn} (lesson 24), {关心|guān xīn} (lesson 20) |
| 注 | to pour; to fix (attention) | zhù | 氵 | 8 | {注意|zhù yì}, {关注|guān zhù} (lesson 20) |
| 用 ✎ | to use | yòng | {用|yòng} | 5 | {不用|bú yòng}, {用|yòng} (lesson 09) |
| 担 (traditional 擔) | to carry (on the shoulder) | dān | 扌 | 8 | {担心|dān xīn} |
| 照 | to shine; to look after | zhào | 灬 | 13 | {照顾|zhào gù}, {照片|zhào piàn} (lesson 14) |

### Sound parts

- 健 *jiàn* is 亻 + 建 *jiàn* (to build): an exact match. Someone well built.
- 锻 *duàn* is 钅 (metal) + {段|duàn} (a section: lesson 21), exact again. {锻炼|duàn liàn} first meant forging
  and refining metal: hammering yourself into shape.
- 炼 *liàn* has the same right side and the same sound as {练|liàn} (to practise, lesson 17). The
  traditional form of 炼 on its own is 煉 (refining with fire: the card and the tracing pad show
  it), but in 鍛鍊 the traditional switch shows the "metal" form 鍊, as Taiwan writes the word.
- 注 *zhù* is 氵 + 主 *zhǔ* (master). 主 gives the sound of {住|zhù} too: {住院|zhù yuàn} and {注意|zhù yì} start with the
  same syllable, written with two different characters.
- 担 *dān* is 扌 + 旦 *dàn* (dawn). 旦 gives the sound of {但|dàn} ({但是|dàn shì}) as well.
- 持 *chí* is 扌 (hand: holding) + 寺 *sì*. In traditional characters 寺 is also in 時 *shí*
  ({时|shí}, time); in all three it once gave the sound.
- 检 *jiǎn* has the right side of last lesson's {脸|liǎn}: they rhyme.
- {照|zhào} is 昭 *zhāo* (bright) over 灬, four dots of fire: light, shining. {照|zhào} is "to shine on" and
  "to look after", and it's the {照|zhào} of {照片|zhào piàn} (photo, lesson 14).
- 感 *gǎn* is 咸 *xián* over 心. Old dictionaries count 咸 as the sound part; the readings have
  drifted.

### The other characters

- 心 is a drawing of the heart. You know it as a radical from HSK 1: 忄 on the left ({忙|máng}, {快|kuài}, {慢|màn},
  {懂|dǒng}), 心 underneath ({想|xiǎng}, 意, 思, {您|nín}). Now it's a word of its own, in {小心|xiǎo xīn} (small heart: careful), {担心|dān xīn}
  (carry in your heart: worry) and later {放心|fàng xīn} (put your heart down: be at ease).
- 冒 is traditionally explained as a hat (the top part) pulled down over an eye (目). A memory aid for
  {感冒|gǎn mào}: you "feel" (感) the cold you "risked" (冒) going out in.
- 坚 is 土 (earth) under the top part; its traditional form 堅 has 臣 on the top left. {坚持|jiān chí} is
  "hold firm".
- 康 is 广 (a building) over the rest. {健康|jiàn kāng} is two "healthy" characters together.
- {用|yòng} is its own radical, five strokes.
- 烧 is 火 + 尧 *yáo*: fire, burning. {发烧|fā shāo} is "to give off heat".

Radical review: 心 / 忄 (heart) in 感, 心; 火 and 灬 (fire) in 烧, 炼, {照|zhào}; 扌 (hand) in 持, 担; 钅 (metal,
HSK 1 lesson 07: 钟, {钱|qián}) in 锻.

### Stroke order

- **心**: the dot on the left, the long curved stroke that hooks up, then the dot in the middle,
  and the dot on the right last.
- **{用|yòng}**: the left-falling stroke on the left, the stroke that goes across and down with a hook,
  the two horizontals inside, and the vertical through the middle last.
- **{查|chá}**: 木 first (horizontal, vertical, left-falling stroke, dot), then {日|rì} below it, then the long
  horizontal at the bottom.
- **感**: 咸 first: horizontal, left-falling stroke, the {一|yī} and {口|kǒu} inside, then the long sweeping
  stroke on the right with its hook, the left-falling stroke and the dot; 心 last.
- **冒**: the top part (a vertical, the turn, two short strokes inside), then 目, wide and tall.
- **{照|zhào}**: {日|rì}, then 召 (刀 over {口|kǒu}), then the four dots of 灬 from left to right.

```trace
感冒烧健康锻炼检
```

```trace
查坚持心注用担照
```

Write it: {查|chá}, 心 and {用|yòng} are on the handwriting list. Write each three times from memory: 心 has
four strokes (dot, hook, dot, dot); in {用|yòng} the middle vertical is last.
=}

## Handwriting review: HSK 1 and 2

These twenty ✎ characters from HSK 1 and HSK 2 are all used in this module. Write each one twice
from memory, then check it against the tracing pad.

> **Handwriting review, module 1**
>
> 爱 ({爱人|ài ren}) · 男 ({男人|nán rén}) · 女 ({女人|nǚ rén}) · 们 ({咱们|zán men}) · 子 ({房子|fáng zi}) · 家 ({搬家|bān jiā}) · 打 ({打扫|dǎ sǎo})
>
> 上 ({上去|shàng qù}) · 下 ({下来|xià lái}) · 来 ({进来|jìn lái}) · 去 ({出去|chū qù}) · 年 ({年轻|nián qīng}) · 可 ({可爱|kě ài}) · 同 ({不同|bù tóng})
>
> 比 ({比|bǐ}) · 长 ({长|cháng}) · 多 ({多了|duō le}) · 时 ({有时候|yǒu shí hou}) · 有 ({没有|méi yǒu}) · 没 ({没有|méi yǒu})

```trace
爱男女们子家打
```

```trace
上下来去年可同
```

```trace
比长多时有没
```

{=Three to watch: {女|nǚ} starts with the turning stroke and ends with the horizontal; in {比|bǐ} the left half
ends with a rising stroke; 长 has only four strokes, and the third one flicks up.=}

## Dialogue: at the doctor's

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) isn't feeling well. She goes to see a doctor (医生).

```dialogue
# At the doctor's
医生: {你好|nǐ hǎo}，{哪儿|nǎr}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}？
= Hello. What seems to be the trouble?
安娜: {我|wǒ}{头|tóu}{疼|téng}，{还|hái}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{发烧|fā shāo}。
= I've got a headache, and a bit of a temperature.
医生: {什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de}？
= When did it start?
安娜: {昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}。{我|wǒ}{一|yì}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{就|jiù}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}，{很|hěn}{想|xiǎng}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。
= Last night. As soon as I got home I felt really tired and just wanted to sleep.
医生: {我|wǒ}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}{检查|jiǎn chá}{一下|yí xià}。……{三十八|sān shí bā}{度|dù}，{你|nǐ}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le}。
= Let me examine you. … 38 degrees: you've got a cold.
安娜: {要|yào}{住院|zhù yuàn}{吗|ma}？
= Do I need to go into hospital?
医生: {不用|bú yòng}{住院|zhù yuàn}。{回|huí}{家|jiā}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}，{多|duō}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}，{吃|chī}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{药|yào}{就|jiù}{好|hǎo}{了|le}。
= No need for that. Go home, rest a lot, drink plenty of water, and take a little medicine, and you'll be fine.
安娜: {我|wǒ}{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{身体|shēn tǐ}，{为什么|wèi shén me}{还|hái}{会|huì}{感冒|gǎn mào}？
= I exercise every day. Why do I still catch colds?
医生: {锻炼|duàn liàn}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{坚持|jiān chí}。{不过|bú guò}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{以后|yǐ hòu}{要|yào}{小心|xiǎo xīn}，{别|bié}{穿|chuān}{得|de}{太|tài}{少|shǎo}。
= Exercise is good; keep it up. But be careful after exercising: don't wear too little.
安娜: {好|hǎo}{的|de}。{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{可以|kě yǐ}{上课|shàng kè}{吗|ma}？
= OK. Can I go to class tomorrow?
医生: {你|nǐ}{这|zhè}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}{注意|zhù yì}{休息|xiū xi}，{别|bié}{去|qù}{上课|shàng kè}{了|le}。{别|bié}{担心|dān xīn}，{过|guò}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}{就|jiù}{好|hǎo}{了|le}。
= Make sure you rest for the next couple of days; don't go to class. Don't worry, you'll be better in a day or two.
安娜: {谢谢|xiè xie}{医生|yī shēng}！
= Thank you, doctor!
```

- {哪儿|nǎr}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}？ (where are you uncomfortable?) is how doctors and friends ask what's wrong.
- {是|shì}…{的|de} in {什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{开始|kāi shǐ}{的|de} is HSK 2's pattern for the time of a past event ({是|shì} left out, as often in
  speech).
- {多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}，{多|duō}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}: {多|duō} before a verb is "do more of it".
- {就|jiù}{好|hǎo}{了|le} is "and then you'll be fine": {就|jiù} (then) from HSK 2.
- {还|hái}{会|huì}{感冒|gǎn mào} is "still catch colds": {会|huì} for something that can happen.
- {过|guò}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān} is "in a couple of days" ({过|guò}, to pass: HSK 2).

## Reading: Grandpa goes into hospital

> {我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{今年|jīn nián}{七十五|qī shí wǔ}{岁|suì}，{身体|shēn tǐ}{一直|yì zhí}{很|hěn}{健康|jiàn kāng}。{上个月|shàng gè yuè}{天气|tiān qì}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{可是|kě shì}{他|tā}{还是|hái shi}{每天|měi tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{去|qù}{小区|xiǎo qū}{里|lǐ}{跑步|pǎo bù}，{衣服|yī fu}{也|yě}{穿|chuān}{得|de}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}。{有一天|yǒu yì tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}，{他|tā}{觉得|jué de}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}，{头|tóu}{也|yě}{疼|téng}。{第二天|dì èr tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}，{他|tā}{一|yì}{起床|qǐ chuáng}{就|jiù}{发烧|fā shāo}{了|le}，{三十九|sān shí jiǔ}{度|dù}。{我们|wǒ men}{马上|mǎ shàng}{带|dài}{他|tā}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}。{医生|yī shēng}{给|gěi}{他|tā}{检查|jiǎn chá}{了|le}{一下|yí xià}，{说|shuō}{他|tā}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le}，{老人|lǎo rén}{发高烧|fā gāo shāo}{要|yào}{小心|xiǎo xīn}，{让|ràng}{他|tā}{住院|zhù yuàn}。
>
> {爷爷|yé ye}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{住|zhù}{了|le}{五|wǔ}{天|tiān}。{我|wǒ}{和|hé}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{每天|měi tiān}{都|dōu}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{照顾|zhào gù}{他|tā}。{爷爷|yé ye}{说|shuō}：“{你们|nǐ men}{工作|gōng zuò}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{忙|máng}，{不用|bú yòng}{天|tiān}{天|tiān}{来|lái}。”{可是|kě shì}{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{担心|dān xīn}{他|tā}，{还是|hái shi}{每天|měi tiān}{去|qù}。
>
> {第六天|dì liù tiān}，{爷爷|yé ye}{出院|chū yuàn}{了|le}。{医生|yī shēng}{对|duì}{他|tā}{说|shuō}：“{您|nín}{要|yào}{注意|zhù yì}{身体|shēn tǐ}，{天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{多|duō}{穿|chuān}{衣服|yī fu}，{锻炼|duàn liàn}{也|yě}{别|bié}{太|tài}{累|lèi}。”{现在|xiàn zài}{爷爷|yé ye}{还|hái}{坚持|jiān chí}{每天|měi tiān}{锻炼|duàn liàn}，{不过|bú guò}{他|tā}{不|bù}{跑步|pǎo bù}{了|le}，{每天|měi tiān}{跟|gēn}{小区|xiǎo qū}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{老人|lǎo rén}{一起|yì qǐ}{走路|zǒu lù}。

- {一直|yì zhí} (all along) is lesson 21's word; {马上|mǎ shàng} (right away) lesson 13's; {带|dài} (to take someone along)
  lesson 09's.
- {还是|hái shi} here is "still, all the same": he kept going despite the cold.
- {天|tiān}{天|tiān} is "every day": a time word doubled (HSK 2).

1. What caused Grandpa's illness?
2. What happened the next morning?
3. Why did the family visit every day, although Grandpa told them not to?
4. How has Grandpa changed his exercise?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. It was very cold, but he still went running every morning, and he didn't wear enough clothes
   ({衣服|yī fu}{也|yě}{穿|chuān}{得|de}{很|hěn}{少|shǎo}).
2. As soon as he got up he had a fever of 39 degrees ({他|tā}{一|yì}{起床|qǐ chuáng}{就|jiù}{发烧|fā shāo}{了|le}); the family took him to hospital
   and he was kept in.
3. They were worried about him ({我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{担心|dān xīn}{他|tā}).
4. He still exercises every day, but he doesn't run any more: he walks with the other old people
   in the compound.

"My grandpa is seventy-five this year, and he's always been very healthy. Last month it was very
cold, but he still went running in the compound every morning, and in very few clothes. One
evening he felt very tired and had a headache. The next morning, as soon as he got up, he had a
temperature: 39 degrees. We took him to the hospital straight away. The doctor examined him and
said he had a cold, but that a high fever in an old person needs care, and had him admitted.

Grandpa was in hospital for five days. My mum and I went every day to look after him. Grandpa
said: 'You're both busy at work; you don't need to come every day.' But we were worried about him,
so we went every day all the same.

On the sixth day Grandpa came out of hospital. The doctor said to him: 'Look after your health:
wear more clothes when it's cold, and don't overdo the exercise.' Now Grandpa still keeps up his
exercise every day, but he doesn't run any more: every day he walks with the other old people in
the compound."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Health
{我|wǒ}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le}，{还|hái}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{发烧|fā shāo}。
= I've got a cold and a bit of a temperature.
{医生|yī shēng}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{检查|jiǎn chá}{了|le}{一下|yí xià}。
= The doctor examined me.
{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{就|jiù}{累|lèi}。
= Whenever I exercise, I get tired.
{天|tiān}{冷|lěng}{了|le}，{小心|xiǎo xīn}{感冒|gǎn mào}！
= It's getting cold: be careful not to catch a cold!
{别|bié}{担心|dān xīn}，{不用|bú yòng}{住院|zhù yuàn}。
= Don't worry, there's no need to go into hospital.
{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{注意|zhù yì}{身体|shēn tǐ}，{照顾|zhào gù}{好|hǎo}{自己|zì jǐ}。
= Look after your health, and take good care of yourself.
```

Now tell the story of a time you were ill, in four or five sentences: what caused it, what
happened ({发烧|fā shāo}, {看病|kàn bìng}, {检查|jiǎn chá}), and how it ended. Use {一|yī}…{就|jiù} once.

## Pronunciation

- {感冒|gǎn mào}: a dip, then a fall. {健康|jiàn kāng}: a fall, then a high level tone.
- {锻炼|duàn liàn}: two falling tones; let the second one fall all the way.
- {检查|jiǎn chá}: the *j* and *ch* are different: *j* is soft, with the tongue flat; *ch* is
  curled back, with a puff of air.
- {坚持|jiān chí}: high, then rising.
- {住院|zhù yuàn} and {注意|zhù yì} both start with *zhù*.
- {担心|dān xīn}, {小心|xiǎo xīn}: {心|xīn} is level and high. {不用|bú yòng}: {不|bù} rises before the fall.
- {照顾|zhào gù}: two falling tones.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving out {就|jiù}: ~~{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{累|lèi}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{一|yí}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{就|jiù}{累|lèi}.
- {就|jiù} before the subject: ~~{你|nǐ}{一|yì}{说|shuō}，{就|jiù}{我|wǒ}{明白|míng bai}{了|le}~~. {就|jiù} goes right before the verb: {你|nǐ}{一|yì}{说|shuō}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{明白|míng bai}{了|le}.
- {不用|bú yòng} as "don't": ~~{不用|bú yòng}{说话|shuō huà}！~~ for "Don't talk!" Say {别|bié}{说话|shuō huà}！ {不用|bú yòng} is "no need to".
- {担心|dān xīn} with a preposition: ~~{我|wǒ}{担心|dān xīn}{关于|guān yú}{你|nǐ}~~ ({关于|guān yú}, about: lesson 28). {担心|dān xīn} takes its object directly: {我|wǒ}{担心|dān xīn}{你|nǐ}.
- {小心|xiǎo xīn} for "look after": ~~{请|qǐng}{小心|xiǎo xīn}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}~~ (means "watch out for my child!"). Say {请|qǐng}{照顾|zhào gù}{一下|yí xià}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{孩子|hái zi}.
- Time after {住院|zhù yuàn}: ~~{我|wǒ}{住院|zhù yuàn}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}{院|yuàn} or {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{医院|yī yuàn}{住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}.
- {健康|jiàn kāng} with {身体|shēn tǐ} the wrong way round: ~~{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{健康|jiàn kāng}{身体|shēn tǐ}~~. Say {我|wǒ}{身体|shēn tǐ}{很|hěn}{健康|jiàn kāng}.

## Key points

- Illness: {感冒|gǎn mào} (a cold; catch a cold), {发烧|fā shāo} (have a fever), {病人|bìng rén}, {检查|jiǎn chá} (examine; {给|gěi}{他|tā}{检查|jiǎn chá}{一下|yí xià}), {住院|zhù yuàn} /
  {出院|chū yuàn} ({住|zhù}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}{院|yuàn}).
- Fitness: {健康|jiàn kāng} (healthy; health), {锻炼|duàn liàn} ({身体|shēn tǐ}), {坚持|jiān chí} + verb (keep doing).
- {一|yī}…{就|jiù}: as soon as; whenever: {我|wǒ}{一|yí}{到|dào}{家|jiā}{就|jiù}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{了|le}, {我|wǒ}{一|yí}{锻炼|duàn liàn}{就|jiù}{累|lèi}. Each subject before its own verb.
- {小心|xiǎo xīn} (watch out; careful: {小心|xiǎo xīn}{感冒|gǎn mào}, {路上|lù shang}{小心|xiǎo xīn}) vs {注意|zhù yì} (pay attention to: {注意|zhù yì}{身体|shēn tǐ}, {注意|zhù yì}{休息|xiū xi}).
- {不用|bú yòng} + verb: no need ({不用|bú yòng}{担心|dān xīn}, {不用谢|bú yòng xiè}); "don't" is {别|bié} / {不要|bú yào}.
- {担心|dān xīn} + person / thing / clause; {照顾|zhào gù} (look after: {照顾|zhào gù}{好|hǎo}{自己|zì jǐ}).
- {=Sound parts: 建 in 健, {段|duàn} in 锻, 主 in 注 and {住|zhù}, 旦 in 担 and {但|dàn}, 寺 in 持. 心 is now a word: {小心|xiǎo xīn},
  {担心|dān xīn}.=}

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete

lessons.title: Courtyard houses and modern flats
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 took you round a modern {小区|xiǎo qū}, and lesson 02 up to the twelfth floor of a tower block. This
honors lesson goes back to an older way of living: the courtyard house of northern China, and above
all of Beijing, called {四合院|sì hé yuàn}, and the narrow lanes between such houses, the {胡同|hú tòng}.
It follows what happened to them in the 20th century, and ends in a modern flat. The Chinese is
mostly what you know from this module, with a few words glossed.

## The courtyard house: {四合院|sì hé yuàn}

{四合院|sì hé yuàn} is "a courtyard ({院|yuàn}) enclosed ({合|hé}) on four ({四|sì}) sides". Single-storey buildings stand round an
open yard, {院子|yuàn zi}, and the house turns its back to the street: from outside you see walls and
a gate; the windows open onto the courtyard.

The plan follows the compass. A large Beijing courtyard house is usually laid out like this:

| Building | Where | Faces | Traditionally used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| {正房|zhèng fáng} (main house) | north side | south | the oldest generation, the head of the family |
| {厢房|xiāng fáng} (side houses) | east and west sides | the courtyard | the younger generations: married sons, children |
| {倒座房|dào zuò fáng} (the "reverse" row) | south side | north | guests, servants, storage: it gets the least sun |
| the gate | usually the south-east corner | the lane | |

The main house faces south, towards the sun: in Beijing's cold winters it gets the most light and
warmth, which is one reason it belongs to the oldest people in the family. Bigger houses have two or
more courtyards one behind the other; small ones are just a single yard with a few rooms.

In Chinese, with the words of lesson 11 to come ({北边|běi bian} north, {南边|nán bian} south, {东边|dōng bian} east, {西边|xī bian} west):

{四合院|sì hé yuàn}{的|de}{正房|zhèng fáng}{在|zài}{北边|běi bian}，{一般|yì bān}{是|shì}{家|jiā}{里|lǐ}{的|de}{老人|lǎo rén}{住|zhù}。{东边|dōng bian}{和|hé}{西边|xī bian}{的|de}{房子|fáng zi}{叫|jiào}{厢房|xiāng fáng}，{孩子们|hái zi men}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{那儿|nàr}。{院子|yuàn zi}{在|zài}{中间|zhōng jiān}，{夏天|xià tiān}{大家|dà jiā}{在|zài}{院子|yuàn zi}{里|lǐ}{聊天儿|liáo tiānr}，{孩子们|hái zi men}{在|zài}{院子|yuàn zi}{里|lǐ}{玩儿|wánr}。 — In a courtyard house the main house is on the north
side; usually the old people of the family live there. The houses on the east and west sides are
called side houses, and the children live there. The courtyard is in the middle: in summer everyone
chats in the courtyard, and the children play there.

({一般|yì bān}, usually, and {夏天|xià tiān}, summer, are lesson 10's words; {中间|zhōng jiān}, the middle, lesson 11's; {聊天儿|liáo tiānr}, to chat, lesson
22's.)

The basic idea of the courtyard house is very old: early forms go back more than two thousand years.
Most of the courtyard houses still standing in Beijing were built in the Ming (1368–1644) and Qing
(1644–1912) dynasties.

## The lanes between: {胡同|hú tòng}

Rows of courtyard houses, wall to wall, leave narrow lanes between them: these are Beijing's {胡同|hú tòng}.
Many were laid out in the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368), when the city was the Yuan capital, and more
were added in the Ming and Qing. The word itself is often said to come from Mongolian, the language of the
Yuan rulers, perhaps from a word for a well; this is one explanation among several.

A {胡同|hú tòng} is a lane and also the neighbourhood along it: people say {我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{胡同|hú tòng}{里|lǐ} (I live in a hutong
neighbourhood). Many have names that tell their history: the trade once carried on there, a temple,
a well.

{胡同|hú tòng}{里|lǐ}{很|hěn}{安静|ān jìng}，{没有|méi yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{车|chē}，{邻居们|lín jū men}{都|dōu}{认识|rèn shi}。 — It's quiet in the hutong; there aren't many cars, and the
neighbours all know each other.

## The 20th century: from one family to many

A courtyard house was built for one large family. In the 20th century many courtyards came to be
shared by several families, each with a room or two. They
built kitchens and extra rooms into the open yard, until in some courtyards little of the yard was
left. A courtyard like that is called a {大杂院|dà zá yuàn}, a "big mixed courtyard": crowded, often
without private toilets, and very sociable.

From the 1970s and 80s the city built more and more blocks of flats, and in the 1990s large areas
of old houses and lanes were pulled down and replaced by apartment buildings and roads. Some {胡同|hú tòng}
neighbourhoods are now protected, and a few courtyard houses have been restored as homes, hotels or
museums.

This history is why older people in Beijing often say two things at once: life in the courtyard was
hard, {不|bù}{方便|fāng biàn} (cold rooms, no toilet of your own), and it was warm, because
everyone knew everyone.

## Modern flats: {楼房|lóu fáng} and the {小区|xiǎo qū}

Most city families now live in {楼房|lóu fáng}, flats in buildings of several storeys, grouped in
a {小区|xiǎo qū} with a gate, paths and often a {保安|bǎo ān} (security guard) at the entrance. An address
inside a compound is a chain of numbers, big to small:

{阳光小区|Yáng guāng xiǎo qū} 3{号楼|hào lóu} 2{单元|dān yuán} 1201

That's Sunshine Compound, Building 3, entrance (staircase) 2, flat 1201. {单元|dān yuán} is one of
a building's entrances, each with its own stairs and lift, and in the flat number the first digits
are usually the floor: 1201 is flat 01 on the twelfth floor, {十二|shí èr}{层|céng}. The whole address is said *sān hào lóu, èr dānyuán, yāo èr líng yāo*: flat numbers are read digit
by digit, with 1 as *yāo*.

Old houses with one storey are {平房|píng fáng}; people who grew up in a {四合院|sì hé yuàn} often say they "lived
in {平房|píng fáng}" ({住平房|zhù píng fáng}) as children and "moved into a {楼房|lóu fáng}" later.

## Reading: Grandma's old home

> {我|wǒ}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{今年|jīn nián}{八十|bā shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}。{她|tā}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}{的|de}{一|yí}{个|gè}{四合院|sì hé yuàn}{里|lǐ}。{那个|nà ge}{院子|yuàn zi}{不|bú}{大|dà}，{可是|kě shì}{住|zhù}{着|zhe}{五|wǔ}{家人|jiā rén}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{是|shì}{邻居|lín jū}。{奶奶|nǎi nai}{说|shuō}，{那|nà}{时候|shí hou}{院子|yuàn zi}{里|lǐ}{没有|méi yǒu}{卫生间|wèi shēng jiān}，{冬天|dōng tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}，{洗澡|xǐ zǎo}{也|yě}{不|bù}{方便|fāng biàn}。{可是|kě shì}{邻居们|lín jū men}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{热情|rè qíng}，{谁|shéi}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{事|shì}，{大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{来|lái}{帮忙|bāng máng}。{后来|hòu lái}，{奶奶|nǎi nai}{搬|bān}{进|jìn}{了|le}{楼房|lóu fáng}，{现在|xiàn zài}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{十二|shí èr}{层|céng}。{她|tā}{家|jiā}{有|yǒu}{电梯|diàn tī}，{有|yǒu}{空调|kōng tiáo}，{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{洗衣机|xǐ yī jī}，{比|bǐ}{以前|yǐ qián}{方便|fāng biàn}{多了|duō le}。{可是|kě shì}{她|tā}{说|shuō}：“{楼房|lóu fáng}{没有|méi yǒu}{四合院|sì hé yuàn}{那么|nà me}{热闹|rè nao}。{我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{了|le}{十|shí}{年|nián}，{楼里|lóu lǐ}{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{邻居|lín jū}{我|wǒ}{不|bú}{认识|rèn shi}。”

- {住|zhù}{着|zhe}{五|wǔ}{家人|jiā rén} is "five families lived there" (an existential sentence with {着|zhe}: lesson 13).
- {热情|rè qíng} (warm, friendly) is lesson 24's word; {后来|hòu lái} (later) and {以前|yǐ qián} (before) are lesson 25's.
- {热闹|rè nao} (lively, bustling) isn't a course word. {冬天|dōng tiān} (winter) is lesson 10's.

1. How many families lived in Grandma's courtyard?
2. What was inconvenient about life there?
3. Why does she miss it?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Five ({住|zhù}{着|zhe}{五|wǔ}{家人|jiā rén}).
2. There was no bathroom in the courtyard, it was cold in winter, and having a wash was difficult.
3. The neighbours were warm and helped each other; her block of flats isn't as lively ({没有|méi yǒu}{四合院|sì hé yuàn}{那么|nà me}
   {热闹|rè nao}), and after ten years she still doesn't know many of her neighbours.

"My grandma is eighty this year. When she was little she lived in a courtyard house in Beijing. The
courtyard wasn't big, but five families lived there, all neighbours. Grandma says there was no
bathroom in the courtyard then, it was very cold in winter, and having a bath wasn't easy. But the
neighbours were all very friendly: if anyone had a problem, everyone came to help. Later Grandma
moved into a block of flats, and now she lives on the twelfth floor. Her building has a lift, and
she has air conditioning and a washing machine: much more convenient than before. But she says: 'A
block of flats isn't as lively as a courtyard. I've lived here ten years, and there are still lots
of neighbours in the building I don't know.'"
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Old homes and new
{我|wǒ}{小时候|xiǎo shí hou}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{四合院|sì hé yuàn}{里|lǐ}。
= When I was little I lived in a courtyard house.
{正房|zhèng fáng}{在|zài}{北边|běi bian}，{门|mén}{在|zài}{东南边|dōng nán bian}。
= The main house is on the north side and the gate is in the south-east corner.
{胡同|hú tòng}{里|lǐ}{很|hěn}{安静|ān jìng}。
= It's quiet in the hutong.
{现在|xiàn zài}{我|wǒ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{楼房|lóu fáng}{里|lǐ}，{比|bǐ}{以前|yǐ qián}{方便|fāng biàn}{多了|duō le}。
= Now I live in a block of flats; it's much more convenient than before.
{楼房|lóu fáng}{没有|méi yǒu}{四合院|sì hé yuàn}{那么|nà me}{热闹|rè nao}。
= A block of flats isn't as lively as a courtyard.
```

Now describe a home you know, old or new, in three or four sentences: where the rooms are, which
floor it's on, what's convenient about it, and how it compares with another home ({比|bǐ}, {没有|méi yǒu}…{那么|nà me}).

## Key points

- {四合院|sì hé yuàn}: a courtyard house, buildings on four sides of a {院子|yuàn zi}. The {正房|zhèng fáng} on the north side faces
  south (the oldest generation); {厢房|xiāng fáng} on the east and west (the younger ones); the gate usually in
  the south-east corner.
- {胡同|hú tòng}: Beijing's lanes between courtyard houses, many laid out in the Yuan dynasty; the word is
  often said to be Mongolian in origin.
- In the 20th century many courtyards were shared by several families ({大杂院|dà zá yuàn}); from the 1990s large
  areas were rebuilt as flats, and some {胡同|hú tòng} are now protected.
- Modern addresses run big to small: {小区|xiǎo qū}, {号楼|hào lóu}, {单元|dān yuán}, flat number (1201: twelfth floor).
- {平房|píng fáng} (one-storey houses) and {楼房|lóu fáng} (flats in a building).

lessons.title: Paper, printing, the compass and gunpowder
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Ask almost anyone who went to school in China to name China's great inventions, and you'll hear the
same four, in one breath: {四大发明|sì dà fā míng}, "the four great inventions". This honors lesson
explains the four words, what is known about each invention, and the people connected with them,
and gives you a short text to read in Chinese. Dates are given as historians give them: often
"about" or "by", because early inventions leave few records.

## The four words

| Word | Parts | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {造纸术|zào zhǐ shù} | {造|zào} (to make) + {纸|zhǐ} (paper) + {术|shù} (art, technique) | papermaking |
| {印刷术|yìn shuā shù} | {印|yìn} (to print) + {刷|shuā} (to brush) + {术|shù} | printing |
| {指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn} | {指|zhǐ} (to point) + {南|nán} (south) + {针|zhēn} (needle) | the compass |
| {火药|huǒ yào} | {火|huǒ} (fire) + {药|yào} (medicine) | gunpowder |

They're good examples of the **[[word formation]]** of lesson 01: {术|shù} works like a suffix, "the art of":
{造纸术|zào zhǐ shù} is "the art of making paper". The {刷|shuā} of {印刷|yìn shuā} is the brush of lesson 03's {牙刷|yá shuā}: early printers
brushed ink onto a carved block. The Chinese compass "points south", where a European one is
thought of as pointing north. And gunpowder is "fire medicine": as you'll see below, it was found by
people trying to make medicines.

{发明|fā míng} is "to invent; an invention". {=Its {发|fā} is the 發 of the Traditional switch, as in {发烧|fā shāo}.=}

## Paper: {造纸术|zào zhǐ shù}

The name linked with paper is {蔡伦|Cài Lún}, an official at the court of the Eastern Han dynasty.
About 105 CE, the historical records say, he presented the emperor with a way of making sheets of
paper from tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets, and was praised for it.

Archaeologists have since found older pieces of paper in north-western China, the oldest from the
2nd century BCE, so paper itself is older than {蔡伦|Cài Lún}. What he is remembered for is improving the
method and making it the standard one. Papermaking then spread slowly westward: it had reached
Samarkand, in Central Asia, by the 8th century.

## Printing: {印刷术|yìn shuā shù}

The first printing in China was **woodblock printing**: a whole page carved in reverse on a block of
wood, inked, and pressed onto paper. It was well developed by the end of the Tang dynasty. The
oldest complete printed book with a date is a copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text, printed in
868 and found in a cave near {敦煌|Dūn huáng} in north-western China; it's now in the British Library.

In the 1040s {毕昇|Bì Shēng}, a commoner who knew woodblock printing, made **movable type**: one small piece of fired clay
for each character, which could be arranged into a page, printed, and used again. We know about it
because the scholar {沈括|Shěn Kuò} described it in his book 《{梦溪笔谈|Mèng xī Bǐ tán}》 *Mèngxī Bǐtán* (Brush Talks
from Dream Brook). Movable type was used in China for centuries, but woodblocks stayed more common:
a language with thousands of characters needs thousands of pieces of type.

## The compass: {指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn}

A lodestone, a naturally magnetic stone, lines up north and south; nobody knows where or when this
was first noticed. A military book of 1044 describes a magnetised iron "fish" that floats on water and
points south. The first clear description of a compass needle is in {沈括|Shěn Kuò}'s book (the one that
describes movable type), which he wrote late in life, at the end of the 11th century. By about 1100 the compass was being used in
China to find the way.

## Gunpowder: {火药|huǒ yào}

Gunpowder was discovered by Daoist alchemists of the Tang dynasty, probably in the 9th century, who
were mixing saltpetre, sulphur and other substances in search of a medicine for long life. The
mixture burned fiercely. One early written recipe is in a military book of 1044; armies used
gunpowder in fire arrows and other weapons, and the knowledge reached the West in the 13th century.

## Other inventions

The list of four is a convention, not a ranking. Other things China gave the world are just as
famous: silk ({丝绸|sī chóu}), for one, is far older than any of the four. Honors
lesson 15h1 follows silk along the trade routes to the west.

## Reading: the four great inventions

> {很|hěn}{多|duō}{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{知道|zhī dào}“{四大发明|sì dà fā míng}”：{造纸术|zào zhǐ shù}、{印刷术|yìn shuā shù}、{指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn}{和|hé}{火药|huǒ yào}。{很早以前|hěn zǎo yǐ qián}，{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}{就|jiù}{会|huì}{做纸|zuò zhǐ}{了|le}。{一千九百多年|yì qiān jiǔ bǎi duō nián}{以前|yǐ qián}，{蔡伦|Cài Lún}{把|bǎ}{做纸|zuò zhǐ}{的|de}{方法|fāng fǎ}{变|biàn}{得|de}{更|gèng}{好|hǎo}，{用|yòng}{的|de}{东西|dōng xi}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{便宜|pián yi}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{能|néng}{用|yòng}{纸|zhǐ}{写字|xiě zì}{了|le}。{后来|hòu lái}，{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}{发明|fā míng}{了|le}{印刷术|yìn shuā shù}。{宋朝|Sòng cháo}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{毕昇|Bì Shēng}{用|yòng}{泥|ní}{做|zuò}{了|le}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{活字|huó zì}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}{一|yí}{个|gè}，{印|yìn}{书|shū}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{放在一起|fàng zài yì qǐ}，{用|yòng}{完|wán}{了|le}{还|hái}{可以|kě yǐ}{再|zài}{用|yòng}。{指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn}{很|hěn}{有用|yǒu yòng}，{有|yǒu}{了|le}{它|tā}，{在|zài}{海上|hǎi shàng}{也|yě}{不|bú}{会|huì}{走|zǒu}{错|cuò}{方向|fāng xiàng}。{火药|huǒ yào}{是|shì}{做|zuò}{药|yào}{的|de}{人|rén}{发现|fā xiàn}{的|de}，{他们|tā men}{本来|běn lái}{想|xiǎng}{做|zuò}{让|ràng}{人|rén}{长寿|cháng shòu}{的|de}{药|yào}。{这|zhè}{四|sì}{个|gè}{发明|fā míng}{后来|hòu lái}{都|dōu}{传|chuán}{到|dào}{了|le}{世界|shì jiè}{上|shàng}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{地方|dì fang}。

- {很早以前|hěn zǎo yǐ qián} is "very long ago" and {一千九百多年|yì qiān jiǔ bǎi duō nián}{以前|yǐ qián} "over 1,900 years ago" ({以前|yǐ qián}, before: lesson 25).
- {变|biàn}{得|de}{更|gèng}{好|hǎo} is "became better": {变|biàn} (to change) and {更|gèng} (even more) are lessons 10 and 12's.
- {宋朝|Sòng cháo} is the Song dynasty (960–1279). {泥|ní} is clay, and {活字|huó zì}, "living
  characters", is movable type: {一|yí}{个|gè}{字|zì}{一|yí}{个|gè} is "one for each character", and {放在一起|fàng zài yì qǐ} "put together".
- {纸|zhǐ} (paper) is lesson 16's word, {方法|fāng fǎ} (method) lesson 17's and {有用|yǒu yòng} (useful) lesson 09's.
- {方向|fāng xiàng} (direction) is lesson 11's word, {世界|shì jiè} (world) lesson 12's, {发现|fā xiàn} (to discover) lesson 28's.
  {本来|běn lái} (originally), {长寿|cháng shòu} (long life) and {传|chuán} (to pass on, to spread: {传到|chuán dào}, to reach by spreading) aren't course words.

1. Did paper exist before {蔡伦|Cài Lún}, according to the text?
2. What was special about {毕昇|Bì Shēng}'s characters?
3. Who discovered gunpowder, and what were they trying to make?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Yes: {很早以前|hěn zǎo yǐ qián}，{中国|Zhōng guó}{人|rén}{就|jiù}{会|huì}{做纸|zuò zhǐ}{了|le} (the Chinese could make paper very early). {蔡伦|Cài Lún} made the method better
   and the materials cheap, so many people could write on paper.
2. They were movable type made of clay, one for each character, put together to print and used
   again afterwards ({用|yòng}{完|wán}{了|le}{还|hái}{可以|kě yǐ}{再|zài}{用|yòng}).
3. People who made medicines; they were trying to make a medicine for a long life.

"Many Chinese people know 'the four great inventions': papermaking, printing, the compass and
gunpowder. The Chinese could make paper very long ago. Over 1,900 years ago, Cai Lun made the
method of making paper better, and the materials it used were cheap, so many people could write on
paper. Later the Chinese invented printing. In the Song dynasty Bi Sheng made lots of pieces of movable
type out of clay, one for each character; to print a book they were put together, and when he'd
finished with them he could use them again. The compass is very useful: with it, you don't go the wrong way even at sea. Gunpowder
was discovered by people who made medicines: they had wanted to make a medicine for a long life.
All four inventions later reached many places in the world."
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# The four great inventions
{中国|Zhōng guó}{的|de}{四大发明|sì dà fā míng}{是|shì}{造纸术|zào zhǐ shù}、{印刷术|yìn shuā shù}、{指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn}{和|hé}{火药|huǒ yào}。
= China's four great inventions are papermaking, printing, the compass and gunpowder.
{蔡伦|Cài Lún}{把|bǎ}{做纸|zuò zhǐ}{的|de}{方法|fāng fǎ}{变|biàn}{得|de}{更|gèng}{好|hǎo}。
= Cai Lun made the method of making paper better.
{毕昇|Bì Shēng}{发明|fā míng}{了|le}{活字印刷|huó zì yìn shuā}。
= Bi Sheng invented printing with movable type.
{有|yǒu}{了|le}{指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn}，{在|zài}{海上|hǎi shàng}{也|yě}{不|bú}{会|huì}{走|zǒu}{错|cuò}{方向|fāng xiàng}。
= With a compass, you don't go the wrong way even at sea.
```

Now say which of the four you think changed the world most, and give one reason with {因为|yīn wèi}. There's
no right answer.

## Key points

- {四大发明|sì dà fā míng}: {造纸术|zào zhǐ shù} (papermaking), {印刷术|yìn shuā shù} (printing), {指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn} (the compass), {火药|huǒ yào} (gunpowder). {术|shù} is "the art
  of"; {指南针|zhǐ nán zhēn} is a "south-pointing needle"; {火药|huǒ yào} is "fire medicine".
- Paper: older pieces exist from the 2nd century BCE; {蔡伦|Cài Lún} (about 105 CE) improved and standardised
  the method.
- Printing: woodblocks by the end of the Tang (the Diamond Sutra, 868); {毕昇|Bì Shēng}'s clay movable type in
  the 1040s, described by {沈括|Shěn Kuò}.
- Compass: first clearly described by {沈括|Shěn Kuò} in the late 11th century; used at sea by about 1100.
- Gunpowder: found by Daoist alchemists, probably in the 9th century; an early recipe in a book of
  1044.

lessons.title: Sweet, fresh and full: 吃得完, 吃不下
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 2 is about the things you buy and use every day: food, drink, clothes, money and the
weather. It starts with snacks and fruit, and with one of the most useful patterns of HSK 3. You
know result complements from HSK 2: {吃完|chī wán} (finish eating), {看见|kàn jiàn} (see),
{买到|mǎi dào} (manage to buy). Put {得|de} or {不|bù} in the middle and they say whether the result
*can* happen:

- {吃得完|chī de wán} (can finish it) and {吃不完|chī bu wán} (can't finish it);
- {买得到|mǎi de dào} / {买不到|mǎi bu dào} (can / can't get hold of), {看不见|kàn bu jiàn} (can't see);
- {吃不下|chī bu xià} (can't eat any more) and {放不下|fàng bu xià} (won't fit);
- how this {得|de} differs from the {得|de} of {吃|chī}{得|de}{很|hěn}{多|duō} (eats a lot).

You'll also say you're hungry, full or thirsty ({饿|è}, {饱|bǎo}, {渴|kě}), taste things
({尝尝|cháng chang}), talk about fruit and sweet things, buy fruit by the {斤|jīn} (half a kilo)
and order a {外卖|wài mài} (takeaway).

## Hungry, full and thirsty

{饿|è} (hungry), {饱|bǎo} (full) and {渴|kě} (thirsty) are adjectives. Like every adjective
predicate they take no {是|shì}, and they usually come with {很|hěn}, {有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}, {太|tài}…{了|le}
or with {了|le} for a change ("I've got hungry"):

{我|wǒ}{饿|è}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{吧|ba}。 — I'm hungry. Let's eat.

{你|nǐ}{饿|è}{不|bu}{饿|è}？ — Are you hungry?

{我|wǒ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{渴|kě}，{有|yǒu}{水|shuǐ}{吗|ma}？ — I'm a bit thirsty. Is there any water?

{饱|bǎo} is most often a result complement after {吃|chī}: {吃饱|chī bǎo}, to eat until you're full.

{我|wǒ}{吃饱|chī bǎo}{了|le}，{谢谢|xiè xie}！ — I'm full, thank you!

{孩子|hái zi}{没|méi}{吃饱|chī bǎo}，{还|hái}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}。 — The child hasn't had enough and wants more.

{我|wǒ}{吃饱|chī bǎo}{了|le} is what you say at the table when you've had enough, and it's the polite way
to refuse more food. English "I am hungry" doesn't become ~~{我|wǒ}{是|shì}{饿|è}~~: say {我|wǒ}{饿|è}{了|le} or
{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{饿|è}.

## Potential complements: can you finish it?

A **[[potential complement]]** is a result or direction complement with {得|de} or {不|bù} between the
verb and the complement. {得|de} says the result can be reached; {不|bù} says it can't:

| Verb + complement | Meaning | Can | Can't |
|---|---|---|---|
| {吃完|chī wán} | finish eating | {吃得完|chī de wán} | {吃不完|chī bu wán} |
| {看见|kàn jiàn} | see | {看得见|kàn de jiàn} | {看不见|kàn bu jiàn} |
| {听懂|tīng dǒng} | understand (hearing) | {听得懂|tīng de dǒng} | {听不懂|tīng bu dǒng} |
| {买到|mǎi dào} | manage to buy | {买得到|mǎi de dào} | {买不到|mǎi bu dào} |
| {吃饱|chī bǎo} | eat your fill | {吃得饱|chī de bǎo} | {吃不饱|chī bu bǎo} |
| {洗干净|xǐ gān jìng} | wash clean | {洗得干净|xǐ de gān jìng} | {洗不干净|xǐ bu gān jìng} |
| {进去|jìn qù} | go in | {进得去|jìn de qù} | {进不去|jìn bu qù} |
| {搬进去|bān jìn qù} | move in | {搬得进去|bān de jìn qù} | {搬不进去|bān bu jìn qù} |

The {得|de} and the {不|bù} in the middle are light: *chī de wán*, *chī bu wán*. The result itself
keeps its tone.

{这么|zhè me}{大|dà}{的|de}{蛋糕|dàn gāo}，{我们|wǒ men}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}{吃不完|chī bu wán}。 — The two of us can't finish a cake this big.

{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{在|zài}{后面|hòu miàn}，{看不见|kàn bu jiàn}。 — I'm sitting at the back; I can't see.

{他|tā}{说|shuō}{得|de}{太|tài}{快|kuài}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{听不懂|tīng bu dǒng}。 — He talks too fast: I can't understand him.

{这么|zhè me}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{还|hái}{买得到|mǎi de dào}{冰激凌|bīng jī líng}{吗|ma}？ — It's so late: can we still get ice cream?

{门|mén}{太|tài}{小|xiǎo}{了|le}，{沙发|shā fā}{搬不进去|bān bu jìn qù}。 — The door's too small: the sofa won't go in.

The last one uses lesson 02's compound direction complement: {搬进去|bān jìn qù} becomes {搬不进去|bān bu jìn qù}.

**Questions** take {吗|ma}, or put the two forms side by side, as an A-not-A question does:

{你|nǐ}{吃得完|chī de wán}{吗|ma}？ — Can you finish it?

{你|nǐ}{吃得完|chī de wán}{吃不完|chī bu wán}？ — Can you finish it or not?

The answer repeats the form: {吃得完|chī de wán}。 / {吃不完|chī bu wán}。

**The object** goes after the whole verb, or, very often, at the front as the topic (HSK 2's
topic-comment sentence):

{我|wǒ}{吃不完|chī bu wán}{这么|zhè me}{多|duō}{菜|cài}。 / {这么|zhè me}{多|duō}{菜|cài}{我|wǒ}{吃不完|chī bu wán}。 — I can't finish this many dishes.

**Not with 把.** Lesson 03's {把|bǎ} sentence reports what was done to a thing, so it can't take a
potential complement: not ~~{我|wǒ}{把|bǎ}{蛋糕|dàn gāo}{吃不完|chī bu wán}~~, but {蛋糕|dàn gāo}{我|wǒ}{吃不完|chī bu wán}.

### Why not just {能|néng}?

{不能|bù néng} + verb says that something isn't allowed or isn't possible in general. A potential
complement says that the *result* won't come, often because of the amount, the distance, the noise
or your ability:

{医生|yī shēng}{说|shuō}{我|wǒ}{不能|bù néng}{吃|chī}{冰激凌|bīng jī líng}。 — The doctor says I mustn't eat ice cream.

{冰激凌|bīng jī líng}{太|tài}{多|duō}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{吃不完|chī bu wán}。 — There's too much ice cream: I can't finish it.

Chinese speakers use the negative potential much more than the positive one. {吃不完|chī bu wán},
{听不懂|tīng bu dǒng}, {看不见|kàn bu jiàn} and {买不到|mǎi bu dào} are everyday phrases; {吃得完|chī de wán}
and {听得懂|tīng de dǒng} come mostly in questions and answers. You'll also hear {吃不了|chī bu liǎo} ("can't
manage to eat", with {了|liǎo}, a different reading of {了|le}); it means much the same as {吃不完|chī bu wán}.

## {下|xià}: there's no more room

{下|xià} after a verb can mean "down" or "into a space". As a potential complement it says whether
something fits:

{我|wǒ}{吃不下|chī bu xià}{了|le}。 — I can't eat any more. (It won't go down.)

{冰箱|bīng xiāng}{里|lǐ}{放不下|fàng bu xià}{这么|zhè me}{大|dà}{的|de}{西瓜|xī guā}。 — A watermelon this big won't fit in the fridge.

{这|zhè}{个|gè}{房间|fáng jiān}{坐不下|zuò bu xià}{二十|èr shí}{个|gè}{人|rén}。 — This room can't seat twenty people.

{吃不下|chī bu xià} is about room in your stomach, {吃不完|chī bu wán} about the amount on the table. After a
big meal both are true: {菜|cài}{太|tài}{多|duō}{了|le}，{我|wǒ}{吃不完|chī bu wán}，{也|yě}{吃不下|chī bu xià}{了|le}。

## Potential or degree? The two kinds of {得|de}

HSK 2 taught the degree complement: verb + {得|de} + description, {他|tā}{吃|chī}{得|de}{很|hěn}{多|duō} (he
eats a lot). Both patterns have {得|de} after the verb, so look at what follows it:

| | Degree: how it's done | Potential: can it be done? |
|---|---|---|
| After {得|de} | a description, usually with {很|hěn}, {太|tài}, {非常|fēi cháng} | the result word straight away ({完|wán}, {到|dào}, {懂|dǒng}, {下|xià}, {进去|jìn qù}) |
| Example | {他|tā}{吃|chī}{得|de}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 He eats a lot. | {他|tā}{吃得完|chī de wán}。 He can finish it. |
| Negative | {不|bù} after {得|de}: {他|tā}{吃|chī}{得|de}{不|bù}{多|duō}。 He doesn't eat much. | {不|bù} replaces {得|de}: {他|tā}{吃不完|chī bu wán}。 He can't finish it. |
| Question | {他|tā}{吃|chī}{得|de}{多|duō}{不|bu}{多|duō}？ | {他|tā}{吃得完|chī de wán}{吃不完|chī bu wán}？ |

So a negative with {不|bù} *right after the verb* and no {得|de} is a potential complement. A {不|bù} after
{得|de} is a degree complement.

{她|tā}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{清楚|qīng chu}，{我|wǒ}{听得懂|tīng de dǒng}。 — She speaks clearly, and I can understand her.

That sentence has both: {说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{清楚|qīng chu} is how she speaks ({清楚|qīng chu}: clear, lesson 18), and
{听得懂|tīng de dǒng} is what you can do.

## Tasting: {尝|cháng} and {尝尝|cháng chang}

{尝|cháng} is "to taste", to try a little to see what it's like. Like other short actions it's
often doubled (HSK 2's verb reduplication), which makes an invitation sound friendly:

{你|nǐ}{尝尝|cháng chang}，{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}！ — Have a taste. It's really good!

{我|wǒ}{可以|kě yǐ}{尝|cháng}{一|yi}{尝|cháng}{吗|ma}？ — May I try a little?

{你|nǐ}{尝|cháng}{一下|yí xià}{这|zhè}{个|gè}{西瓜|xī guā}，{甜|tián}{不|bu}{甜|tián}？ — Try this watermelon. Is it sweet?

The second {尝|cháng} in {尝尝|cháng chang} is light. {尝|cháng} sounds like {常|cháng} (often) and {长|cháng} (long); {唱|chàng}
(to sing) falls.

## Fruit and sweet things

| Word | Meaning | Note |
|---|---|---|
| {西瓜|xī guā} | watermelon | "western melon" |
| {香蕉|xiāng jiāo} | banana | {香|xiāng} means fragrant |
| {苹果|píng guǒ} | apple | HSK 1 |
| {蛋糕|dàn gāo} | cake | {蛋|dàn} egg + {糕|gāo} cake |
| {冰激凌|bīng jī líng} | ice cream | also {冰淇淋|bīng qí lín} |
| {糖|táng} | sugar; sweets | {一|yí}{块|kuài}{糖|táng}, a sweet |
| {方便面|fāng biàn miàn} | instant noodles | "convenient noodles" |

{甜|tián} (sweet) and {新鲜|xīn xiān} (fresh) describe them:

{这些|zhè xiē}{西瓜|xī guā}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{甜|tián}。 — These watermelons are all sweet.

{这|zhè}{个|gè}{蛋糕|dàn gāo}{太|tài}{甜|tián}{了|le}。 — This cake is too sweet.

{这里|zhè lǐ}{的|de}{水果|shuǐ guǒ}{很|hěn}{新鲜|xīn xiān}。 — The fruit here is very fresh.

{香蕉|xiāng jiāo}{不|bù}{新鲜|xīn xiān}{了|le}，{别|bié}{买|mǎi}{了|le}。 — The bananas aren't fresh any more: don't buy them.

{糖|táng} is sugar, and also a sweet or a piece of candy. {吃|chī}{糖|táng} (eat sweets) is something children
love and parents count: {别|bié}{吃|chī}{太|tài}{多|duō}{糖|táng}！

{冰激凌|bīng jī líng} is "ice" + {激凌|jī líng}, which is usually explained as a borrowing of the sound of
"cream". Both {冰激凌|bīng jī líng} and {冰淇淋|bīng qí lín} are common; the first is the one you'll see in
HSK 3. {方便面|fāng biàn miàn} is the food students and travellers live on: lesson 02's {方便|fāng biàn}
(convenient) + noodles, as in {面条儿|miàn tiáor}.

## Buying by the {斤|jīn}

At a market, fruit and vegetables are sold by the {斤|jīn}. A {斤|jīn} is half a kilo, 500 grams, in
mainland China (in Taiwan and Hong Kong the traditional {斤|jīn} is heavier, about 600 grams).
{斤|jīn} is a measure word, so the number comes straight before it, with {两|liǎng} for two:

{苹果|píng guǒ}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}{一|yì}{斤|jīn}？ — How much is a jin of apples?

{五|wǔ}{块|kuài}{钱|qián}{一|yì}{斤|jīn}。 / {一|yì}{斤|jīn}{五|wǔ}{块|kuài}。 — Five kuai a jin.

{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{两|liǎng}{斤|jīn}{香蕉|xiāng jiāo}。 — I'd like two jin (a kilo) of bananas.

{半|bàn}{斤|jīn} is 250 grams. The kilogram, {公斤|gōng jīn}, is lesson 07's word: supermarket labels and
scales often use it, and people translate between the two all the time.

## Takeaway: {外卖|wài mài}

{外卖|wài mài} is food sent out from a restaurant: takeaway, and above all food delivered to your
door, ordered on a phone app. The verbs that go with it:

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {点|diǎn}{外卖|wài mài} / {叫|jiào}{外卖|wài mài} | order a takeaway |
| {送|sòng}{外卖|wài mài} | deliver takeaways |
| {外卖|wài mài}{到|dào}{了|le} | the takeaway's here |
| {外卖员|wài mài yuán} | delivery rider (lesson 01's suffix {员|yuán}) |

{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{做饭|zuò fàn}，{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{外卖|wài mài}{吧|ba}。 — I don't feel like cooking today. Let's order a takeaway.

{这么|zhè me}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{还|hái}{叫得到|jiào de dào}{外卖|wài mài}{吗|ma}？ — It's so late: can we still get a delivery?

Food delivery is a big part of city life in China, and riders in company jackets are a
common sight on every street.

### Sound parts

Most of these characters are a meaning part plus a sound part, and several sound parts are
characters you know:

| Sound part | Characters | Note |
|---|---|---|

| {包|bāo} (wrap; bag) | 饱 *bǎo*, 跑 *pǎo* (HSK 2: run) | 饱 is food 饣 + 包: a "wrapped-up" stomach is a memory aid, not history |
| 曷 (an old word, *hé*) | 喝 *hē* (drink), 渴 *kě* (thirsty) | mouth 口 for drinking, water 氵 for thirst |
| 唐 *táng* (the Tang dynasty) | 糖 *táng* | rice 米 + 唐: an exact sound match |
| 羔 *gāo* (lamb) | 糕 *gāo* | rice 米 + 羔: cakes were made of rice flour |
| 焦 *jiāo* (scorched) | 蕉 *jiāo* | grass 艹 + 焦 |
| 夌 *líng* | 凌 *líng* | ice 冫 + 夌 |

The others are built from meanings:

- **甜** is 舌 (tongue) + 甘 (sweet): what the tongue finds sweet. 甘 is the radical.
- **香** has 禾 (grain) on top; the bottom was once 甘 (sweet) and is written 日 today.
- **瓜** is a drawing: a melon hanging between the lines of its vine.
- **斤** began as a drawing of an axe; it became a weight later. It's also the sound part of {近|jìn}
  (near, HSK 2).
- **鲜** is fish 鱼 + sheep 羊. The character first named a kind of fish; "fresh like fish and lamb"
  is a good memory aid, not its history.

### Stroke order

- **饣**: three strokes, the left-falling stroke, the short turning stroke, then the vertical that
  flicks up to the right. Write it first in 饺, 饿 and 饱.
- **瓜**: the short left-falling stroke on top, then the long left-falling stroke down the left side,
  the vertical inside that turns up to the right, the dot, and the long right-falling stroke last.
- **斤**: two left-falling strokes, then the horizontal, then the vertical.
- **甜**: 舌 first (left-falling stroke, horizontal, vertical, 口), then 甘 (horizontal, two verticals,
  the short horizontal inside, the bottom horizontal).
- **鲜**: 鱼 on the left, its last horizontal written as a rising stroke; then 羊, whose long vertical
  comes last.

## Dialogue: at the fruit stall

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) buys fruit at a market stall. She calls the stallholder {叔叔|shū shu} (叔叔), the
friendly "uncle" of lesson 01.

```dialogue
# At the fruit stall
安娜: {叔叔|shū shu}，{西瓜|xī guā}{多少|duō shao}{钱|qián}{一|yì}{斤|jīn}？
= Excuse me, how much is the watermelon a jin?
叔叔: {两|liǎng}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ}{一|yì}{斤|jīn}。{今天|jīn tiān}{的|de}{西瓜|xī guā}{很|hěn}{新鲜|xīn xiān}，{你|nǐ}{尝尝|cháng chang}！
= Two fifty a jin. Today's watermelons are really fresh. Have a taste!
安娜: {真|zhēn}{甜|tián}！{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{一|yí}{个|gè}。
= So sweet! I'll take one.
叔叔: {这|zhè}{个|gè}{大|dà}{的|de}{怎么样|zěn me yàng}？{十四|shí sì}{斤|jīn}。
= How about this big one? Fourteen jin.
安娜: {太|tài}{大|dà}{了|le}！{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{吃不完|chī bu wán}，{冰箱|bīng xiāng}{里|lǐ}{也|yě}{放不下|fàng bu xià}。
= Too big! I can't finish that on my own, and it won't fit in the fridge either.
叔叔: {那|nà}{你|nǐ}{买|mǎi}{半|bàn}{个|gè}{吧|ba}。{半|bàn}{个|gè}{七|qī}{斤|jīn}，{十七|shí qī}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ}。
= Then buy half. Half is seven jin: seventeen fifty.
安娜: {好|hǎo}。{香蕉|xiāng jiāo}{怎么|zěn me}{卖|mài}？
= OK. How much are the bananas?
叔叔: {三|sān}{块|kuài}{一|yì}{斤|jīn}。
= Three kuai a jin.
安娜: {我|wǒ}{要|yào}{两|liǎng}{斤|jīn}。{一|yí}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}{吃得完|chī de wán}。
= I'll have two jin. I can finish them in a week.
叔叔: {西瓜|xī guā}{十七|shí qī}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ}，{香蕉|xiāng jiāo}{六|liù}{块|kuài}，{二十三|èr shí sān}{块|kuài}{五|wǔ}。
= Watermelon seventeen fifty, bananas six: twenty-three fifty.
```
