## Pronunciation

- {春天|chūn tiān}: *ch* + *un* (short for *uen*), level, and {天|tiān} level. {秋天|qiū tiān}: *q* + *iu*, level.
- {夏天|xià tiān}: a strong fall, then level. {冬天|dōng tiān}: two level tones.
- {季节|jì jié}: 4 + 2. {季|jì} sounds like {记|jì} (remember, lesson 18).
- {风|fēng}: *f* + *eng*, level. Don't let it become *fōng*.
- {凉快|liáng kuai}, {太阳|tài yang}, {月亮|yuè liang}: the second syllable is light in all three.
- {伞|sǎn}: *s* + *an*, dipping. {三|sān} (three) is level.
- {一般|yì bān}: {一|yì} falls before a first tone. {一半|yí bàn} (half) rises before a fourth tone.
- {突然|tū rán}: *t* with a puff of air, level, then a rising *rán*, with the Chinese *r* (tongue curled,
  close to the *s* in "pleasure").

## Common mistakes

- ~~{今天|jīn tiān}{比|bǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{很|hěn}{冷|lěng}~~: no {很|hěn} in a {比|bǐ} sentence. {今天|jīn tiān}{比|bǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{冷|lěng}, or {冷|lěng}{一点儿|yì diǎnr} / {冷|lěng}{多|duō}{了|le}.
- ~~{今天|jīn tiān}{比|bǐ}{昨天|zuó tiān}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{冷|lěng}~~: the amount comes after the adjective: {冷|lěng}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}.
- ~~{风|fēng}{刮|guā}{很|hěn}{大|dà}~~: "it's windy" is {风|fēng}{很|hěn}{大|dà} or {刮|guā}{大|dà}{风|fēng}.
- ~~{天气|tiān qì}{换|huàn}{了|le}~~: the weather {变|biàn}; {换|huàn} is swapping one thing for another.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{一般|yì bān}{的|de}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{起床|qǐ chuáng}~~: as an adverb, {一般|yì bān} goes straight before the verb phrase.
- {=Writing {冬|dōng} without its two dots, or {伞|sǎn} with only one of its two short strokes: both have two.=}

## Key points

- {春天|chūn tiān}, {夏天|xià tiān}, {秋天|qiū tiān}, {冬天|dōng tiān}; {季节|jì jié} (season), {季|jì} (in words), {四季|sì jì}, {一年四季|yì nián sì jì} (all year round).
- {刮风|guā fēng} / {刮|guā}{大|dà}{风|fēng}, {风|fēng}{很|hěn}{大|dà}; {冰|bīng}; {凉快|liáng kuai} (pleasantly cool); {出|chū}{太阳|tài yang}{了|le}; {月亮|yuè liang}; {一|yì}{把|bǎ}{伞|sǎn}, {带|dài}{伞|sǎn}.
- Weather scenes with {着|zhe}: {外面|wài miàn}{下|xià}{着|zhe}{雨|yǔ}, {刮|guā}{着|zhe}{大|dà}{风|fēng}.
- {变|biàn} + adj. + {了|le} ({变|biàn}{冷|lěng}{了|le}); {变化|biàn huà} (change, noun and verb); {突然|tū rán} (suddenly).
- {一般|yì bān}: usually ({我|wǒ}{一般|yì bān}…); ordinary ({很|hěn}{一般|yì bān}: nothing special).
- Comparison of degree: {比|bǐ}…{一点儿|yì diǎnr} / {多|duō}{了|le} / {得|de}{多|duō} / + amount; {比|bǐ}…{更|gèng}; {没有|méi yǒu}…{那么|nà me}; {跟|gēn}…{一样|yí yàng}. No {很|hěn} with {比|bǐ}.
- {越来越|yuè lái yuè} + adj.: more and more (lesson 12).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: The 24 solar terms: 二十四节气
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 10 gave you the four seasons. The traditional Chinese year divides them much more finely,
into twenty-four "solar terms" of about fifteen days each, with names like "Start of Spring",
"Grain Rain" and "Frost's Descent". You met them in passing in HSK 1's calendar lesson. This honors
lesson explains what they are, gives all twenty-four names with a rhyme for remembering them, and
looks at two of them that are also festivals, {清明|qīng míng} and {冬至|dōng zhì}, and the foods that go with them.
New words are glossed; they aren't added to your reviews.

## The sun's calendar

The solar terms are {二十四节气|èr shí sì jié qì}. {节气|jié qì} is lesson 10's {节|jié} (section) + {气|qì} (air,
weather): a section of the year's weather.

They follow the sun, not the moon. Over a year the sun seems to travel once round the sky, 360
degrees, against the stars. Divide that path into twenty-four equal parts of 15 degrees and you get
the solar terms: the sun takes about fifteen days to cross each one (a little less around January, when
the earth is nearest the sun, and a little more around July). Because they're
tied to the sun, the terms fall on almost the same Western date every year, give or take a day.
{立春|lì chūn}, "Start of Spring", is around 4 February, and {冬至|dōng zhì}, the winter solstice, around 22 December.

That makes them different from the festivals of the lunar calendar ({农历|nóng lì}, HSK 1), such as
the Spring Festival and the Mid-Autumn Festival, whose Western dates move from year to year. The
traditional calendar keeps both: the moon for the months, the solar terms for the seasons.

The system grew out of observations of the seasons in the Yellow River valley. The solstices and
equinoxes came first; all twenty-four terms were part of the official calendar by 104 BCE, under
the Han dynasty. For farmers they were a timetable: when to plough, sow and harvest. Many still use
them, and weather forecasts and calendars in China mark each one.

## The twenty-four names

| | Term | Meaning | Around |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | {立春|lì chūn} | Start of Spring | 4 Feb |
| 2 | {雨水|yǔ shuǐ} | Rain Water | 19 Feb |
| 3 | {惊蛰|jīng zhé} | Insects Awaken | 6 Mar |
| 4 | {春分|chūn fēn} | Spring Equinox | 21 Mar |
| 5 | {清明|qīng míng} | Clear and Bright | 5 Apr |
| 6 | {谷雨|gǔ yǔ} | Grain Rain | 20 Apr |
| 7 | {立夏|lì xià} | Start of Summer | 6 May |
| 8 | {小满|xiǎo mǎn} | Grain Fills a Little | 21 May |
| 9 | {芒种|máng zhòng} | Grain in Ear | 6 Jun |
| 10 | {夏至|xià zhì} | Summer Solstice | 21 Jun |
| 11 | {小暑|xiǎo shǔ} | Lesser Heat | 7 Jul |
| 12 | {大暑|dà shǔ} | Greater Heat | 23 Jul |
| 13 | {立秋|lì qiū} | Start of Autumn | 8 Aug |
| 14 | {处暑|chǔ shǔ} | End of Heat | 23 Aug |
| 15 | {白露|bái lù} | White Dew | 8 Sep |
| 16 | {秋分|qiū fēn} | Autumn Equinox | 23 Sep |
| 17 | {寒露|hán lù} | Cold Dew | 8 Oct |
| 18 | {霜降|shuāng jiàng} | Frost's Descent | 23 Oct |
| 19 | {立冬|lì dōng} | Start of Winter | 7 Nov |
| 20 | {小雪|xiǎo xuě} | Lesser Snow | 22 Nov |
| 21 | {大雪|dà xuě} | Greater Snow | 7 Dec |
| 22 | {冬至|dōng zhì} | Winter Solstice | 22 Dec |
| 23 | {小寒|xiǎo hán} | Lesser Cold | 6 Jan |
| 24 | {大寒|dà hán} | Greater Cold | 20 Jan |

The names follow a few patterns you can read with what you know:

- {立|lì} (to stand, to set up) + a season: the start of that season. {立春|lì chūn}, {立夏|lì xià}, {立秋|lì qiū}, {立冬|lì dōng}.
- {分|fēn} (to divide) after spring or autumn: the equinoxes, when day and night are divided equally.
- {至|zhì} (to arrive, the furthest point) after summer or winter: the solstices, the longest and the
  shortest day.
- {小|xiǎo} and {大|dà}: lesser and greater heat, snow and cold.
- The rest are about weather and farming: rain ({雨|yǔ}), dew ({露|lù}), frost ({霜|shuāng}), heat ({暑|shǔ}), cold
  ({寒|hán}), grain (in {谷雨|gǔ yǔ}), and in {惊蛰|jīng zhé}, insects "startled" awake by spring thunder.

{清明|qīng míng} uses HSK 1's {明|míng} (bright) and lesson 18's {清|qīng} (clear). In {处暑|chǔ shǔ}, {处|chǔ} is read *chǔ*, not the
*chù* of {到处|dào chù} (everywhere, lesson 14).

## A rhyme for remembering them

Children in China learn the terms with a rhyme, the {节气歌|jié qì gē} ("solar terms song"). Each line is
one season, and almost every syllable stands for one term in order:

> {春雨惊春清谷天|chūn yǔ jīng chūn qīng gǔ tiān}，
>
> {夏满芒夏暑相连|xià mǎn máng xià shǔ xiāng lián}，
>
> {秋处露秋寒霜降|qiū chǔ lù qiū hán shuāng jiàng}，
>
> {冬雪雪冬小大寒|dōng xuě xuě dōng xiǎo dà hán}。

| Line | Terms, in order |
|---|---|
| spring | {立春|lì chūn}, {雨水|yǔ shuǐ}, {惊蛰|jīng zhé}, {春分|chūn fēn}, {清明|qīng míng}, {谷雨|gǔ yǔ}; the last syllable, {天|tiān}, just completes the line |
| summer | {立夏|lì xià}, {小满|xiǎo mǎn}, {芒种|máng zhòng}, {夏至|xià zhì}, then {小暑|xiǎo shǔ} and {大暑|dà shǔ} in one syllable and {相连|xiāng lián}, "following each other" |
| autumn | {立秋|lì qiū}, {处暑|chǔ shǔ}, {白露|bái lù}, {秋分|qiū fēn}, {寒露|hán lù}, {霜降|shuāng jiàng} |
| winter | {立冬|lì dōng}, {小雪|xiǎo xuě}, {大雪|dà xuě}, {冬至|dōng zhì}, {小寒|xiǎo hán}, {大寒|dà hán} |

The rhyme is a traditional folk verse; versions with more lines add the dates.

## {清明|qīng míng}: a term and a festival

{清明|qīng míng}, around 5 April, is also a festival, {清明节|qīng míng jié}, and the only solar term that is a public holiday:
it has been one in mainland China since 2008. Families go to the graves of their relatives
to clean them and leave offerings: {扫墓|sǎo mù}, "sweeping the tomb" (lesson 03's {扫|sǎo}). It's also a day
for going out into the spring countryside, {踏青|tà qīng} ("treading the green"), and for flying kites
({放风筝|fàng fēng zheng}). The food most linked with it is {青团|qīng tuán}: sticky rice balls, green from the juice
of a spring plant, filled with sweet bean paste.

{清明|qīng míng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{人|rén}{回|huí}{老家|lǎo jiā}{扫墓|sǎo mù}。 — At Qingming many people go back to their home town to sweep their
family's graves. ({老家|lǎo jiā}: home town)

## {冬至|dōng zhì}: the shortest day

{冬至|dōng zhì} is the day with the shortest daylight of the year, and for a long time it was one of the
year's great feasts: an old saying puts it on a level with New Year. What people eat on the day
often depends on the region, as a broad tendency:

- In the **north** the custom is {饺子|jiǎo zi}. Folk tradition says that eating dumplings at the winter
  solstice keeps your ears from freezing.
- In the **south** many families eat {汤圆|tāng yuán}, little balls of sticky rice flour, often filled and
  served in a sweet soup.

{冬至|dōng zhì}{北方|běi fāng}{人|rén}{一般|yì bān}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{南方|nán fāng}{人|rén}{一般|yì bān}{吃|chī}{汤圆|tāng yuán}。 — At the winter solstice northerners usually eat
dumplings, and southerners usually eat tangyuan. ({北方|běi fāng}, {南方|nán fāng}: the north, the south: lesson 12)

Other terms have their own local customs too. The Zhuang people of southern China, for example,
hold a festival at {霜降|shuāng jiàng}, Frost's Descent, to give thanks for the rice harvest.

## On the UNESCO list

In 2016 the solar terms were inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural
Heritage of Humanity, under the name "The Twenty-Four Solar Terms, knowledge in China of time and
practices developed through observation of the sun's annual motion". The listing describes them as
shared by many ethnic groups in China and still important to farmers, passed on through rhymes,
proverbs and festivals.

## Reading: the shortest day

> {今天|jīn tiān}{是|shì}{冬至|dōng zhì}，{一|yì}{年|nián}{里|lǐ}{白天|bái tiān}{最|zuì}{短|duǎn}{的|de}{一|yì}{天|tiān}。{下午|xià wǔ}{四|sì}{点|diǎn}{多|duō}，{太阳|tài yang}{就|jiù}{下山|xià shān}{了|le}，{外面|wài miàn}{刮|guā}{着|zhe}{大|dà}{风|fēng}，{非常|fēi cháng}{冷|lěng}。{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{北京|Běi jīng}，{冬至|dōng zhì}{我们|wǒ men}{家|jiā}{一般|yì bān}{吃|chī}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。{晚上|wǎn shang}{妈妈|mā ma}{包|bāo}{了|le}{好多|hǎo duō}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{我|wǒ}{吃|chī}{了|le}{二十|èr shí}{个|gè}，{吃饱|chī bǎo}{了|le}。{妈妈|mā ma}{笑|xiào}{着|zhe}{说|shuō}：“{今天|jīn tiān}{吃|chī}{了|le}{饺子|jiǎo zi}，{冬天|dōng tiān}{耳朵|ěr duo}{就|jiù}{不|bù}{冷|lěng}{了|le}！”{我|wǒ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{是|shì}{广州|Guǎng zhōu}{人|rén}，{她|tā}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{发|fā}{了|le}{一|yì}{张|zhāng}{照片|zhào piàn}：{她|tā}{家|jiā}{今天|jīn tiān}{吃|chī}{汤圆|tāng yuán}，{甜甜|tián tián}{的|de}，{很|hěn}{好吃|hǎo chī}。{从|cóng}{明天|míng tiān}{起|qǐ}，{白天|bái tiān}{就|jiù}{会|huì}{越来越|yuè lái yuè}{长|cháng}{了|le}。

{下山|xià shān} is "to go down behind the hills": to set. {包|bāo}{饺子|jiǎo zi} is "to make (wrap) dumplings", and {照片|zhào piàn}
(photo) is lesson 14's word.

1. What is special about today?
2. What did the family eat, and why did the mother laugh?
3. What did the classmate in Guangzhou eat?
4. What happens from tomorrow?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. It's the winter solstice, the day with the shortest daylight of the year.
2. Dumplings, which the mother made; she joked that after eating dumplings at the solstice your ears
   won't get cold all winter.
3. Tangyuan, sweet and delicious ({甜甜|tián tián}{的|de}).
4. The days start getting longer and longer ({白天|bái tiān}{就|jiù}{会|huì}{越来越|yuè lái yuè}{长|cháng}{了|le}).

"Today is the winter solstice, the day with the shortest daylight of the year. The sun set before
five in the afternoon, and outside a strong wind was blowing: it was freezing. My family
lives in Beijing, and at the winter solstice we usually eat dumplings. In the evening Mum made lots
of dumplings; I ate twenty and was full. Mum laughed and said, 'You've had your dumplings today, so
your ears won't get cold this winter!' My classmate is from Guangzhou, and she sent me a photo:
her family had tangyuan today, nice and sweet. From tomorrow on, the days will get longer and
longer."
</details>

## Key points

- {二十四节气|èr shí sì jié qì}: the sun's path divided into 24 parts of 15 degrees, about fifteen days each, on
  nearly fixed Western dates; a farming calendar, complete by 104 BCE.
- Patterns: {立|lì} + season (start), {春分|chūn fēn} / {秋分|qiū fēn} (equinoxes), {夏至|xià zhì} / {冬至|dōng zhì} (solstices), {小|xiǎo} / {大|dà} + heat,
  snow, cold.
- The rhyme: {春雨惊春清谷天|chūn yǔ jīng chūn qīng gǔ tiān}… one syllable per term.
- {清明|qīng míng} (about 5 April): tomb sweeping, spring outings, kites, {青团|qīng tuán}; a public holiday since 2008.
- {冬至|dōng zhì} (about 22 December): {饺子|jiǎo zi} in the north, {汤圆|tāng yuán} in the south, as a tendency.
- On UNESCO's Representative List since 2016.

lessons.title: Regional food and customs: noodles, dim sum, hot pot
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

HSK 1 contrasted northern wheat and southern rice, and HSK 2's cuisines lesson introduced the
regional styles ({川菜|chuān cài}, {粤菜|yuè cài} and the others) and the custom of sharing dishes. This honors
lesson looks closely at four regional foods that people across China talk about, and at the
customs around them: Lanzhou beef noodles, the noodles of Shanxi, dim sum in Guangdong, and hot
pot in Chongqing, Sichuan and Beijing. Everything here is a tendency, not a rule: every city has
all kinds of food, and every family its own habits. New words are glossed and aren't added to your
reviews.

## Lanzhou beef noodles: {兰州牛肉面|Lán zhōu niú ròu miàn}

{兰州|Lán zhōu}, in the north-west, is the capital of Gansu province, and its best-known dish is a bowl of
beef noodle soup. The noodles are {拉面|lā miàn}, "pulled noodles": the cook stretches a piece of dough
between the hands, folds it and stretches it again until it's a bundle of thin strands, then drops
them into the boiling water. Across China the shops are often just called {兰州拉面|Lán zhōu lā miàn}. In
2021 the craft of making them was added to China's national list of intangible cultural heritage.

A good bowl is described with a five-colour formula, {一清二白三红四绿五黄|yī qīng èr bái sān hóng sì lǜ wǔ huáng}:

| | Colour | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| {一|yī}{清|qīng} | clear | the soup, a clear beef broth |
| {二|èr}{白|bái} | white | slices of white radish |
| {三|sān}{红|hóng} | red | chilli oil |
| {四|sì}{绿|lǜ} | green | coriander and garlic shoots |
| {五|wǔ}{黄|huáng} | yellow | the noodles, a pale yellow |

When you order, you say how thick you want the noodles. The names include {毛细|máo xì} ("thin as a
hair": lesson 09's {毛|máo} + {细|xì}, thin), then {一细|yī xì}, {二细|èr xì} and {三细|sān xì} (round noodles, each a little thicker),
and the flat {韭叶|jiǔ yè} ("chive leaf") and {小宽|xiǎo kuān} ("a little wide").

{老板|lǎo bǎn}，{一|yì}{碗|wǎn}{牛肉面|niú ròu miàn}，{要|yào}{二细|èr xì}{的|de}，{多|duō}{加|jiā}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{辣|là}。 — A bowl of beef noodles, please: medium-thin, with a bit
more chilli. ({老板|lǎo bǎn}: boss, the owner; {辣|là}: chilli, spicy)

Local records credit a Hui man named {马保子|Mǎ Bǎo zi} with creating the dish as it's known today: he
sold it in the streets and opened his own shop in 1915. A poem from around 1800 suggests beef
noodles were known in Lanzhou even before that. Many people in Lanzhou start the day with a bowl, and some
go early in the morning to get the first, freshest broth.

## Shanxi: the home of noodles

{山西|Shān xī}, in the north, west of Beijing, is often called China's "home of noodles", with hundreds of
kinds. The most famous is {刀削面|dāo xiāo miàn}, "knife-shaved noodles". The cook holds a big block of
dough on one arm or shoulder and, with a curved blade, shaves strip after strip straight into the
pot of boiling water, each one landing "like a leaf". The noodles come out thick in the middle and
thin at the edges, chewy and good with a meat sauce. A few drops of {醋|cù} (vinegar) finish the bowl:
Shanxi is also known for its aged vinegar, {老陈醋|lǎo chén cù}.

{山西|Shān xī}{人|rén}{吃|chī}{面条|miàn tiáo}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{一般|yì bān}{要|yào}{加|jiā}{醋|cù}。 — People in Shanxi usually add vinegar when they eat noodles.

## Guangdong: morning tea and dim sum

You met {点心|diǎn xin} (dim sum) and {喝|hē}{早茶|zǎo chá} ("drinking morning tea") in HSK 2. In Guangdong and Hong
Kong, families and old friends meet in a teahouse in the morning, sometimes for hours. The tea comes
first; then small dishes in bamboo steamers, three or four pieces in each, shared by everyone. A few
classics:

| Dish | What it is |
|---|---|
| {虾饺|xiā jiǎo} | shrimp dumplings in a thin, almost clear wrapper: this module's {饺|jiǎo} |
| {烧卖|shāo mài} | open-topped dumplings of pork and shrimp |
| {叉烧包|chā shāo bāo} | soft steamed buns filled with sweet roast pork ({包子|bāo zi}: HSK 1) |

Because there are so many small dishes, the table can order a lot: {点心|diǎn xin}{个个|gè gè}{都|dōu}{很|hěn}{小|xiǎo}，{但是|dàn shì}{点|diǎn}{了|le}{好多|hǎo duō}，
{最后|zuì hòu}{总是|zǒng shì}{吃不完|chī bu wán} (each dish is small, but you order loads and never finish them all; {最后|zuì hòu}: in
the end, {总是|zǒng shì}: always). HSK 1's tea lesson
mentioned tapping the table with your fingers to thank someone who pours your tea: you'll see it
here.

## Hot pot: {火锅|huǒ guō}

{火锅|huǒ guō} ("fire pot") is a pot of broth kept simmering on the table. Everyone puts in raw meat,
vegetables and tofu, cooks them, fishes them out and dips them in a sauce. It's eaten all year,
but above all on cold evenings with friends.

**Chongqing and Sichuan.** Chongqing is often called the capital of hot pot. Its broth is {麻辣|má là},
numbing and hot (HSK 2: chilli for the heat, Sichuan pepper for the tingle), cooked with beef fat,
and {毛肚|máo dǔ} (beef tripe) is a classic thing to cook in it. One popular story says it began with
boatmen on the Yangtze who cooked whatever they had in a spicy broth on the riverbank; there are
several other stories, and nobody knows for sure. For a mixed group there's the {鸳鸯锅|yuān yang guō}, a pot
divided down the middle, spicy on one side and mild on the other. ({鸳鸯|yuān yang} are mandarin ducks,
which swim in pairs.)

**Beijing.** Old Beijing's hot pot is {涮羊肉|shuàn yáng ròu}, "dip-boiled mutton": paper-thin slices of
mutton swished for a few seconds in a clear broth in a copper pot ({铜锅|tóng guō}), then dipped in sesame
sauce ({麻酱|má jiàng}). It's much milder than Chongqing's.

{我|wǒ}{吃不了|chī bu liǎo}{太|tài}{辣|là}{的|de}，{我们|wǒ men}{点|diǎn}{一|yí}{个|gè}{鸳鸯锅|yuān yang guō}{吧|ba}。 — I can't handle very spicy food: let's order a
split pot. ({吃不了|chī bu liǎo}: lesson 06's "can't manage to eat")

## Dumplings by weight

Dumplings are the north's best-known food at New Year (HSK 1) and at the winter solstice (the
previous honors lesson). In many dumpling restaurants they're sold by weight, by the {两|liǎng}: a
traditional unit of 50 grams, a tenth of lesson 06's {斤|jīn}. One {两|liǎng} is usually six or seven
dumplings, and some places now sell by the plate instead.

{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{三|sān}{两|liǎng}{饺子|jiǎo zi}。 — I'd like three liang (150 g) of dumplings.

{三|sān}{两|liǎng} uses {两|liǎng} as a measure, not the number two; {二|èr}{两|liǎng} is two {两|liǎng}.

## Dialogue: which pot?

{王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) has taken {大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫) to a hot pot restaurant in Chongqing.

```dialogue
# Which pot?
王芳: {来|lái}{重庆|Chóng qìng}{一定|yí dìng}{要|yào}{吃|chī}{火锅|huǒ guō}！{你|nǐ}{能|néng}{吃|chī}{辣|là}{吗|ma}？
= You can't come to Chongqing without having hot pot! Can you eat spicy food?
大卫: {一点儿|yì diǎnr}{可以|kě yǐ}，{太|tài}{辣|là}{的|de}{我|wǒ}{吃不了|chī bu liǎo}。
= A little is fine, but I can't handle very spicy.
王芳: {那|nà}{我们|wǒ men}{要|yào}{鸳鸯锅|yuān yang guō}，{一|yì}{边|biān}{辣|là}{的|de}，{一|yì}{边|biān}{不|bú}{辣|là}{的|de}。
= Then let's get a split pot: spicy on one side, mild on the other.
大卫: {好|hǎo}{主意|zhǔ yi}。{点|diǎn}{什么|shén me}{菜|cài}？
= Good idea. What shall we order?
王芳: {毛肚|máo dǔ}{一定|yí dìng}{要|yào}{点|diǎn}，{还有|hái yǒu}{牛肉|niú ròu}、{豆腐|dòu fu}{和|hé}{青菜|qīng cài}。{再|zài}{加|jiā}{两|liǎng}{瓶|píng}{啤酒|pí jiǔ}{吧|ba}。
= We have to have tripe, and beef, tofu and greens. And let's add two beers.
大卫: {这么|zhè me}{多|duō}，{我们|wǒ men}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{人|rén}{吃得完|chī de wán}{吗|ma}？
= That much? Can the two of us finish it?
王芳: {差不多|chà bu duō}。{吃|chī}{火锅|huǒ guō}{要|yào}{慢慢|màn màn}{吃|chī}，{吃|chī}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}{很|hěn}{正常|zhèng cháng}。
= About right. You take your time with hot pot: two hours is quite normal.
大卫: {这|zhè}{个|gè}{毛肚|máo dǔ}{要|yào}{煮|zhǔ}{多|duō}{长|cháng}{时间|shí jiān}？
= How long do you cook the tripe?
王芳: {十几|shí jǐ}{秒|miǎo}{就|jiù}{好|hǎo}{了|le}。{你|nǐ}{尝尝|cháng chang}！
= Just ten-odd seconds. Have a taste!
大卫: {又|yòu}{麻|má}{又|yòu}{辣|là}……{但是|dàn shì}{真|zhēn}{好吃|hǎo chī}！
= Numbing and hot… but delicious!
```

{一定|yí dìng} (definitely, must) is lesson 27's word. {主意|zhǔ yi} is an idea; {豆腐|dòu fu} tofu; {青菜|qīng cài} green
vegetables; {正常|zhèng cháng} normal; {煮|zhǔ} to boil; {秒|miǎo} a second. {一|yì}{边|biān}…{一|yì}{边|biān}… here is "one side…, the other
side…" (lesson 14 uses {一边|yì biān}…{一边|yì biān}… for doing two things at once).

## Reading: a message from Lanzhou

> {王芳|Wáng Fāng}，{你|nǐ}{好|hǎo}！{我|wǒ}{到|dào}{兰州|Lán zhōu}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}{了|le}。{这里|zhè lǐ}{的|de}{人|rén}{早上|zǎo shang}{一般|yì bān}{吃|chī}{牛肉面|niú ròu miàn}，{所以|suǒ yǐ}{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{去|qù}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{面馆|miàn guǎn}。{店|diàn}{里|lǐ}{已经|yǐ jīng}{有|yǒu}{好多|hǎo duō}{人|rén}{了|le}。{老板|lǎo bǎn}{问|wèn}{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{哪|nǎ}{种|zhǒng}{面条|miàn tiáo}，{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}{怎么|zěn me}{选|xuǎn}，{他|tā}{就|jiù}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{做|zuò}{了|le}{二细|èr xì}。{汤|tāng}{很|hěn}{清|qīng}，{萝卜|luó bo}{是|shì}{白|bái}{的|de}，{辣椒油|là jiāo yóu}{是|shì}{红|hóng}{的|de}，{上面|shàng miàn}{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{绿色|lǜ sè}{的|de}{香菜|xiāng cài}，{真|zhēn}{漂亮|piào liang}！{一|yì}{碗|wǎn}{面|miàn}{只|zhǐ}{要|yào}{十|shí}{块|kuài}{钱|qián}，{又|yòu}{便宜|pián yi}{又|yòu}{好吃|hǎo chī}。{明天|míng tiān}{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{山西|Shān xī}，{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{尝尝|cháng chang}{刀削面|dāo xiāo miàn}。{大卫|Dà wèi}

{汤|tāng} is the soup, {萝卜|luó bo} a radish, {辣椒油|là jiāo yóu} chilli oil and {香菜|xiāng cài} coriander. {只|zhǐ}{要|yào} is "only costs" ({={只|zhǐ}=}, only: lesson
26). The price is David's: prices change and differ from shop to shop.

1. Why did David go for noodles so early?
2. How did he choose his noodles?
3. Which of the five colours does he describe?
4. What does he think of the bowl, and what will he try next?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. People in Lanzhou usually eat beef noodles in the morning ({早上|zǎo shang}{一般|yì bān}{吃|chī}{牛肉面|niú ròu miàn}).
2. He didn't know how to choose, so the owner made him medium-thin noodles ({二细|èr xì}).
3. Clear soup, white radish, red chilli oil and green coriander (he doesn't mention the yellow
   noodles).
4. Cheap and delicious ({又|yòu}{便宜|pián yi}{又|yòu}{好吃|hǎo chī}); knife-cut noodles in Shanxi tomorrow.

"Hi Wang Fang! I've been in Lanzhou for two days. People here usually have beef noodles in the
morning, so today I went to a noodle shop at seven. There were already lots of people there. The
owner asked what kind of noodles I wanted. I didn't know how to choose, so he made me
medium-thin ones. The soup was very clear, the radish white, the chilli oil red, and there was
green coriander on top: beautiful! A bowl only costs ten kuai, cheap and delicious. Tomorrow I'm
going to Shanxi; I want to try knife-cut noodles. David"
</details>

## Key points

- {兰州牛肉面|Lán zhōu niú ròu miàn}: pulled noodles ({拉面|lā miàn}) in clear beef soup; {一清二白三红四绿五黄|yī qīng èr bái sān hóng sì lǜ wǔ huáng}; you choose
  the thickness ({毛细|máo xì}, {二细|èr xì}, {韭叶|jiǔ yè}…).
- {山西|Shān xī}: "home of noodles"; {刀削面|dāo xiāo miàn}, shaved into the pot; a few drops of {醋|cù}.
- Guangdong: {早茶|zǎo chá} and {点心|diǎn xin} ({虾饺|xiā jiǎo}, {烧卖|shāo mài}, {叉烧包|chā shāo bāo}), small dishes shared over tea.
- {火锅|huǒ guō}: Chongqing and Sichuan {麻辣|má là} with {毛肚|máo dǔ}; {鸳鸯锅|yuān yang guō} for mixed groups; Beijing's milder
  {涮羊肉|shuàn yáng ròu} in a copper pot with sesame sauce.
- Dumplings by weight: {一|yì}{两|liǎng} = 50 g, about six or seven.

lessons.title: Finding your way in the city: 东南西北, 中间, 哪儿都
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In HSK 2 you learned to put things on the left and right ({左边|zuǒ bian}, {右边|yòu bian}, {旁边|páng biān}) and to say how far
away they are ({离|lí}, {从|cóng}…{到|dào}…, {往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu}). This module takes you out into the city and beyond it. This
lesson gives you:

- the four points of the compass, {东|dōng}, {南|nán}, {西|xī} and {北|běi}, with -{边|biān} and -{面|miàn};
- {中间|zhōng jiān} (in the middle, between) and {附近|fù jìn} (nearby);
- the words of a street: {马路|mǎ lù}, {街|jiē}, {路口|lù kǒu}, {路边|lù biān};
- {地方|dì fang} (a place) and {地点|dì diǎn} (the place where something happens), {地图|dì tú} (map), {方向|fāng xiàng} (direction), and the
  character {地|dì} read on its own: the ground;
- {城市|chéng shì} and {市|shì} (city), {有名|yǒu míng} (famous) and {环境|huán jìng} (surroundings);
- a pattern you'll use every day: question words used without asking ({哪儿|nǎr}{都|dōu}{有|yǒu}, {什么|shén me}{都|dōu}{知道|zhī dào},
  {谁|shéi}{都|dōu}{认识|rèn shi}).

At the end you can follow and give directions with the compass, describe a neighbourhood and
say "everywhere", "everything" and "nobody".

## {东|dōng}, {南|nán}, {西|xī}, {北|běi}: the four directions

The four directions are {东|dōng} (east), {南|nán} (south), {西|xī} (west) and {北|běi} (north). Chinese lists them starting
from the east: {东|dōng}{南|nán}{西|xī}{北|běi} or {东|dōng}{西|xī}{南|nán}{北|běi}. English starts from the north: "north, south, east and west".

On their own they are used mostly after {往|wǎng} (towards) and in a few set phrases. To name a side or
an area, add -{边|biān} or -{面|miàn}, just as with {左边|zuǒ bian} and {前面|qián miàn}:

| Direction | + {边|biān} | + {面|miàn} | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| {东|dōng} | {东边|dōng bian} | {东面|dōng miàn} | the east side, to the east |
| {南|nán} | {南边|nán bian} | {南面|nán miàn} | the south side, to the south |
| {西|xī} | {西边|xī bian} | {西面|xī miàn} | the west side, to the west |
| {北|běi} | {北边|běi bian} | {北面|běi miàn} | the north side, to the north |

-{边|biān} is the everyday spoken form (its *bian* is light); -{面|miàn} means the same and is a little more
common in writing. As with {左边|zuǒ bian}, "to the north of X" is X ({的|de}) {北边|běi bian}, with the place first:

{银行|yín háng}{在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{的|de}{北边|běi bian}。 — The bank is to the north of the supermarket.

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{东边|dōng bian}，{走路|zǒu lù}{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng}。 — My home is east of the school, ten minutes on foot.

{这个|zhè ge}{城市|chéng shì}{的|de}{西边|xī bian}{很|hěn}{安静|ān jìng}。 — The west side of this city is very quiet.

With {往|wǎng} (HSK 2 lesson 07) the direction stands alone:

{从|cóng}{这儿|zhèr}{往|wǎng}{南|nán}{走|zǒu}，{到|dào}{了|le}{路口|lù kǒu}{往|wǎng}{东|dōng}{走|zǒu}。 — Go south from here, and at the crossing go east.

You already know {东西|dōng xi}, "thing", from HSK 1. Written the same, {东|dōng} and {西|xī} read with their
full tones are simply "east and west". The light *xi* makes the difference: {我|wǒ}{去|qù}{买|mǎi}{东西|dōng xi} (I'm going
to buy some things).

Two city names you know contain these characters: {北京|Běi jīng} (Beijing) is "the northern capital", and
{南京|Nán jīng} (Nanjing, a city on the Yangtze) is "the southern capital".

How people give directions varies. In cities with streets laid out in a grid, such as Beijing,
you'll often hear {往|wǎng}{北|běi}{走|zǒu} or {在|zài}{东边|dōng bian}. In many other places people find {往|wǎng}{左|zuǒ}{走|zǒu}, {往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu} more natural.
Learn both.

## {中间|zhōng jiān} and {在|zài}…{中间|zhōng jiān}: in the middle, between

{中间|zhōng jiān} is "the middle". With two places it means "between": {在|zài} A {和|hé} B {中间|zhōng jiān}.

{银行|yín háng}{在|zài}{书店|shū diàn}{和|hé}{超市|chāo shì}{中间|zhōng jiān}。 — The bank is between the bookshop and the supermarket.

{我|wǒ}{坐|zuò}{在|zài}{爸爸|bà ba}{和|hé}{妈妈|mā ma}{中间|zhōng jiān}。 — I'm sitting between Dad and Mum.

{马路|mǎ lù}{中间|zhōng jiān} — in the middle of the road

{中间|zhōng jiān}{的|de}{那个|nà ge}{人|rén}{是|shì}{我|wǒ}{哥哥|gē ge}。 — The person in the middle is my older brother.

Put the two places first, joined by {和|hé}, and {中间|zhōng jiān} last. English order (~~{在|zài}{中间|zhōng jiān}{银行|yín háng}{和|hé}{超市|chāo shì}~~) doesn't work.

{中间|zhōng jiān} also works for time: {中间|zhōng jiān}{休息|xiū xi}{十|shí}{分钟|fēn zhōng} (there's a ten-minute break in the middle).

## {附近|fù jìn}: nearby

{附近|fù jìn} is "the area nearby". Like other place words it follows a place ({我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{附近|fù jìn}, {学校|xué xiào}{附近|fù jìn}, {这|zhè}{附近|fù jìn})
and goes before {有|yǒu} to say what there is:

{我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{附近|fù jìn}{有|yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}。 — There's a supermarket near my home.

{这|zhè}{附近|fù jìn}{有|yǒu}{没有|méi yǒu}{银行|yín háng}？ — Is there a bank around here?

It can also describe a noun, with {的|de}: {附近|fù jìn}{的|de}{饭馆|fàn guǎn} (the restaurants nearby).

{附近|fù jìn} says where something is; {近|jìn} (HSK 2) says how close it is. {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{离|lí}{学校|xué xiào}{很|hěn}{近|jìn} (my home is close to
school) but {我|wǒ}{家|jiā}{在|zài}{学校|xué xiào}{附近|fù jìn} (my home is near the school).

## The street: {马路|mǎ lù}, {街|jiē}, {路口|lù kǒu}, {路边|lù biān}

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {马路|mǎ lù} | a road (for traffic, in a town) | {过|guò}{马路|mǎ lù} to cross the road |
| {街|jiē} | a street (with shops and people) | {这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{街|jiē} this street |
| {路口|lù kǒu} | a junction, a crossing | {第|dì}{二|èr}{个|gè}{路口|lù kǒu} the second crossing |
| {路边|lù biān} | the roadside | {在|zài}{路边|lù biān}{等|děng}{我|wǒ} wait for me by the road |

{马路|mǎ lù} has {马|mǎ} (horse) in it, but today it's simply a road with traffic. {路|lù}
(HSK 2) is the general word for any road or way. {街|jiē} is the street as a place where people walk
and shop, and it is used in street names ({东大街|Dōng Dà jiē}, East Street). {上|shàng}{街|jiē} is "to go into town, to go
shopping". All three take {条|tiáo}, the measure word for long thin things: {一|yì}{条|tiáo}{马路|mǎ lù}, {这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{街|jiē}.

{过|guò}{马路|mǎ lù}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}，{你|nǐ}{要|yào}{看|kàn}{车|chē}。 — When you cross the road, look out for cars.

{到|dào}{了|le}{第|dì}{二|èr}{个|gè}{路口|lù kǒu}{往|wǎng}{右|yòu}{走|zǒu}。 — Go right at the second crossing.

{路边|lù biān}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{小|xiǎo}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}。 — There are lots of little restaurants along the road.

A crossroads where two roads meet is a {十字路口|shí zì lù kǒu}: a crossing shaped like
the character {十|shí}.

## {地方|dì fang} and {地点|dì diǎn}; {地|dì} on its own

{地方|dì fang} (*dìfang*, light *fang*) is "a place" of any kind:

{这个|zhè ge}{地方|dì fang}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — This place is beautiful.

{你|nǐ}{住|zhù}{在|zài}{什么|shén me}{地方|dì fang}？ — Where do you live? (What place do you live in?)

{我们|wǒ men}{去|qù}{一|yí}{个|gè}{安静|ān jìng}{的|de}{地方|dì fang}{吧|ba}。 — Let's go somewhere quiet.

{地点|dì diǎn} is "the location": the place where something happens, as it appears on notices, tickets and
invitations, often next to {时间|shí jiān}:

> {时间|shí jiān}：{星期|xīng qī}{六|liù}{上午|shàng wǔ}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}
>
> {地点|dì diǎn}：{学校|xué xiào}{门口|mén kǒu}

In conversation, say {地方|dì fang}; {地点|dì diǎn} belongs to notices and plans.

{地图|dì tú} is a map: {看|kàn}{地图|dì tú}, {手机|shǒu jī}{上|shàng}{的|de}{地图|dì tú}, {在|zài}{地图|dì tú}{上|shàng} (on the map). {方向|fāng xiàng} is a direction: {往|wǎng}{哪个|nǎ ge}{方向|fāng xiàng}{走|zǒu}？ (which
way do I go?), {方向|fāng xiàng}{不|bú}{对|duì} (it's the wrong way).

In {地方|dì fang}, {地点|dì diǎn} and {地图|dì tú}, and in {地铁|dì tiě} (metro), the first character is {地|dì}, "ground, land". On its own
{地|dì} is "the ground" or "the floor":

{别|bié}{把|bǎ}{手机|shǒu jī}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{地|dì}{上|shàng}。 — Don't put your phone on the floor.

{孩子|hái zi}{们|men}{坐|zuò}{在|zài}{地|dì}{上|shàng}{看|kàn}{电视|diàn shì}。 — The children are sitting on the floor watching TV.

Don't confuse it with the light particle {地|de} of HSK 2 ({慢|màn}{慢|màn}{地|de}{说|shuō}, "say it slowly"), which comes
after a description and before a verb. Same character, different word.

## {城市|chéng shì} and {市|shì}

{城市|chéng shì} is "a city, a town" in general: {大|dà}{城市|chéng shì}, {小|xiǎo}{城市|chéng shì}, {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{这个|zhè ge}{城市|chéng shì}. {市|shì} is the city as a place with a
name and an administration: {北京市|Běi jīng shì} (the city of Beijing), {上海市|Shàng hǎi shì}, and compounds such as {市中心|shì zhōng xīn}
(the city centre) and {市里|shì lǐ} (in town). For "a city" in general, say {一|yí}{个|gè}{城市|chéng shì}: {市|shì} is
the city as a unit of government.

## {有名|yǒu míng} and {环境|huán jìng}

{有名|yǒu míng} is "famous", literally "having a name". It's an adjective, so it needs no {是|shì}:

{这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{街|jiē}{很|hěn}{有名|yǒu míng}。 — This street is famous.

{他|tā}{是|shì}{一|yí}{个|gè}{很|hěn}{有名|yǒu míng}{的|de}{医生|yī shēng}。 — He's a very famous doctor.

{环境|huán jìng} is "surroundings, environment": where you live, study or work, and (in lesson 15) the natural
environment.

{这个|zhè ge}{小区|xiǎo qū}{的|de}{环境|huán jìng}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{又|yòu}{安静|ān jìng}{又|yòu}{方便|fāng biàn}。 — The surroundings of this housing estate are very good:
quiet and convenient. ({又|yòu}…{又|yòu}, "both… and…", is lesson 08's.)

## Question words without a question: {哪儿|nǎr}{都|dōu}, {什么|shén me}{都|dōu}, {谁|shéi}{都|dōu}

You know {哪儿|nǎr}, {什么|shén me} and {谁|shéi} as question words. Followed by {都|dōu} (or {也|yě}) and a verb, they stop asking
and mean "every" or "any": "everywhere", "everything", "everybody".

| Pattern | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {哪儿|nǎr} + {都|dōu} + verb | {这|zhè}{种|zhǒng}{小|xiǎo}{店|diàn}{哪儿|nǎr}{都|dōu}{有|yǒu}。 | These little shops are everywhere. |
| {什么|shén me} + {都|dōu} + verb | {他|tā}{什么|shén me}{都|dōu}{知道|zhī dào}。 | He knows everything. |
| {谁|shéi} + {都|dōu} + verb | {我|wǒ}{奶奶|nǎi nai}{谁|shéi}{都|dōu}{认识|rèn shi}。 | My grandma knows everybody. |
| {谁|shéi} as subject | {谁|shéi}{都|dōu}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{她|tā}。 | Everybody likes her. |
| {什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou} + {都|dōu} | {什么|shén me}{时候|shí hou}{都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}。 | Any time is fine. |
| {哪个|nǎ ge} + {都|dōu} | {哪个|nǎ ge}{都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}。 | Either one is fine. / Any of them is fine. |

With {不|bù} or {没|méi} the meaning becomes "nowhere", "nothing", "nobody". {也|yě} is the more usual word here,
though {都|dōu} is fine too:

{我|wǒ}{今天|jīn tiān}{哪儿|nǎr}{也|yě}{不|bú}{去|qù}。 — I'm not going anywhere today.

{我|wǒ}{什么|shén me}{也|yě}{没|méi}{买|mǎi}。 — I didn't buy anything.

{这儿|zhèr}{谁|shéi}{也|yě}{不|bú}{认识|rèn shi}{我|wǒ}。 — Nobody here knows me.

Three rules:

1. The question word comes **before** {都|dōu} / {也|yě}, which comes before the verb. It does not stay in its
   question position after the verb: ~~{他|tā}{都|dōu}{知道|zhī dào}{什么|shén me}~~ is a question ("what all does he know?"), and
   ~~{我|wǒ}{买|mǎi}{什么|shén me}{也|yě}{没|méi}~~ is not Chinese.
2. As an object, the question word moves to the front, before {都|dōu} / {也|yě}: {他|tā}{什么|shén me}{都|dōu}{吃|chī} (he eats
   anything), {我|wǒ}{谁|shéi}{也|yě}{没|méi}{看见|kàn jiàn} (I didn't see anybody).
3. Don't leave out {都|dōu} / {也|yě}: ~~{我|wǒ}{哪儿|nǎr}{不|bú}{去|qù}~~ means nothing; {我|wǒ}{哪儿|nǎr}{都|dōu}{不|bú}{去|qù}.

In speech the question word is stressed: in {他|tā}{什么|shén me}{都|dōu}{知道|zhī dào} the {什么|shén me} is the loud part. There's no question mark, because there's no
question.

| 向 | towards; direction | xiàng | 口 | 6 | {方向|fāng xiàng} |

As in module 1, the notes look at the part of a character that gives its sound (its phonetic
component) as well as the radical, which hints at the meaning. Most characters are built this way.

- {城|chéng}: 土 (earth) for the meaning, since early city walls were built of rammed earth, and {成|chéng}
  for the sound ({成|chéng} is a lesson 17 character, in {成绩|chéng jì}). {城|chéng} first meant the wall itself.
- {境|jìng}: 土 again, and {竟|jìng} for the sound ({竟|jìng} isn't a course character). A {境|jìng} is the edge of a
  territory, and so the area inside it.
- {附|fù}: 阝 on the left is the "mound" radical you know from {阿|ā} and {院|yuàn} ({左耳旁|zuǒ ěr páng}, "left ear",
  by its shape); {付|fù} (to pay; not a course character) on the right gives the sound exactly.
- {环|huán} ({環|huán}): 王 on the left is really 玉 (jade): a {环|huán} was first a ring of jade. The right side of
  the traditional form, 睘, is also in 還, the traditional form of {还|hái} and {还|huán}, and
  gives both their sound. The simplified form puts 不 there: just a shape, not a sound.
- {马|mǎ} ({馬|mǎ}): a drawing of a horse, simplified to three strokes. It's the phonetic component of
  {妈|mā}, {吗|ma}, {码|mǎ} (in {号码|hào mǎ}, lesson 09) and {骂|mà} (to scold; not a course word): each says
  *ma* with its own tone. In {骑|qí} (to ride, lesson 13) {马|mǎ} gives the meaning instead.
- {北|běi}: the usual explanation is two people sitting back to back. It first meant "the back", and
  came to mean "north", it's said, because houses faced south, with the north behind them.
- {向|xiàng}: a dictionary of nearly 2,000 years ago explains it as a window in the north wall of a house.
  Use that as a story to remember the shape: a short stroke on top, a frame, and 口 inside.
- {南|nán}: where the shape comes from is debated. Learn its parts: 十 on top, then 冂, and inside 丷
  over 干. Dictionaries file it under 十.
- {图|tú} ({圖|tú}): 囗 (an enclosure) with 冬 inside in the simplified form. {冬|dōng} (winter, lesson 10)
  only lends its shape; it has nothing to do with the meaning.
- {街|jiē}: the character {行|xíng} (to go, as in {银行|yín háng} and {自行车|zì xíng chē}) split in two, with
  圭 in the middle. 圭 once gave the sound, but no longer matches it: treat it as a shape.

### Stroke order

- **{北|běi}**: the left side first: a vertical, a short horizontal, and a rising stroke. Then the
  right side: a left-falling stroke and a vertical that bends into a hook at the bottom.
- **{马|mǎ}**: three strokes: a horizontal that turns down, a vertical that turns twice and ends in a
  hook, and a rising horizontal at the bottom.
- **{南|nán}**: 十, then 冂, then a dot and a short left-falling stroke, and 干 last (two horizontals and the vertical).
- **{图|tú}** and other enclosures: the left side and the top corner first, then what goes inside,
  and the bottom stroke last to "close the door".
- **{向|xiàng}**: the short left-falling stroke on top first, then the frame (vertical, then the
  horizontal with its hook), then 口 inside.
- **{城|chéng}**: 土 first, its last stroke a rising one; then {成|chéng}, with its dot at the top right last.
- **{街|jiē}**: from left to right: 彳, then 圭 (two 土, one above the other), then 亍.

## Dialogue: looking for a famous restaurant

("Old Beijing Restaurant"; the name is made up) and asks a man in the street, whom she calls
{叔叔|shū shu} (叔叔), "uncle": a friendly way to address a man of your parents' age (lesson 01).
