lessons.title: Painting and calligraphy
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since the pinyin course you've written characters stroke by stroke, in a fixed order. For more than
two thousand years, people in China have done the same with a brush, and writing well became an
art of its own: calligraphy, {书法|shū fǎ} ("the method of writing"). This honors lesson is about that art
and its close relative, painting with ink: the tools, the main styles of script, one famous
calligrapher, and why the stroke order you've learned matters for a brush. A few words outside the
course are glossed where they come; you don't need to learn them.

## The four treasures of the study

A calligrapher's tools are called the {文房四宝|wén fáng sì bǎo}, "the four treasures of the study" ({文房|wén fáng}
is a scholar's study, {宝|bǎo} a treasure):

| Tool | Chinese | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| brush | {毛笔|máo bǐ} | a "hair pen": animal hair tied into a point, on a bamboo handle |
| ink | {墨|mò} | a stick of solid ink, ground with a little water to make liquid ink |
| paper | {纸|zhǐ} | absorbent paper; the best known kind is {宣纸|xuān zhǐ}, xuan paper |
| inkstone | {砚|yàn} | a flat stone with a hollow, where the ink stick is ground |

You know {笔|bǐ} (pen) and {纸|zhǐ} (paper) from HSK 2 and lesson 16: {毛笔|máo bǐ} is "a pen made of hair", since {毛|máo} is
hair or fur (lesson 09's {毛|máo} for ten cents is the same character). The brush is held upright, and
the soft tip can make a line thin or thick, wet or dry, in a single stroke. Ink soaks into the
paper at once: a stroke can't be corrected, so each one has to be right the first time.

## Five styles of script

UNESCO inscribed Chinese calligraphy on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural
Heritage of Humanity in 2009. Its description names five styles of script, and calligraphers
still practise all five. Here they are with their Chinese names ({书|shū} here is "script, writing"),
roughly from oldest to newest, though they overlapped for centuries:

| Style | Chinese | What it looks like |
|---|---|---|
| seal script | {篆书|zhuàn shū} | even, rounded lines of the same width, tall shapes; the oldest style still written, now used for seals (name stamps) |
| clerical script | {隶书|lì shū} | flat, wide characters; horizontal strokes end in a flared "tail"; the script of the Han dynasty |
| regular script | {楷书|kǎi shū} | every stroke separate and clear; the model for printed characters and for learners |
| running script | {行书|xíng shū} | strokes joined where the brush runs on; quicker, the everyday hand |
| cursive script | {草书|cǎo shū} | whole characters in one or two sweeps; beautiful, and hard to read |

Take the character {山|shān} (mountain) in words. In seal script it is three rounded peaks on a curved
base, close to a picture. In clerical script it sits low and wide, the bottom stroke ending in a
little flare. In regular script it is the {山|shān} you know: a vertical, a bent stroke, a vertical. In
running script the bent stroke and the last vertical run together, and the brush barely lifts. In
cursive the whole character can shrink to a single looping line.

{行书|xíng shū} uses {行|xíng} (to go, to walk: lesson 28's {行|xíng} means "OK"), and {草书|cǎo shū} uses {草|cǎo}, grass (lesson 15),
which also means "rough, hasty": "grass script" is the quick, rough hand.

## Learning calligraphy

Most learners start with regular script: its strokes are clear, and it teaches the shape and
balance of each character. They copy model characters by famous calligraphers, again and again,
first tracing over them, then writing beside them. Calligraphy is still taught by a teacher to
students, as it has always been, and UNESCO notes that it is now also taught in schools. Many
people practise it as a hobby for the rest of their lives; in parks you may see older people
writing large characters on the pavement with a big brush and plain water, which dries away in a
few minutes.

This is where stroke order comes in. The order you've learned (top before bottom, left before
right, horizontal before a crossing vertical, inside before the closing stroke) is the order of the
brush. In regular script you can't see it; in running and cursive script you can, because the
brush goes straight from the end of one stroke to the start of the next, and the joins show the
path. Write a character in the wrong order and its running form comes out a different shape. The
tracing pads in this course have a link to the brush too: their stroke data comes from
Make Me a Hanzi, which was made from Kai typefaces, printed regular script ({楷书|kǎi shū}).

## The "Sage of Calligraphy"

The most famous name in Chinese calligraphy is {王羲之|Wáng Xī zhī}, Wang Xizhi, who lived in the 4th
century, in the Eastern Jin dynasty (his dates are usually given as 303–361). He is traditionally
called the {书圣|shū shèng}, "Sage of Calligraphy". His best-known work is the {兰亭集序|Lán tíng Jí Xù}, the
"Preface to the Orchid Pavilion Poems", written in running script in 353 for a collection of
poems that friends wrote at a gathering by a stream. The original has long been lost: what
survives are early copies, tracings and rubbings from stone, and calligraphers still copy them
today.

## Painting with the same brush

Chinese painting uses the same brush, ink and paper, and the same strokes, so painters and
calligraphers were often the same people. A painting is usually made with black ink in many
shades, from deep black to pale grey, sometimes with light colours, and much of the paper may be
left empty, for sky, water or mist.

The greatest subject became the landscape, in Chinese {山水画|shān shuǐ huà}, "mountains-and-water
painting": {山|shān} (mountain, lesson 15) and {水|shuǐ} (water). Earlier, landscapes were mostly the setting for
people and stories; in the 10th and 11th centuries, in the Five Dynasties and the Song dynasty,
mountains and rivers became the main subject. One of the best-known works of that time is
Travellers among Mountains and Streams by Fan Kuan, painted in the early 11th century: a huge
mountain fills the scroll, and the travellers on the path below are tiny.

Many paintings also carry writing: a poem in the painter's hand, a date, and red seals with the
names of the painter and later owners. Painting, poetry and calligraphy were seen as three
sides of one art.

## Reading: Grandpa's brush

> {我|wǒ}{爷爷|yé ye}{今年|jīn nián}{七十|qī shí}{岁|suì}{了|le}，{他|tā}{对|duì}{书法|shū fǎ}{特别|tè bié}{感兴趣|gǎn xìng qù}。{他|tā}{平时|píng shí}{早上|zǎo shang}{六|liù}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{起床|qǐ chuáng}{了|le}，{先|xiān}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{走|zǒu}{一|yì}{走|zǒu}，{然后|rán hòu}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{写字|xiě zì}。{他|tā}{有|yǒu}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{毛笔|máo bǐ}，{大|dà}{的|de}、{小|xiǎo}{的|de}{都|dōu}{有|yǒu}。
>
> {上|shàng}{个|gè}{周末|zhōu mò}，{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{爷爷|yé ye}{家|jiā}。{爷爷|yé ye}{让|ràng}{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{试|shì}{一|yí}{试|shì}。{他|tā}{先|xiān}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{讲|jiǎng}{了|le}{怎么|zěn me}{拿|ná}{笔|bǐ}，{然后|rán hòu}{在|zài}{纸|zhǐ}{上|shàng}{写|xiě}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}“{山|shān}”{字|zì}。{我|wǒ}{写|xiě}{了|le}{半天|bàn tiān}，{写|xiě}{得|de}{非常|fēi cháng}{难看|nán kàn}，{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{不|bù}{开心|kāi xīn}。{爷爷|yé ye}{笑|xiào}{着|zhe}{说|shuō}：“{别|bié}{急|jí}，{我|wǒ}{写|xiě}{了|le}{六十|liù shí}{年|nián}，{才|cái}{写|xiě}{得|de}{这么|zhè me}{好|hǎo}！”
>
> {我们|wǒ men}{一直|yì zhí}{写|xiě}{到|dào}{中午|zhōng wǔ}。{最后|zuì hòu}，{我|wǒ}{终于|zhōng yú}{写|xiě}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{不错|bú cuò}{的|de}“{山|shān}”{字|zì}。{爷爷|yé ye}{很|hěn}{高兴|gāo xìng}，{把|bǎ}{它|tā}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{了|le}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。{他|tā}{说|shuō}：“{你|nǐ}{看|kàn}，{书法|shū fǎ}{跟|gēn}{做事|zuò shì}{一样|yí yàng}，{要|yào}{慢|màn}{慢|màn}{来|lái}。”

{书法|shū fǎ} is calligraphy, {毛笔|máo bǐ} a brush. {做事|zuò shì} is "doing things" in general.

1. What does Grandpa usually do in the morning?
2. Why wasn't the writer happy at first?
3. What did Grandpa say about calligraphy at the end?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. He's up by six, goes for a walk in the park first, then goes home and writes ({先|xiān}{去|qù}{公园|gōng yuán}{走|zǒu}{一|yì}{走|zǒu}，{然后|rán hòu}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{写字|xiě zì}).
2. The writer wrote for ages and the characters came out really ugly ({写|xiě}{得|de}{非常|fēi cháng}{难看|nán kàn}).
3. That calligraphy is like doing anything else: you have to take it slowly ({要|yào}{慢|màn}{慢|màn}{来|lái}).

"My grandpa is seventy this year, and he's especially interested in calligraphy. Normally he's up
by six in the morning: first he goes for a walk in the park, then he comes home and writes. He has
lots of brushes, big ones and small ones.

Last weekend I went to Grandpa's. He had me try too. First he told me how to hold the brush, then
he wrote the character 'mountain' on the paper. I wrote for ages, and it came out really ugly,
and I was a bit unhappy. Grandpa laughed and said, 'Don't worry: I've been writing for sixty
years, and only now do I write this well!'

We kept writing until noon. In the end I finally wrote a pretty good 'mountain'. Grandpa was very
pleased and put it on the table. He said, 'You see, calligraphy is like everything else: you have
to take it slowly.'"
</details>

## Key points

- {书法|shū fǎ}: calligraphy. The four treasures of the study: brush ({毛笔|máo bǐ}), ink ({墨|mò}), paper ({纸|zhǐ}), inkstone ({砚|yàn}).
- Chinese calligraphy is on UNESCO's Representative List (2009). Five styles: seal, clerical,
  regular, running and cursive script ({篆书|zhuàn shū}, {隶书|lì shū}, {楷书|kǎi shū}, {行书|xíng shū}, {草书|cǎo shū}). Learners start with regular script.
- Stroke order is the brush's order; it shows in running and cursive script.
- Wang Xizhi (4th century), the "Sage of Calligraphy": the Orchid Pavilion Preface (353), in
  running script; the original is lost.
- Painting uses the same tools. Landscape ({山水画|shān shuǐ huà}, "mountains and water") became the main subject in
  the 10th–11th centuries; paintings often carry poems and red seals.

Words outside the course in this lesson: {文房四宝|wén fáng sì bǎo} (the four treasures of the study), {毛笔|máo bǐ} (brush),
{墨|mò} (ink), {宣纸|xuān zhǐ} (xuan paper), {砚|yàn} (inkstone), {书法|shū fǎ} (calligraphy), {篆书|zhuàn shū}, {隶书|lì shū}, {楷书|kǎi shū}, {行书|xíng shū}, {草书|cǎo shū} (the five
scripts), {书圣|shū shèng} (Sage of Calligraphy), {山水画|shān shuǐ huà} (landscape painting).

lessons.title: Peking opera
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 22 gave you the words for shows: {表演|biǎo yǎn}, {节目|jié mù}, {音乐|yīn yuè}, {故事|gù shi}, {声音|shēng yīn}. This honors lesson is about the
best-known show of all in Chinese culture, Peking opera, {京剧|jīng jù} ("the Beijing drama"): where it
came from, its four kinds of role, the painted faces, the music, and how it is kept alive. A few
words outside the course are glossed where they come; you don't need to learn them.

## Singing, speaking, acting and fighting

Peking opera is a whole theatre in one: the performers sing, speak their lines in a special
stylised voice, act with fixed gestures and movements, and fight with acrobatic leaps and spears.
Chinese sums it up in four words, {唱|chàng} (singing), {念|niàn} (reciting), {做|zuò} (acting) and {打|dǎ}
(fighting), and UNESCO's description names the same four: singing, reciting, acting and martial
arts. The costumes are bright and rich, and the stage is almost empty: a table and two chairs can
be a palace, a mountain or a city wall. A walk round the stage is a long journey; a whip in the
hand means the actor is riding a horse.

UNESCO inscribed Peking opera on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of
Humanity in 2010. Its description says the art is performed all over China but centred on
Beijing, Tianjin and Shanghai, that it is sung and recited mainly in the Beijing dialect, and that
it is passed on mostly from master to student, by teaching, watching and copying.

## How it began

The traditional story is that Peking opera began in 1790, when four famous theatre companies
from Anhui province came to Beijing for the celebrations of the Qianlong emperor's 80th birthday.
They stayed, mixed their music with other styles they met in the capital, and the new form took
its shape during the 19th century. That is why its home is Beijing, though its roots are in the
south.

In the early years, all the female roles were played by men. The most famous of these performers
was {梅兰芳|Méi Lán fāng}, Mei Lanfang (1894–1961), who played mostly female roles and became known around the
world; in 1930 he toured the United States. Today both women and men perform.

## Four kinds of role

Every character in Peking opera belongs to one of four main role types. An actor usually trains
in one type for life.

| Role | Chinese | Who they are |
|---|---|---|
| sheng | {生|shēng} | male roles: young scholars, old officials, generals |
| dan | {旦|dàn} | female roles: young women, older women, women warriors |
| jing | {净|jìng} | "painted faces": strong men, generals, heroes and villains, with boldly painted faces |
| chou | {={丑|chǒu}=} | the clown: comic parts, from servants to officials, with a small white patch around the eyes and nose |

You know {生|shēng} from {学生|xué sheng} and {生日|shēng rì}. The clown's name, {={丑|chǒu}=}, is also the word for "ugly" (in traditional characters "ugly" is a different
character, {=醜=}); on stage it means comedy, not ugliness.

## Painted faces

The painted faces, {脸谱|liǎn pǔ} ("face charts", {脸|liǎn}: face, lesson 04), worn mostly by the jing roles, are the best-known
image of Peking opera. The colours and patterns tell the audience at once what kind of person a
character is. These are conventions with many exceptions, but three are taught everywhere:

| Colour | Meaning | Famous example |
|---|---|---|
| red | loyalty, courage, uprightness | Guan Yu ({关羽|Guān Yǔ}), a general of the Three Kingdoms period (on stage usually a red-faced sheng role) |
| black | honesty, integrity, a straight and blunt character | Judge Bao ({包公|Bāo gōng}), the incorruptible judge |
| white | cunning, a schemer | Cao Cao ({曹操|Cáo Cāo}), the Three Kingdoms warlord, as the stories show him |

The stories behind these characters come from history and from old novels, so the audience
usually knows them before the curtain rises. Cao Cao, for example, was a real ruler and an able
general and poet; the white face belongs to the cunning villain of the stories, not to the
historical man.

## The music

The orchestra sits at the side of the stage. The leading instrument is the {京胡|jīng hú}, a small
two-stringed fiddle with a high, bright sound, played with a bow. UNESCO's description puts it
like this: "civilian" plays emphasise string and wind instruments, while "military" plays, with
their battles, feature percussion: drums and gongs.
Drums and gongs mark the actors' movements and every fight, and a performance often opens with a
big gong.

Most of the arias follow two families of melody, called xipi and erhuang: one generally brighter,
the other often used for serious or sad moments. The voice of a young dan role is high and
clear; that of a jing role big and rough.

## Peking opera today

Peking opera is performed in theatres in Beijing and many other cities and on television. Young performers
still train for years in opera schools and with masters, starting as children, because the singing,
the movements and the fighting all take a long time to learn. Its painted faces appear on
everything from posters to stamps.

## Reading: my first Peking opera

> {上|shàng}{个|gè}{周末|zhōu mò}，{爷爷|yé ye}{带|dài}{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{看|kàn}{京剧|jīng jù}。{爷爷|yé ye}{对|duì}{京剧|jīng jù}{特别|tè bié}{感兴趣|gǎn xìng qù}，{他|tā}{年轻|nián qīng}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{也|yě}{唱|chàng}{过|guo}。{我|wǒ}{以前|yǐ qián}{觉得|jué de}{京剧|jīng jù}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{奇怪|qí guài}，{没有|méi yǒu}{兴趣|xìng qù}。
>
> {我们|wǒ men}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{就|jiù}{到|dào}{了|le}。{表演|biǎo yǎn}{开始|kāi shǐ}{以前|yǐ qián}，{爷爷|yé ye}{先|xiān}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{讲|jiǎng}{了|le}{今天|jīn tiān}{的|de}{故事|gù shi}。{表演|biǎo yǎn}{开始|kāi shǐ}{了|le}，{表演|biǎo yǎn}{的|de}{人|rén}{穿|chuān}{的|de}{衣服|yī fu}{漂亮|piào liang}{极|jí}{了|le}，{他们|tā men}{的|de}{脸|liǎn}{也|yě}{画|huà}{得|de}{很|hěn}{特别|tè bié}：{有|yǒu}{红色|hóng sè}{的|de}、{黑色|hēi sè}{的|de}，{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{白色|bái sè}{的|de}。{爷爷|yé ye}{告诉|gào su}{我|wǒ}，{红脸|hóng liǎn}{是|shì}{好人|hǎo rén}，{白|bái}{脸|liǎn}{常常|cháng cháng}{是|shì}{坏|huài}{人|rén}。{音乐|yīn yuè}{的|de}{声音|shēng yīn}{很|hěn}{大|dà}，{我|wǒ}{刚|gāng}{开始|kāi shǐ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{害怕|hài pà}，{后来|hòu lái}{就|jiù}{习惯|xí guàn}{了|le}。
>
> {表演|biǎo yǎn}{完|wán}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{直到|zhí dào}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{才|cái}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。{我|wǒ}{跟|gēn}{爷爷|yé ye}{说|shuō}：“{京剧|jīng jù}{挺|tǐng}{有意思|yǒu yì si}{的|de}！{下次|xià cì}{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{想|xiǎng}{来|lái}。”{爷爷|yé ye}{听|tīng}{了|le}，{开心|kāi xīn}{极|jí}{了|le}。

{京剧|jīng jù} is Peking opera. {常常|cháng cháng} (often) is lesson 27's word; {下次|xià cì} is "next time".

1. What did the writer think of Peking opera before?
2. What did Grandpa do before the show started?
3. How did the writer feel about the music, at first and later?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. The writer used to find Peking opera a bit strange and wasn't interested ({我|wǒ}{以前|yǐ qián}{觉得|jué de}{京剧|jīng jù}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{奇怪|qí guài}，{没有|méi yǒu}{兴趣|xìng qù}).
2. He told the writer the story of that evening's opera ({爷爷|yé ye}{先|xiān}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{讲|jiǎng}{了|le}{今天|jīn tiān}{的|de}{故事|gù shi}).
3. At first the loud music was a bit frightening; later the writer got used to it ({我|wǒ}{刚|gāng}{开始|kāi shǐ}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{害怕|hài pà}，{后来|hòu lái}{就|jiù}{习惯|xí guàn}{了|le}).

"Last weekend Grandpa took me to see Peking opera. Grandpa is especially interested in Peking
opera; he sang it himself when he was young. I used to think Peking opera was a bit strange and
had no interest in it.

We got there as early as seven. Before the performance began, Grandpa first told me that day's
story. The show began: the performers' clothes were extremely beautiful, and their faces were
painted in a very special way: some red, some black and some white. Grandpa told me the red faces
are good people and the white faces are often bad people. The music was very loud, and at first I
was a bit scared, but later I got used to it.

When the show was over, we didn't get home until half past ten. I said to Grandpa, 'Peking opera
is pretty interesting! I'd like to come again next time.' Grandpa was delighted to hear it."
</details>

## Key points

- {京剧|jīng jù}, Peking opera: singing, reciting, acting and fighting ({唱|chàng}, {念|niàn}, {做|zuò}, {打|dǎ}) on an almost empty stage.
  On UNESCO's Representative List since 2010; centred on Beijing, Tianjin and Shanghai; passed on
  from master to student.
- By tradition it began in 1790, when four Anhui companies came to Beijing; it took shape in the
  19th century. Female roles were once played by men; Mei Lanfang (1894–1961) is the most famous.
- Four role types: sheng ({男|nán}), dan ({女|nǚ}), jing (painted faces), chou (clown).
- Painted faces ({脸谱|liǎn pǔ}): red for loyalty (Guan Yu), black for integrity (Judge Bao), white for
  cunning (Cao Cao), as stage conventions.
- Music: the jinghu fiddle leads; drums and gongs carry the battle plays and mark every movement.

Words outside the course in this lesson: {京剧|jīng jù} (Peking opera), {念|niàn} (to recite), {生|shēng} / {旦|dàn} / {净|jìng} / {={丑|chǒu}=}
(the four roles), {脸谱|liǎn pǔ} (painted faces), {京胡|jīng hú} (the jinghu fiddle), and the names {梅兰芳|Méi Lán fāng}, {关羽|Guān Yǔ}, {包公|Bāo gōng} and {曹操|Cáo Cāo}.

lessons.title: If, as long as, only if: conditions and purpose
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You already join two clauses in several ways: {因为|yīn wèi}…{所以|suǒ yǐ} (cause and effect), {虽然|suī rán}…{但是|dàn shì} (contrast),
{又|yòu}…{又|yòu} (lesson 08), {一边|yì biān}…{一边|yì biān} (lesson 14), {先|xiān}…{然后|rán hòu} (lesson 25) and {越|yuè}…{越|yuè} (lesson 12). Each of
these is a **[[complex sentence]]**: two clauses held together by a pair of linking words. Module 6
finishes the set. This lesson adds the ones that set conditions and say what something is for:

- {如果|rú guǒ}…({的话|de huà})，{就|jiù}…: if… (then);
- {只要|zhǐ yào}…{就|jiù}…: as long as…;
- {只有|zhǐ yǒu}…{才|cái}…: only if…, only when…;
- {不但|bú dàn}…{而且|ér qiě}…: not only… but also…;
- {为了|wèi le}: in order to; {为|wèi}: for (someone); {向|xiàng}: towards, to ({向|xiàng}{他|tā}{学习|xué xí});
- {或|huò} / {或者|huò zhě} (or) in statements and {还是|hái shi} in questions;
- {又|yòu} and {再|zài} (again: past or future);
- {={只|zhǐ}=} zhǐ (only) and {只能|zhǐ néng} (can only).

At the end you can set conditions, make plans that depend on the weather or on other people, and
read a notice full of rules.

## {如果|rú guǒ}…{就|jiù}…: if…

{如果|rú guǒ} starts a supposition, and {就|jiù} introduces what follows from it. This is a **[[hypothetical sentence]]**: the first half imagines a situation, the second says what happens then.

{如果|rú guǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{我们|wǒ men}{就|jiù}{不|bú}{去|qù}{爬|pá}{山|shān}{了|le}。 — If it rains tomorrow, we won't go hiking.

{如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{累|lèi}{了|le}，{就|jiù}{休息|xiū xi}{一会儿|yí huìr}{吧|ba}。 — If you're tired, have a rest.

{如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{这|zhè}{本|běn}{书|shū}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{送|sòng}{给|gěi}{你|nǐ}。 — If you like this book, I'll give it to you.

Two positions matter:

- {如果|rú guǒ} goes at the very start or straight after the subject: {如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{有|yǒu}{问题|wèn tí}… or {你|nǐ}{如果|rú guǒ}{有|yǒu}{问题|wèn tí}… (if
  you have a question…). Both are fine.
- {就|jiù} is an adverb, so it goes after the subject of the second clause and before its verb: {如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{去|qù}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{去|qù}
  (if you go, I'll go), never ×{如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{去|qù}，{就|jiù}{我|wǒ}{去|qù}.

The particle {的话|de huà} can close the {如果|rú guǒ} clause, or replace {如果|rú guǒ} altogether. All three say the same,
and the {的话|de huà} forms are a little more spoken:

{如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{就|jiù}{别|bié}{去|qù}{了|le}。 — If you don't want to go, don't.

{如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{的话|de huà}，{就|jiù}{别|bié}{去|qù}{了|le}。

{你|nǐ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}{的话|de huà}，{就|jiù}{别|bié}{去|qù}{了|le}。

When the second half is a suggestion, speakers often leave out {就|jiù}: {如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{累|lèi}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{吧|ba}。 (If
you're tired, let's go home.)

## {只要|zhǐ yào}…{就|jiù}…: as long as…

{只要|zhǐ yào} names a condition that is **enough**: if it's met, the result follows, whatever else is true.
English says "as long as" or "all you need is…":

{只要|zhǐ yào}{你|nǐ}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{练习|liàn xí}，{你|nǐ}{的|de}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{就|jiù}{会|huì}{越|yuè}{来|lái}{越|yuè}{好|hǎo}。 — As long as you practise every day, your Chinese will keep
getting better.

{只要|zhǐ yào}{不|bú}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{我们|wǒ men}{就|jiù}{去|qù}。 — As long as it doesn't rain, we'll go.

{只要|zhǐ yào}{你|nǐ}{说|shuō}{慢|màn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{听|tīng}{得|de}{懂|dǒng}。 — As long as you speak a little more slowly, I can understand.

The last example has a potential complement ({听|tīng}{得|de}{懂|dǒng}, lesson 06): conditions and possibility go
together naturally. Like {如果|rú guǒ}, {只要|zhǐ yào} can follow the subject: {你|nǐ}{只要|zhǐ yào}{说|shuō}{慢|màn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{听|tīng}{得|de}{懂|dǒng}。

## {只有|zhǐ yǒu}…{才|cái}…: only if…

{只有|zhǐ yǒu} names a condition that is **necessary**: it's the only way, and without it the result won't
happen. The second half takes {才|cái} (only then), not {就|jiù}:

{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{多|duō}{听|tīng}{多|duō}{说|shuō}，{才|cái}{能|néng}{学|xué}{好|hǎo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 — Only by listening and speaking a lot can you learn Chinese well.

{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{周末|zhōu mò}，{我|wǒ}{才|cái}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{看|kàn}{电影|diàn yǐng}。 — I only have time to watch films at the weekend.

{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{你|nǐ}{去|qù}，{他|tā}{才|cái}{会|huì}{去|qù}。 — He'll only go if you go.

{才|cái} is the {才|cái} of lesson 25 ({他|tā}{十|shí}{点|diǎn}{才|cái}{来|lái}: "not until ten"), and it keeps that feeling of "not before,
not otherwise". After {才|cái} you'll often find {能|néng} or {会|huì}. Both {只要|zhǐ yào}…{就|jiù} and {只有|zhǐ yǒu}…{才|cái} are **[[conditional sentences]]**;
the difference is how strong the condition is:

| Pattern | The condition is… | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {只要|zhǐ yào}…{就|jiù}… | enough (other ways may work too) | {只要|zhǐ yào}{你|nǐ}{努力|nǔ lì}，{就|jiù}{能|néng}{考|kǎo}{好|hǎo}。 As long as you work hard, you'll do well. |
| {只有|zhǐ yǒu}…{才|cái}… | the only way (nothing else will do) | {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{努力|nǔ lì}，{才|cái}{能|néng}{考|kǎo}{好|hǎo}。 Only hard work will get you a good result. |
| {如果|rú guǒ}…{就|jiù}… | just a supposition | {如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{努力|nǔ lì}，{就|jiù}{能|néng}{考|kǎo}{好|hǎo}。 If you work hard, you'll do well. |

{只有|zhǐ yǒu} has a second, simpler use: "only" before a noun or a person, with no {才|cái} clause. {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{他|tā}{知道|zhī dào}{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}。
(Only he knows about this.) {这儿|zhèr}{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{一|yí}{个|gè}{超市|chāo shì}。 (There's only one supermarket here.)

## {不但|bú dàn}…{而且|ér qiě}…: not only… but also…

{不但|bú dàn}…{而且|ér qiě} adds a second point on top of the first, usually a stronger one. This is a sentence of
**[[progression]]**: the second clause goes further than the first.

{他|tā}{不但|bú dàn}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{而且|ér qiě}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}。 — Not only can he speak Chinese, he speaks it very well.

{这|zhè}{家|jiā}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}{的|de}{菜|cài}{不但|bú dàn}{好吃|hǎo chī}，{而且|ér qiě}{很|hěn}{便宜|pián yi}。 — This restaurant's food is not only good but cheap too.

Where the subject goes depends on whether the two clauses share it:

- **Same subject**: the subject comes first, then {不但|bú dàn}: {他|tā}{不但|bú dàn}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{而且|ér qiě}…
- **Two subjects**: {不但|bú dàn} comes before the first subject, and the second clause often has {也|yě} or {还|hái}
  as well: {不但|bú dàn}{我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{这个|zhè ge}{电影|diàn yǐng}，{而且|ér qiě}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}。 (Not only do I like this film, my mum likes
  it too.)

{而且|ér qiě} also works on its own, like "and what's more": {这个|zhè ge}{房子|fáng zi}{很|hěn}{大|dà}，{而且|ér qiě}{离|lí}{地铁|dì tiě}{站|zhàn}{很|hěn}{近|jìn}。 (This flat is
big, and it's close to the metro station too.) {不但|bú dàn}, on the other hand, always needs a second clause, with {而且|ér qiě}, {也|yě} or {还|hái}.

## {为了|wèi le} (in order to) and {为|wèi} (for)

{为了|wèi le} + a goal states a **[[purpose]]**: what you do something for. The {为了|wèi le} phrase normally comes
first:

{为了|wèi le}{学|xué}{好|hǎo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{他|tā}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{看|kàn}{中国|Zhōng guó}{电影|diàn yǐng}。 — To learn Chinese well, he watches Chinese films every day.

{为了|wèi le}{健康|jiàn kāng}，{我|wǒ}{爸爸|bà ba}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{早上|zǎo shang}{去|qù}{锻炼|duàn liàn}。 — My dad goes to exercise every morning for his health.

English often puts the purpose at the end ("…every day to learn Chinese"). In Chinese, a purpose
at the end takes {是|shì}{为了|wèi le}: {他|tā}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{看|kàn}{中国|Zhōng guó}{电影|diàn yǐng}，{是|shì}{为了|wèi le}{学|xué}{好|hǎo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。 (He watches Chinese films every day in
order to learn Chinese well.)

{为|wèi} on its own is "for", for the person who benefits or who your feeling is about:

{妈妈|mā ma}{为|wèi}{我|wǒ}{做|zuò}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{生日|shēng rì}{蛋糕|dàn gāo}。 — Mum made a birthday cake for me.

{你|nǐ}{考|kǎo}{得|de}{这么|zhè me}{好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{真|zhēn}{为|wèi}{你|nǐ}{高兴|gāo xìng}！ — You did so well in the exam: I'm really happy for you!

You've known {为|wèi} since HSK 2's {为什么|wèi shén me} (for what, why) and {因为|yīn wèi} (because). In all of these
{为|wèi} is wèi, fourth tone.

## {向|xiàng}: towards, to

{向|xiàng} marks a direction. With a direction word it is the same as {往|wǎng} (HSK 2): {向|xiàng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu} = {往|wǎng}{前|qián}{走|zǒu} (go
straight ahead), {向|xiàng}{左|zuǒ}{看|kàn} (look to the left). Unlike {往|wǎng}, {向|xiàng} can also take a person: the person your
action is aimed at.

{我|wǒ}{向|xiàng}{老师|lǎo shī}{请|qǐng}{了|le}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}{假|jià}。 — I asked the teacher for two days off.

{他|tā}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{要|yào}{向|xiàng}{他|tā}{学习|xué xí}。 — He speaks Chinese very well: I want to learn from him.

{向|xiàng}{大家|dà jiā}{问好|wèn hǎo}！ — Greetings to everyone! (a speaker greeting an audience; {问好|wèn hǎo}: to send greetings)

So {向|xiàng} + person + verb covers "ask someone for", "learn from someone", "say something to someone".
{往|wǎng} never takes a person.

## {或|huò} / {或者|huò zhě} and {还是|hái shi}: two kinds of "or"

English "or" has two jobs that Chinese keeps apart. In a statement, offering choices, say {或者|huò zhě}:

{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{或者|huò zhě}{后天|hòu tiān}{来|lái}{都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}。 — You can come tomorrow or the day after.

{我们|wǒ men}{坐|zuò}{地铁|dì tiě}{或者|huò zhě}{打车|dǎ chē}{去|qù}{吧|ba}。 — Let's take the metro or a taxi.

In a question asking someone to choose, say {还是|hái shi} (HSK 2):

{你|nǐ}{明天|míng tiān}{来|lái}{还是|hái shi}{后天|hòu tiān}{来|lái}？ — Are you coming tomorrow or the day after?

{你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}？ — Would you like tea or coffee?

{或|huò} is the short, written form of {或者|huò zhě}, typical of notices and forms: {星期|xīng qī}{六|liù}{或|huò}{星期日|xīng qī rì} (Saturday or
Sunday). A question that is only reported, inside a statement, still takes {还是|hái shi}, because it's still
a choice to be made: {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}{他|tā}{明天|míng tiān}{来|lái}{还是|hái shi}{后天|hòu tiān}{来|lái}。 (I don't know whether he's coming tomorrow or the
day after.)

| | Statement | Question |
|---|---|---|
| "or" | {或者|huò zhě} (written: {或|huò}) | {还是|hái shi} |
| example | {茶|chá}{或者|huò zhě}{咖啡|kā fēi}{都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}。 Tea or coffee, either is fine. | {茶|chá}{还是|hái shi}{咖啡|kā fēi}？ Tea or coffee? |

## {又|yòu} and {再|zài}: again, before and after

Both mean "again", but they look in different directions:

- {又|yòu} for a repetition that **has happened**: {他|tā}{昨天|zuó tiān}{迟到|chí dào}{了|le}，{今天|jīn tiān}{又|yòu}{迟到|chí dào}{了|le}。 (He was late yesterday, and
  he was late again today.)
- {再|zài} for a repetition that **will happen** (or that you ask for): {这个|zhè ge}{电影|diàn yǐng}{很|hěn}{好看|hǎo kàn}，{我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{再|zài}{看|kàn}{一|yí}{遍|biàn}。 (This
  film is great: I'd like to see it again.) {请|qǐng}{明天|míng tiān}{再|zài}{来|lái}。 (Please come again tomorrow.)

One exception you'll hear: {又|yòu} is used for something future that is sure to come round again, such
as a day of the week: {明天|míng tiān}{又|yòu}{是|shì}{星期|xīng qī}{一|yī}{了|le}！ (Tomorrow's Monday again!) And you know {又|yòu} from {又|yòu}…{又|yòu}
(lesson 08): {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{又|yòu}{便宜|pián yi}{又|yòu}{好看|hǎo kàn} (both cheap and nice).

## {={只|zhǐ}=} (only) and {只能|zhǐ néng} (can only)

{={只|zhǐ}=} is an adverb, so it goes before the verb:

{我|wǒ}{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{十|shí}{块|kuài}{钱|qián}。 — I've only got ten yuan.

{他|tā}{只|zhǐ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}，{不|bù}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}。 — He only drinks tea, not coffee.

"Only he…" can't be ×{只|zhǐ}{他|tā}…: {={只|zhǐ}=} can't stand before a subject. Use {只有|zhǐ yǒu}: {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{他|tā}{知道|zhī dào}。 (Only he knows.)

{只能|zhǐ néng} is "can only", "have no choice but to":

{公园|gōng yuán}{里|lǐ}{只能|zhǐ néng}{走路|zǒu lù}，{不|bù}{能|néng}{骑|qí}{自行车|zì xíng chē}。 — In the park you can only walk: no cycling.

{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}{了|le}，{没有|méi yǒu}{地铁|dì tiě}{了|le}，{我们|wǒ men}{只能|zhǐ néng}{打车|dǎ chē}{回|huí}{家|jiā}。 — It's too late, there's no metro: we'll have to take a taxi home.

This {={只|zhǐ}=} is a different word from the measure word in HSK 1's {一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo} (a cat): same
character, different tone and meaning. With the traditional script on you'll see them apart: the
measure word is written 隻 ({一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo}), while "only" stays {={只|zhǐ}=}.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 如 | if; like | rú | 女 | 6 | {如果|rú guǒ}, {比如|bǐ rú} (lesson 28) |
| 而 | and; but (written) | ér | 而 | 6 | {而且|ér qiě} |
| 且 | moreover | qiě | 一 | 5 | {而且|ér qiě} |
| 或 | or | huò | 戈 | 8 | {或|huò}, {或者|huò zhě} |

None of the six has a different traditional form.

- {如|rú}: {女|nǚ} on the left and {口|kǒu} on the right. It's in {如果|rú guǒ} (if) and, in lesson 28, {比如|bǐ rú} (for
  example).
- {而|ér}: a grammar word of written Chinese ("and, yet"). In speech you meet it in {而且|ér qiě}. Its oldest
  shapes are usually explained as a picture of a beard; today the character keeps only its sound
  and grammar uses.
- {且|qiě} is also a sound part. You already write it in {姐|jiě} jiě ({女|nǚ} + {且|qiě}, HSK 1), where it still
  gives a close sound. It's in {租|zū} zū (禾 + {且|qiě}: {出租车|chū zū chē}, taxi) and, in lesson 29, {助|zhù} zhù ({且|qiě} + {力|lì}: {帮助|bāng zhù}).
  There the sound has drifted too far to help: it gave the sound once, but no longer matches.
- {或|huò}: 戈 (an old dagger-axe) on the right, {口|kǒu} and a short stroke below on the left. With the
  traditional script on you'll find {或|huò} inside 國 (country): 囗 around {或|huò}.
- {者|zhě}: 耂 on top, as in {老|lǎo} and {考|kǎo}, and {日|rì} below. {者|zhě} is the left half of {都|dōu} dōu: the sound no longer
  matches. As a suffix it makes "a person who…" in words you'll learn later ({记者|jì zhě}, journalist).
- {又|yòu} first drew a right hand. In simplified characters it often stands in for a complicated
  part that has nothing to do with hands: {对|duì} (traditional 對), {欢|huān} (歡), {汉|hàn} (漢), {难|nán} (難), {鸡|jī} (雞),
  {双|shuāng} (雙). {又|yòu} there is just a simple shape, not a meaning or a sound.

### Stroke order

- **而**: the top horizontal, then the short left-falling stroke under it, then the frame (the left
  vertical, then the horizontal-turn-hook on the right), and the two short verticals inside last.
- **且**: the left vertical, the top-and-right stroke, the two short horizontals inside, and the long
  bottom horizontal last.
- **或**: the long horizontal first, then {口|kǒu} and the short rising stroke below it, then 戈's long
  slanting hook, its left-falling stroke, and the dot at the top right last.
- **者**: the short horizontal and the vertical of the top, the long horizontal, the long
  left-falling stroke, then {日|rì}.
- **又**: two strokes only: the horizontal that turns down to the left, then the long right-falling
  stroke across it.

```trace
如而且或者又
```

2. Yes: buy a ticket at the door for 25 yuan ({如果|rú guǒ}{没有|méi yǒu}{卡|kǎ}，{可以|kě yǐ}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}{买|mǎi}{票|piào}).
3. Feeling unwell, having a cold or a fever ({如果|rú guǒ}{身体|shēn tǐ}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}，{或者|huò zhě}{感冒|gǎn mào}{发烧|fā shāo}{了|le}，{就|jiù}{别|bié}{来|lái}{游泳|yóu yǒng}{了|le}).
4. Only water ({不|bù}{能|néng}{吃|chī}{东西|dōng xi}，{只能|zhǐ néng}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}).

"**Swimming pool notice.** So that everyone can swim safely and happily, please note the following.
1. The pool opens at 8 a.m. and closes at 9 p.m. every day. It is closed on Monday mornings. 2. As
long as you have a swimming card, you can go in and swim. If you don't have a card, you can buy a
ticket at the door: 25 yuan a ticket. 3. Only children 1.4 metres tall and over may swim on their
own. Children under 1.4 metres must come with an adult. 4. Please shower before you go in. If you
feel unwell, or have a cold or a fever, please don't come swimming. 5. No food in the pool hall:
water only. 6. If something of yours goes missing, please tell a member of staff at once. 7. Every day from
12 to 1 the pool is cleaned, and no one can swim. 8. For safety, an adult must watch children while
they swim. Swimming
not only keeps you fit, it's a way to make new friends too. Everyone is welcome! City Swimming
Pool, 1 June."
</details>

## Write it: your own conditions

Write two sentences in characters, one with {如果|rú guǒ}…{就|jiù} and one with {只要|zhǐ yào}…{就|jiù} or {只有|zhǐ yǒu}…{才|cái}, about your
own plans. Say them aloud afterwards.

<details>
<summary>Model answers</summary>

- {如果|rú guǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{天气|tiān qì}{好|hǎo}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{骑|qí}{自行车|zì xíng chē}{去|qù}{上班|shàng bān}。 — If the weather's good tomorrow, I'll cycle to work.
- {只要|zhǐ yào}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{看|kàn}{中文|Zhōng wén}{书|shū}。 — Whenever I have time (as long as I have time), I read Chinese books.
- {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{复习|fù xí}，{才|cái}{能|néng}{记住|jì zhù}{这些|zhè xiē}{汉字|hàn zì}。 — Only by reviewing every day can I remember these characters.
  ({记住|jì zhù}: to remember, {记|jì} + the result {住|zhù}.)
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Conditions and plans
{如果|rú guǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{下雨|xià yǔ}，{我们|wǒ men}{就|jiù}{不|bú}{去|qù}{了|le}。
= If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.
{只要|zhǐ yào}{你|nǐ}{说|shuō}{慢|màn}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{听|tīng}{得|de}{懂|dǒng}。
= As long as you speak a little more slowly, I can understand.
{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{多|duō}{听|tīng}{多|duō}{说|shuō}，{才|cái}{能|néng}{学|xué}{好|hǎo}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}。
= Only by listening and speaking a lot can you learn Chinese well.
{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}？
= Tea or coffee?
{茶|chá}{或者|huò zhě}{咖啡|kā fēi}{都|dōu}{可以|kě yǐ}。
= Tea or coffee, either's fine.
{请|qǐng}{您|nín}{再|zài}{说|shuō}{一|yí}{遍|biàn}。
= Could you say that again, please?
```

## Pronunciation

- {如果|rú guǒ} rú guǒ: a rising tone, then a dipping one. Keep the *r* of {如|rú} soft, close to the *r* in
  "pleasure", not an English *r*.
- {而且|ér qiě} ér qiě: ér is the same syllable as {儿|ér} (HSK 1). {且|qiě} qiě has *q* (like *ch* in "cheese") and *ie*.
- {或者|huò zhě} huò zhě: a falling tone, then a dipping *zhě*. {或|huò} and {活|huó} (huó, {生活|shēng huó}) differ only in tone.
- {又|yòu} yòu and {有|yǒu} yǒu (to have) are the same syllable: fourth tone for "again", third for "have". {右|yòu}
  yòu (right, HSK 2) is said exactly like {又|yòu}.
- {={只|zhǐ}=} (only) is third tone; the measure word in {一|yì}{只|zhī}{猫|māo} is first tone.
- {为了|wèi le} wèi le: {为|wèi} is fourth tone here, and {了|le} is light.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{去|qù}，{就|jiù}{我|wǒ}{去|qù}~~: {就|jiù} is an adverb and goes after the subject: {如果|rú guǒ}{你|nǐ}{去|qù}，{我|wǒ}{就|jiù}{去|qù}.
- ~~{只有|zhǐ yǒu}{多|duō}{练习|liàn xí}，{就|jiù}{能|néng}{学|xué}{好|hǎo}~~: {只有|zhǐ yǒu} pairs with {才|cái}: {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{多|duō}{练习|liàn xí}，{才|cái}{能|néng}{学|xué}{好|hǎo}. ({只要|zhǐ yào} pairs with {就|jiù}.)
- ~~{你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{或者|huò zhě}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}？~~ as a question: a choice question takes {还是|hái shi}: {你|nǐ}{喝|hē}{茶|chá}{还是|hái shi}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}？
- ~~{他|tā}{昨天|zuó tiān}{来|lái}{了|le}，{今天|jīn tiān}{再|zài}{来|lái}{了|le}~~: a repetition that has happened takes {又|yòu}: {今天|jīn tiān}{又|yòu}{来|lái}{了|le}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{为了|wèi le}{去|qù}{中国|Zhōng guó}{工作|gōng zuò}~~: put {为了|wèi le} first, or use {是|shì}{为了|wèi le} at the end: {为了|wèi le}{去|qù}{中国|Zhōng guó}{工作|gōng zuò}，{我|wǒ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ} /
  {我|wǒ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{是|shì}{为了|wèi le}{去|qù}{中国|Zhōng guó}{工作|gōng zuò}.
- ~~{只|zhǐ}{他|tā}{知道|zhī dào}~~: "only he" is {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{他|tā}: {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{他|tā}{知道|zhī dào}.
- ~~{不但|bú dàn}{他|tā}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{而且|ér qiě}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}~~ with one subject: the subject goes first: {他|tā}{不但|bú dàn}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{而且|ér qiě}{会|huì}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}.

## Key points

- {如果|rú guǒ} (…{的话|de huà})，(subject) {就|jiù}…: if; {的话|de huà} can close the clause or replace {如果|rú guǒ}.
- {只要|zhǐ yào}…{就|jiù}…: the condition is enough (as long as). {只有|zhǐ yǒu}…{才|cái}…: the only way (only if).
- {不但|bú dàn}…{而且|ér qiě} (…{也|yě} / {还|hái}): not only… but also; one subject goes before {不但|bú dàn}.
- {为了|wèi le} + goal (first) or {是|shì}{为了|wèi le} + goal (at the end): purpose. {为|wèi} + person: for someone.
- {向|xiàng} + direction (= {往|wǎng}) or + person: {向|xiàng}{老师|lǎo shī}{请假|qǐng jià}, {向|xiàng}{他|tā}{学习|xué xí}.
- {或者|huò zhě} / {或|huò} in statements, {还是|hái shi} in questions.
- {又|yòu}: again (it happened); {再|zài}: again (it will).
- {={只|zhǐ}=} zhǐ + verb: only; {只能|zhǐ néng}: can only. "Only he" is {只有|zhǐ yǒu}{他|tā}.
- New characters: {如|rú} {而|ér} {且|qiě} {或|huò} {者|zhě} {又|yòu}, all handwriting characters.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Advice, obligation and exceptions: 应该, 得, 必须, 除了
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 26 set conditions. This lesson is about what people should do, have to do and don't need
to do, and about the small adverbs that make advice sound natural:

- {应该|yīng gāi}, {该|gāi}, {得|děi} and {必须|bì xū}: should, have to, must, and their negatives ({不|bù}{应该|yīng gāi}, {不用|bú yòng}, {不必|bú bì});
- {最好|zuì hǎo}: had better;
- {除了|chú le}…({以外|yǐ wài}): except, and besides;
- {总|zǒng} / {总是|zǒng shì} (always), {常|cháng} / {常常|cháng cháng} (often) and {一直|yì zhí} (all along), {几乎|jī hū} (almost);
- {大概|dà gài} (probably), {一定|yí dìng} (certainly, must be), {看来|kàn lái} (it seems);
- {可是|kě shì} and {可|kě} (but), {只是|zhǐ shì} (it's just that);
- {其他|qí tā} and {别的|bié de} (other).

At the end you can give advice, explain rules, and say what you think is probably true.

## Should, have to, must: four modal verbs

All four go before the verb, like the other **[[modal verbs]]** you know ({会|huì}, {能|néng}, {可以|kě yǐ}, {想|xiǎng}, {要|yào}, {需要|xū yào}).
They differ in strength and in style:

| Word | Strength | Style | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {应该|yīng gāi} yīng gāi | should (it's right, it's sensible) | everyday, any register | {你|nǐ}{应该|yīng gāi}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}。 You should rest more. |
| {该|gāi} gāi | should; it's time to | spoken | {十一|shí yī}{点|diǎn}{了|le}，{你|nǐ}{该|gāi}{睡觉|shuì jiào}{了|le}。 It's eleven: time you went to bed. |
| {得|děi} děi | have to, need to | spoken, informal | {我|wǒ}{得|děi}{走|zǒu}{了|le}。 I have to go. |
| {必须|bì xū} bì xū | must (a rule, no choice) | firm; rules and notices | {你|nǐ}{必须|bì xū}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{以前|yǐ qián}{到|dào}。 You must arrive before eight. |

{应该|yīng gāi} also makes a reasonable guess: {他|tā}{七|qī}{点|diǎn}{出发|chū fā}{的|de}，{现在|xiàn zài}{应该|yīng gāi}{到|dào}{了|le}。 (He left at seven: he should
be there by now.)

{该|gāi} has two set uses worth learning whole: {该|gāi}{你|nǐ}{了|le}！ (Your turn!) and {该|gāi} + verb + {了|le} (it's time to…):
{该|gāi}{吃|chī}{饭|fàn}{了|le} (time to eat), {我|wǒ}{该|gāi}{回|huí}{家|jiā}{了|le} (I should be getting home).

{得|děi} is the same character as the particle {得|de} of {说|shuō}{得|de}{很|hěn}{好|hǎo} and the verb {得|dé} "to get" of
lesson 21 ({得分|dé fēn}). As "have to" it comes before a verb and is third tone: {我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{得|děi}{早|zǎo}{起|qǐ}。 (I have to get
up early tomorrow.)

## Saying "don't have to"

The negatives aren't simply {不|bù} + the word. This table is the one to remember:

| Positive | Negative | Meaning of the negative |
|---|---|---|
| {应该|yīng gāi} | {不|bù}{应该|yīng gāi} | shouldn't: {你|nǐ}{不|bù}{应该|yīng gāi}{这么|zhè me}{说|shuō}。 You shouldn't say that. |
| {该|gāi} | {不|bù}{该|gāi} | shouldn't (spoken): {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{该|gāi}{告诉|gào su}{他|tā}。 I shouldn't have told him. |
| {得|děi} | {不用|bú yòng} (never ×{不得|bù dé}) | don't have to: {你|nǐ}{不用|bú yòng}{去|qù}。 You don't have to go. |
| {必须|bì xū} | {不用|bú yòng} / {不必|bú bì} | needn't: {明天|míng tiān}{不用|bú yòng} / {不必|bú bì}{来|lái}。 You needn't come tomorrow. |

{不用|bú yòng} (lesson 05) is the everyday "no need to". {不必|bú bì} says the same, a little more formally;
it's made of {不|bù} and the {必|bì} of {必须|bì xū}. ×{不|bú}{必须|bì xū} doesn't exist. You'll see {不得|bù dé} on notices with a
different meaning, "may not", so don't use it for "don't have to".

## {最好|zuì hǎo}: had better

{最好|zuì hǎo} before a verb gives advice: "you'd best…". It's softer than {应该|yīng gāi}.

{你|nǐ}{最好|zuì hǎo}{早点儿|zǎo diǎnr}{去|qù}，{晚|wǎn}{了|le}{人|rén}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 — You'd better go early: later it gets crowded.

{外面|wài miàn}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}，{你|nǐ}{最好|zuì hǎo}{带|dài}{伞|sǎn}。 — It's raining outside: you'd better take an umbrella.

{你|nǐ}{最好|zuì hǎo}{别|bié}{告诉|gào su}{他|tā}。 — You'd better not tell him.

The negative is {最好|zuì hǎo}{别|bié} or {最好|zuì hǎo}{不要|bú yào}. On its own {最好|zuì hǎo} is also the plain "best": {这个|zhè ge}{办法|bàn fǎ}{最好|zuì hǎo} (this way is
best).

## {除了|chú le}…({以外|yǐ wài}): except and besides

{除了|chú le} X ({以外|yǐ wài}) takes X out of the picture, and the second clause says what is true of the rest. What
follows decides the meaning:

- with {都|dōu}: **except** (X is the exception):
  {除了|chú le}{小王|Xiǎo Wáng}{以外|yǐ wài}，{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}。 — We've all been to Beijing except Xiao Wang.
- with {还|hái} or {也|yě}: **besides, as well as** (X is included, and there's more):
  {除了|chú le}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{他|tā}{还|hái}{会|huì}{说|shuō}{英语|Yīng yǔ}。 — Besides Chinese, he speaks English too.
  {除了|chú le}{米饭|mǐ fàn}，{我|wǒ}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}。 — As well as rice, I really like noodles too.

{以外|yǐ wài} is optional, and so is a comma after the {除了|chú le} phrase when it is short. English "except" and
"besides" are different words; Chinese uses one frame and lets {都|dōu} or {还|hái} / {也|yě} decide.

## Always, often, all along, almost

| Word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {总是|zǒng shì} / {总|zǒng} | always, every time (a habit; often a complaint) | {他|tā}{总是|zǒng shì}{迟到|chí dào}。 He's always late. |
| {常常|cháng cháng} / {常|cháng} | often | {我们|wǒ men}{常常|cháng cháng}{去|qù}{那|nà}{家|jiā}{饭馆|fàn guǎn}。 We often go to that restaurant. |
| {经常|jīng cháng} (HSK 2) | often, regularly | {他|tā}{经常|jīng cháng}{出国|chū guó}。 He often travels abroad. |
| {一直|yì zhí} (lesson 21) | all along, without a break | {雨|yǔ}{一直|yì zhí}{下|xià}{了|le}{三|sān}{天|tiān}。 It rained non-stop for three days. |
| {几乎|jī hū} | almost | {他|tā}{几乎|jī hū}{每|měi}{天|tiān}{都|dōu}{锻炼|duàn liàn}。 He exercises almost every day. |

- {总|zǒng} is the short form of {总是|zǒng shì}, common before a negative: {他|tā}{总|zǒng}{不|bú}{在|zài}{家|jiā}。 (He's never at home.)
- {常|cháng} and {常常|cháng cháng} mean the same; {常|cháng} is shorter and a little more written. The negative is {不|bù}{常|cháng}: {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{常|cháng}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}。
  (I don't often drink coffee.) ×{不|bù}{常常|cháng cháng} is wrong.
- {总是|zǒng shì} is "again and again"; {一直|yì zhí} is "without stopping, the whole time". {他|tā}{总是|zǒng shì}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} (he keeps
  ringing me) vs {他|tā}{一直|yì zhí}{给|gěi}{我|wǒ}{打电话|dǎ diàn huà} (he's been ringing me non-stop).
- {几乎|jī hū} goes before what it qualifies, and often brings {都|dōu} or {没|méi}: {几乎|jī hū}{每|měi}{个|gè}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{知道|zhī dào} (almost everyone knows),
  {我|wǒ}{几乎|jī hū}{没|méi}{睡|shuì} (I hardly slept). Note its tone: jī hū, first and first, not the jǐ of {几|jǐ}{个|gè}.

## Probably, certainly, it seems: {大概|dà gài}, {一定|yí dìng}, {看来|kàn lái}

These three show how sure you are.

- {大概|dà gài}: probably; roughly. {他|tā}{大概|dà gài}{不|bù}{来|lái}{了|le}。 (He probably isn't coming.) {从|cóng}{这儿|zhèr}{到|dào}{机场|jī chǎng}{大概|dà gài}{要|yào}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。 (It's
  about an hour from here to the airport.)
- {一定|yí dìng}: certainly, definitely. With a plan it's a promise: {我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{一定|yí dìng}{来|lái}。 (I'll definitely come
  tomorrow.) With a guess it's "must be": {你|nǐ}{一定|yí dìng}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}{了|le}{吧|ba}！ (You must be tired!) {一定|yí dìng}{要|yào} + verb is "be sure
  to": {你|nǐ}{一定|yí dìng}{要|yào}{来|lái}！ {不|bù}{一定|yí dìng} is "not necessarily": {贵|guì}{的|de}{不|bù}{一定|yí dìng}{好|hǎo}。 (Expensive isn't necessarily good.)
- {看来|kàn lái}: it looks as if (judging from what you can see). It usually starts the sentence: {看来|kàn lái}{要|yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。
  (Looks like rain.) {看来|kàn lái}{他|tā}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}。 (It seems he doesn't know about it.)

{一定|yí dìng} is yí dìng: {一|yī} changes to the rising tone before a fourth tone.

## But: {可是|kě shì}, {可|kě} and {只是|zhǐ shì}

- {可是|kě shì} means "but", like {但是|dàn shì}, and is a little more spoken: {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{可是|kě shì}{没有|méi yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}。 It pairs with {虽然|suī rán} too:
  {虽然|suī rán}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}，{可是|kě shì}{很|hěn}{开心|kāi xīn}。
- {可|kě} alone is a short spoken "but": {我|wǒ}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}，{可|kě}{我|wǒ}{没|méi}{时间|shí jiān}。 It has a second, very common use: it
  stresses what follows, like "really" or "do". {今天|jīn tiān}{可|kě}{冷|lěng}{了|le}！ (It's so cold today!) {你|nǐ}{可|kě}{别|bié}{忘|wàng}{了|le}！ (Whatever you
  do, don't forget!)
- {只是|zhǐ shì} is a soft "it's just that", which keeps the good part in front: {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{衣服|yī fu}{很|hěn}{好看|hǎo kàn}，{只是|zhǐ shì}{有点儿|yǒu diǎnr}{贵|guì}。
  (It's a nice top, it's just a bit expensive.) It is also "only, merely": {我|wǒ}{只是|zhǐ shì}{问|wèn}{一下|yí xià}。 (I'm only
  asking.)

Don't stack two "but"s: ×{可是|kě shì}…{但是|dàn shì}.

## {其他|qí tā} and {别的|bié de}: other

Both mean "other". {其他|qí tā} is more general and can mean "the rest"; {别的|bié de} is more spoken.

{其他|qí tā}{人|rén}{都|dōu}{走|zǒu}{了|le}。 — The others have all gone.

{还|hái}{有|yǒu}{别的|bié de}{问题|wèn tí}{吗|ma}？ — Any other questions?

{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{吃|chī}{面条儿|miàn tiáor}，{有|yǒu}{别的|bié de}{吗|ma}？ — I don't want noodles: is there anything else?

{别的|bié de} can stand alone ("anything else"); {其他|qí tā} alone usually takes {的|de}: {其他|qí tā}{的|de}.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 除 | remove; except | chú | 阝 | 9 | {除了|chú le} |
| 总 (traditional 總) | always; total | zǒng | 心 | 9 | {总|zǒng}, {总是|zǒng shì} |
| 乎 | (in {几乎|jī hū}; a classical question particle) | hū | 丿 | 5 | {几乎|jī hū} |
| 概 | general; roughly | gài | 木 | 13 | {大概|dà gài} |
| 其 | his, its; that | qí | 八 | 8 | {其他|qí tā}, {其实|qí shí} (lesson 28) |
| 必 | certainly; must | bì | 心 | 5 | {必须|bì xū} |
| 须 (traditional 須) | must; (once) beard | xū | 彡 | 9 | {必须|bì xū} |
| 应 (traditional 應) | should; respond | yīng | 广 | 7 | {应该|yīng gāi} |
| 该 (traditional 該) | should; owe | gāi | 讠 | 8 | {应该|yīng gāi}, {该|gāi} |

- {除|chú}: 阝 on the left, as in {阿|ā} ({阿姨|ā yí}) and {院|yuàn} ({医院|yī yuàn}), and 余 on the right, which once gave the sound
  (yú): it no longer matches chú.
- {总|zǒng}: a dot and a short left-falling stroke, {口|kǒu} and {心|xīn}. Traditional 總 is built quite differently, with the silk radical 糸
  on the left and 17 strokes.
- {乎|hū}: a left-falling stroke, a dot and a short left-falling stroke under it, a horizontal and a vertical hook. In classical Chinese {乎|hū} ends
  a question, much as {吗|ma} does today; if you read the Analects lesson (20h1), you met it in {不|bú}{亦|yì}{说|yuè}{乎|hū}.
- {概|gài}: 木 (tree) on the left and 既 on the right, which gave the sound long ago (jì): it no longer
  matches gài.
- {其|qí} is a good sound part today: {其|qí} qí gives the sound of {期|qī} qī in {星期|xīng qī} and {学期|xué qī}, with {月|yuè} added.
  It's also the first character of {其他|qí tā} and {其实|qí shí}.
- {必|bì}: it looks like {心|xīn} with a stroke through it, and that's how most dictionaries describe it, but it
  isn't written as {心|xīn} plus a stroke (see Stroke order).
- {须|xū}: 彡 (three strokes of hair) and {页|yè} (the head). The character first meant "beard"; "must" is a
  meaning it took on later. In traditional script, {必须|bì xū} is 必須, and a beard is 鬚.
- {应|yīng}: 广 (a roof with a wall) over two dots, a left-falling stroke and a long horizontal. Traditional
  應 has {心|xīn} at the bottom and 17 strokes.
- {该|gāi}: 讠 (speech) and 亥 (hài), a sound part you know from {孩|hái} hái ({孩子|hái zi}) and {刻|kè} kè (lesson 21's
  {一|yí}{刻|kè}, a quarter of an hour). In {孩|hái} and {该|gāi} it still sounds close; in {刻|kè} it no longer matches.

### Stroke order

- **必**: follow the pad's numbers: the dots and the bent hook come one at a time, and the long
  left-falling stroke comes fourth, cutting through the hook, before the last dot on the right. It is
  not {心|xīn} with a stroke added at the end.
- **乎**: the short left-falling stroke on top first, then the dot on the left and the short
  left-falling stroke on the right, the horizontal, and the vertical hook last.
- **总**: the dot and the short left-falling stroke on top, then {口|kǒu}, then {心|xīn} (the dot, the bent hook, two dots).
- **其**: the top horizontal, then the two verticals, the two short
  horizontals inside, the long horizontal, and the left-falling stroke and the dot at the bottom.
- **应**, like every character with 广: the dot and the horizontal, the long left-falling stroke,
  then what's inside, and the bottom horizontal last.

```trace
除总乎概其必须
```

```trace
应该
```

**Write it**: {除|chú} {总|zǒng} {其|qí} {必|bì} {须|xū} {应|yīng} {该|gāi} are handwriting characters (✎). Write each three times from memory,
then the words {除了|chú le}, {总是|zǒng shì}, {其他|qí tā}, {必须|bì xū} and {应该|yīng gāi}.

### Handwriting review

Five handwriting characters of HSK 1 and 2 used in this lesson's sentences: 要 去 来 过 比. Write each
with a word: {需要|xū yào}, {回去|huí qù}, {看来|kàn lái}, {过去|guò qù}, {比较|bǐ jiào}.

```trace
要去来过比
```

## Dialogue: you should see a doctor

{大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫, David) has a cold. His friend {王芳|Wáng Fāng} (王芳) gives him advice.

```dialogue
# You should see a doctor
王芳: {大卫|Dà wèi}，{你|nǐ}{怎么|zěn me}{了|le}？{你|nǐ}{看起来|kàn qǐ lai}{很|hěn}{累|lèi}。
= David, what's wrong? You look tired.
大卫: {我|wǒ}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le}，{昨天|zuó tiān}{晚上|wǎn shang}{几乎|jī hū}{没|méi}{睡|shuì}。
= I've got a cold. I hardly slept last night.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{应该|yīng gāi}{去|qù}{医院|yī yuàn}{看看|kàn kan}。
= You should go and see a doctor.
大卫: {不用|bú yòng}，{只是|zhǐ shì}{感冒|gǎn mào}，{休息|xiū xi}{两|liǎng}{天|tiān}{就|jiù}{好|hǎo}{了|le}。
= No need. It's only a cold; a couple of days' rest and I'll be fine.
王芳: {你|nǐ}{总是|zǒng shì}{这么|zhè me}{说|shuō}！{上|shàng}{次|cì}{你|nǐ}{也|yě}{说|shuō}{不用|bú yòng}，{可是|kě shì}{后来|hòu lái}{病|bìng}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{星期|xīng qī}。
= You always say that! Last time you said there was no need too, and then you were ill for a week.
大卫: {好|hǎo}{吧|ba}，{好|hǎo}{吧|ba}。{可|kě}{我|wǒ}{明天|míng tiān}{得|děi}{上班|shàng bān}。
= All right, all right. But I have to go to work tomorrow.
王芳: {看来|kàn lái}{你|nǐ}{得|děi}{请假|qǐng jià}{了|le}。{你们|nǐ men}{经理|jīng lǐ}{一定|yí dìng}{会|huì}{同意|tóng yì}{的|de}。
= Looks like you'll have to take time off. Your manager's sure to agree.
大卫: {大概|dà gài}{吧|ba}。{除了|chú le}{请假|qǐng jià}，{我|wǒ}{还|hái}{该|gāi}{做|zuò}{什么|shén me}？
= Probably. Apart from taking time off, what else should I do?
王芳: {你|nǐ}{最好|zuì hǎo}{多|duō}{喝|hē}{水|shuǐ}，{早点儿|zǎo diǎnr}{睡觉|shuì jiào}。{还|hái}{有|yǒu}，{别的|bié de}{事情|shì qing}{都|dōu}{别|bié}{做|zuò}{了|le}！
= You'd better drink plenty of water and go to bed early. And don't do anything else!
大卫: {你|nǐ}{可|kě}{真|zhēn}{像|xiàng}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}！
= You really are just like my mum!
```

- {看起来|kàn qǐ lai}: "it looks (as if)", from {看|kàn} + {起来|qǐ lái} (HSK 2): said of how someone or something looks.
- {一定|yí dìng}{会|huì}…{的|de}: a promise or a confident guess; the {的|de} at the end makes it sound sure.
- {你|nǐ}{可|kě}{真|zhēn}{像|xiàng}{我|wǒ}{妈妈|mā ma}: {可|kě} stresses {真|zhēn}{像|xiàng}, "you really are…". {像|xiàng} is lesson 04's "to look like".

## Reading: before the exam

A message from a teacher to her class, the kind of notice the level-3 reading section uses.

> **{关于|guān yú}{明天|míng tiān}{的|de}{考试|kǎo shì}** ({关于|guān yú}: about, lesson 28)
>
> {同学|tóng xué}{们|men}：
>
> {明天|míng tiān}{上午|shàng wǔ}{九|jiǔ}{点|diǎn}{考试|kǎo shì}，{考试|kǎo shì}{大概|dà gài}{要|yào}{两|liǎng}{个|gè}{小时|xiǎo shí}。{请|qǐng}{注意|zhù yì}{下面|xià miàn}{几|jǐ}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}：
>
> {第|dì}{一|yī}，{大家|dà jiā}{必须|bì xū}{在|zài}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{以前|yǐ qián}{到|dào}{教室|jiào shì}，{迟到|chí dào}{十五|shí wǔ}{分钟|fēn zhōng}{以上|yǐ shàng}{就|jiù}{不|bù}{能|néng}{进去|jìn qù}{了|le}。
>
> {第|dì}{二|èr}，{一定|yí dìng}{要|yào}{带|dài}{学生卡|xué sheng kǎ}，{没有|méi yǒu}{学生卡|xué sheng kǎ}{的|de}{同学|tóng xué}{可以|kě yǐ}{带|dài}{护照|hù zhào}。{除了|chú le}{笔|bǐ}{以外|yǐ wài}，{其他|qí tā}{东西|dōng xi}{都|dōu}{不|bù}{能|néng}{带|dài}{进|jìn}{教室|jiào shì}。{手机|shǒu jī}{得|děi}{关机|guān jī}，{放|fàng}{在|zài}{门口|mén kǒu}{的|de}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}。
>
> {第|dì}{三|sān}，{不用|bú yòng}{带|dài}{词典|cí diǎn}，{也|yě}{不用|bú yòng}{带|dài}{书|shū}。
>
> {考试|kǎo shì}{的|de}{时候|shí hou}{不|bù}{能|néng}{说话|shuō huà}。{如果|rú guǒ}{有|yǒu}{问题|wèn tí}，{就|jiù}{请|qǐng}{举手|jǔ shǒu}{问|wèn}{老师|lǎo shī}。{如果|rú guǒ}{身体|shēn tǐ}{不|bù}{舒服|shū fu}，{可以|kě yǐ}{告诉|gào su}{老师|lǎo shī}，{但是|dàn shì}{不|bù}{能|néng}{离开|lí kāi}{教室|jiào shì}。{考|kǎo}{完|wán}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{请|qǐng}{先|xiān}{把|bǎ}{纸|zhǐ}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{桌子|zhuō zi}{上|shàng}，{然后|rán hòu}{再|zài}{离开|lí kāi}。
>
> {最近|zuì jìn}{天气|tiān qì}{冷|lěng}，{很|hěn}{多|duō}{同学|tóng xué}{感冒|gǎn mào}{了|le}。{考试|kǎo shì}{以前|yǐ qián}，{大家|dà jiā}{最好|zuì hǎo}{早点儿|zǎo diǎnr}{睡觉|shuì jiào}，{别|bié}{太|tài}{晚|wǎn}。{几乎|jī hū}{每|měi}{次|cì}{考试|kǎo shì}{都|dōu}{有|yǒu}{同学|tóng xué}{因为|yīn wèi}{没|méi}{睡|shuì}{好|hǎo}{考|kǎo}{得|de}{不|bù}{好|hǎo}，{希望|xī wàng}{这|zhè}{次|cì}{不|bú}{会|huì}。
>
> {祝|zhù}{大家|dà jiā}{考|kǎo}{得|de}{好|hǎo}！
>
> {王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}

{学生卡|xué sheng kǎ} is a student card, {举手|jǔ shǒu} is "to raise your hand", and {祝|zhù} is "to wish
(someone well)". {第|dì}{一|yī}, {第|dì}{二|èr} count the points (first, second).

1. What time must the students be in the classroom?
2. What may they take into the room?
3. Name two things they don't need to bring.
4. What is the teacher's advice for the night before?

<details>
<summary>Answers and translation</summary>

1. Before half past eight ({必须|bì xū}{在|zài}{八|bā}{点|diǎn}{半|bàn}{以前|yǐ qián}{到|dào}{教室|jiào shì}); fifteen minutes late or more and they can't go in.
2. Only a pen, and their student card or passport ({除了|chú le}{笔|bǐ}{以外|yǐ wài}，{其他|qí tā}{东西|dōng xi}{都|dōu}{不|bù}{能|néng}{带|dài}{进|jìn}{教室|jiào shì}). Phones are switched off
   and left on the table by the door.
3. A dictionary and books ({不用|bú yòng}{带|dài}{词典|cí diǎn}，{也|yě}{不用|bú yòng}{带|dài}{书|shū}).
4. Go to bed early ({最好|zuì hǎo}{早点儿|zǎo diǎnr}{睡觉|shuì jiào}): almost every exam, someone does badly from lack of sleep.

"**About tomorrow's exam.** Dear students, the exam is at nine tomorrow morning and will take about
two hours. Please note the following. First, everyone must be in the classroom by half past eight;
if you're fifteen minutes late or more you can't go in. Second, be sure to bring your student card;
if you don't have one you can bring your passport. Apart from a pen, nothing else may be taken
into the classroom. Phones have to be switched off and put on the table by the door. Third, you
don't need to bring a dictionary or books. No talking during the exam. If you have a question,
raise your hand and ask the teacher. If you feel unwell you can tell the teacher, but you can't
leave the room. When you've finished, put your paper on the desk first, then leave. It's cold at the moment and many of you have colds. You'd
best go to bed early before the exam, not too late. Almost every exam, someone does badly because
they didn't sleep well; I hope this time no one will. Good luck, everyone! Ms Wang"
</details>

## Write it: give some advice

A friend is going to China for the first time. Write two sentences of advice, one with {应该|yīng gāi} or {最好|zuì hǎo}
and one with {一定|yí dìng}{要|yào} or {别|bié}.

<details>
<summary>Model answers</summary>

- {你|nǐ}{最好|zuì hǎo}{带|dài}{一|yì}{张|zhāng}{银行卡|yín háng kǎ}，{那儿|nàr}{很|hěn}{多|duō}{地方|dì fang}{不|bù}{能|néng}{用|yòng}{信用卡|xìn yòng kǎ}。 — You'd better take a bank card: a lot of places there
  don't take credit cards. (A claim about your own trip: check before you go.)
- {你|nǐ}{应该|yīng gāi}{学|xué}{一点儿|yì diǎnr}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{这样|zhè yàng}{会|huì}{方便|fāng biàn}{很|hěn}{多|duō}。 — You should learn a bit of Chinese: it will make things much easier.
- {你|nǐ}{一定|yí dìng}{要|yào}{去|qù}{爬|pá}{山|shān}，{那儿|nàr}{的|de}{山|shān}{很|hěn}{漂亮|piào liang}。 — Be sure to go hiking: the mountains there are beautiful.
</details>

## Say it

```speak
# Advice and obligation
{你|nǐ}{应该|yīng gāi}{多|duō}{休息|xiū xi}。
= You should rest more.
{我|wǒ}{得|děi}{走|zǒu}{了|le}，{明天|míng tiān}{见|jiàn}！
= I have to go: see you tomorrow!
{你|nǐ}{不用|bú yòng}{来|lái}，{我|wǒ}{一|yí}{个|gè}{人|rén}{可以|kě yǐ}。
= You don't need to come: I can manage on my own.
{你|nǐ}{最好|zuì hǎo}{早点儿|zǎo diǎnr}{去|qù}。
= You'd better go early.
{除了|chú le}{他|tā}{以外|yǐ wài}，{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}{去|qù}{过|guo}。
= We've all been, except him.
{看来|kàn lái}{要|yào}{下雨|xià yǔ}{了|le}。
= Looks like rain.
```

## Pronunciation

- {应该|yīng gāi} yīng gāi: two high, level tones. Hold them both up.
- {得|děi} as "have to" is děi, third tone: {我|wǒ}{得|děi}{走|zǒu}{了|le} wǒ děi zǒu le (three third tones in a row: usually said wó déi zǒu le, with the first two rising).
  The particle {得|de} is a light de; {得|dé} "to get" is dé.
- {必须|bì xū} bì xū: a short fall, then a level *xū* with rounded lips (ü).
- {几乎|jī hū} jī hū: both first tone. {几|jǐ} is jǐ in {几|jǐ}{个|gè} (how many) but jī in {几乎|jī hū}.
- {其他|qí tā} qí tā: a rise, then a level tone. {其实|qí shí} (lesson 28) is qí shí.
- {总是|zǒng shì} zǒng shì: the *z* is a "dz" sound, *ong* as in {东|dōng} dōng.
- {大概|dà gài} dà gài and {一定|yí dìng} yí dìng: two falling tones in a row in {大概|dà gài}; {一|yī} rises before {定|dìng}.

## Common mistakes

- ~~{你|nǐ}{得|děi}{不|bú}{去|qù}~~ or ~~{你|nǐ}{不得|bù dé}{去|qù}~~ for "you don't have to go": the negative of {得|děi} is {不用|bú yòng}: {你|nǐ}{不用|bú yòng}{去|qù}.
- ~~{不|bú}{必须|bì xū}~~: say {不用|bú yòng} or {不必|bú bì}.
- ~~{我|wǒ}{常常|cháng cháng}{不|bù}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}~~ for "I don't often drink coffee": {我|wǒ}{不|bù}{常|cháng}{喝|hē}{咖啡|kā fēi}. ({常常|cháng cháng}{不|bù} means "often don't", a different
  idea.)
- {除了|chú le} with the wrong partner: {除了|chú le}{他|tā}{以外|yǐ wài}，{我们|wǒ men}{都|dōu}… (except him) vs {除了|chú le}{他|tā}{以外|yǐ wài}，{我们|wǒ men}{还|hái}… (him, and others too).
- ~~{可是|kě shì}…{但是|dàn shì}~~ in one sentence: one "but" is enough.
- {几乎|jī hū} said jǐ hū: it's jī hū.
- ~~{他|tā}{应该|yīng gāi}{去|qù}{必须|bì xū}~~: a modal verb goes before the main verb, one at a time: {他|tā}{必须|bì xū}{去|qù}.

## Key points

- {应该|yīng gāi} (should; should be), {该|gāi} (should; it's time: {该|gāi}{你|nǐ}{了|le}), {得|děi} (have to, spoken), {必须|bì xū} (must).
- Negatives: {不|bù}{应该|yīng gāi}, {不|bù}{该|gāi}, and for "don't have to" {不用|bú yòng} / {不必|bú bì} (never {不得|bù dé}, {不|bú}{必须|bì xū}).
- {最好|zuì hǎo} + verb: had better; {最好|zuì hǎo}{别|bié} + verb: had better not.
- {除了|chú le}…({以外|yǐ wài}) + {都|dōu}: except; + {还|hái} / {也|yě}: besides.
- {总是|zǒng shì} (always), {常常|cháng cháng} / {常|cháng} (often; not often = {不|bù}{常|cháng}), {一直|yì zhí} (non-stop), {几乎|jī hū} (almost, jī hū).
- {大概|dà gài} (probably; about), {一定|yí dìng} (definitely; must be; {不|bù}{一定|yí dìng} not necessarily), {看来|kàn lái} (it seems).
- {可是|kě shì} / {可|kě} (but; {可|kě} also stresses), {只是|zhǐ shì} (it's just that; only), {其他|qí tā} / {别的|bié de} (other).
- New characters: {除|chú} {总|zǒng} {乎|hū} {概|gài} {其|qí} {必|bì} {须|xū} {应|yīng} {该|gāi}; handwriting: {除|chú} {总|zǒng} {其|qí} {必|bì} {须|xū} {应|yīng} {该|gāi}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Telling a story: what happened
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

One of the tasks HSK 3 sets is to tell what happened: an event with its cause, how it went and
how it ended. You already have most of the tools: {了|le} and {过|guo}, {是|shì}…{的|de}, time words, {先|xiān}…{然后|rán hòu},
{后来|hòu lái} and {最后|zuì hòu} (lesson 25), {突然|tū rán} (lesson 10), {终于|zhōng yú} (lesson 21), {被|bèi} (lesson 13). This lesson adds:

- verbs of meeting and finding: {遇到|yù dào}, {遇见|yù jiàn}, {发现|fā xiàn};
- verbs of ending and changing: {结束|jié shù}, {分开|fēn kāi}, {变成|biàn chéng};
- {长|zhǎng} (to grow; head of…) and {过去|guò qù} (the past);
- words for an argument: {当然|dāng rán} (of course), {其实|qí shí} (actually), {比如|bǐ rú} (for example), {关于|guān yú} (about),
  {主要|zhǔ yào} and {重要|zhòng yào} (main, important);
- {怎样|zěn yàng} and {怎么办|zěn me bàn}, {行|xíng} and {不行|bù xíng}, {常见|cháng jiàn} and {常用|cháng yòng};
- **[[rhetorical questions]]**: questions that aren't really asking ({你|nǐ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}{吗|ma}？).

At the end you can tell a short story in order, and argue a point in a few sentences.

## A story in three parts

A good short narrative, in speech or in writing, has the shape the HSK 3 task asks for:

| Part | What it says | Useful words |
|---|---|---|
| Cause (the start) | when, where, who, and what started it | {那|nà}{天|tiān}, {去年|qù nián}, {有一次|yǒu yí cì} (once), …{的|de}{时候|shí hou}, {因为|yīn wèi} |
| Process (what happened) | the events in order | {先|xiān}, {然后|rán hòu}, {后来|hòu lái}, {突然|tū rán}, {这|zhè}{时候|shí hou} (at that moment), {遇到|yù dào}, {发现|fā xiàn} |
| Result (the end) | how it ended, and what it meant | {最后|zuì hòu}, {终于|zhōng yú}, {从|cóng}{那|nà}{天|tiān}{以后|yǐ hòu}, {所以|suǒ yǐ}, {变成|biàn chéng} |

{有一次|yǒu yí cì} (once, one time) is the classic way to begin. Here is a short example, in five sentences:

{有一次|yǒu yí cì}，{我|wǒ}{去|qù}{北京|Běi jīng}{出差|chū chāi} (on a work trip)，{在|zài}{机场|jī chǎng}{发现|fā xiàn}{护照|hù zhào}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}。{我|wǒ}{很|hěn}{着急|zháo jí}，{先|xiān}{给|gěi}{公司|gōng sī}{打|dǎ}{了|le}{电话|diàn huà}，{然后|rán hòu}{去|qù}{找|zhǎo}{了|le}{机场|jī chǎng}{的|de}{工作人员|gōng zuò rén yuán}。{后来|hòu lái}，{一|yí}{个|gè}{服务员|fú wù yuán}{找|zhǎo}{到|dào}{了|le}{我|wǒ}{的|de}{护照|hù zhào}：{它|tā}{在|zài}{卫生间|wèi shēng jiān}{里|lǐ}！{最后|zuì hòu}，{我|wǒ}{终于|zhōng yú}{上|shàng}{了|le}{飞机|fēi jī}。{从|cóng}{那|nà}{天|tiān}{以后|yǐ hòu}，{我|wǒ}{出门|chū mén}{以前|yǐ qián}{总是|zǒng shì}{先|xiān}{看看|kàn kan}{护照|hù zhào}{在|zài}{不|bu}{在|zài}。

— Once, on a work trip to Beijing, I found at the airport that my passport was missing. I was very
worried: first I rang the office, then I went to find the airport staff. Later a member of staff
found my passport: it was in the toilets! In the end I made it onto the plane. Since that day,
before I go out I always check my passport is there.

{出差|chū chāi} (to go on a business trip) and {工作人员|gōng zuò rén yuán} (staff) are glossed: the rest is course
Chinese. Note how {先|xiān}…{然后|rán hòu} gives the order, {后来|hòu lái} moves the story on, and {最后|zuì hòu} and {从|cóng}{那|nà}{天|tiān}{以后|yǐ hòu} close it.

## {遇到|yù dào}, {遇见|yù jiàn} and {发现|fā xiàn}

| Word | Meaning | Object | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| {遇到|yù dào} | to come across, to run into | people, and also problems or situations | {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{路上|lù shang}{遇到|yù dào}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{老|lǎo}{同学|tóng xué}。 {我们|wǒ men}{遇到|yù dào}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{问题|wèn tí}。 |
| {遇见|yù jiàn} | to meet (by chance) | people | {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{超市|chāo shì}{遇见|yù jiàn}{了|le}{王老师|Wáng lǎo shī}。 |
| {发现|fā xiàn} | to discover, to find out, to notice | facts, things | {我|wǒ}{发现|fā xiàn}{手机|shǒu jī}{不见|bú jiàn}{了|le}。 {我|wǒ}{发现|fā xiàn}{他|tā}{说|shuō}{得|de}{不|bú}{对|duì}。 |

- {遇到|yù dào} and {遇见|yù jiàn} both mean meeting without planning to. {遇到|yù dào} is wider: you {遇到|yù dào} problems ({遇到|yù dào}{问题|wèn tí}),
  bad weather and good luck too. With people, the two are interchangeable.
- A planned meeting is {见面|jiàn miàn} (lesson 29) or {见|jiàn}: {我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{见面|jiàn miàn}.
- {发现|fā xiàn} is about knowing something new: it is often followed by a whole clause ({发现|fā xiàn}{他|tā}{已经|yǐ jīng}{走|zǒu}{了|le}, found that
  he'd already left). For "find something you were looking for", Chinese uses {找|zhǎo}{到|dào} (look for + reach).

## {结束|jié shù}, {分开|fēn kāi} and {变成|biàn chéng}

{结束|jié shù} is "to end, to finish" (of an event): {比赛|bǐ sài}{结束|jié shù}{了|le}。 (The match is over.) {会议|huì yì}{几|jǐ}{点|diǎn}{结束|jié shù}？ (What time
does the meeting finish?) A person finishing a task says {完|wán} ({做|zuò}{完|wán}, {写|xiě}{完|wán}): {我|wǒ}{写|xiě}{完|wán}{了|le}{作业|zuò yè}, not ×{我|wǒ}{结束|jié shù}{了|le}{作业|zuò yè}.

{分开|fēn kāi} is "to separate, to part": {我们|wǒ men}{在|zài}{路口|lù kǒu}{分开|fēn kāi}{了|le}。 (We went our separate ways at the crossroads.) It
works for things too: {把|bǎ}{白|bái}{衣服|yī fu}{和|hé}{黑|hēi}{衣服|yī fu}{分开|fēn kāi}{洗|xǐ}。 (Wash the white and dark clothes separately.)

{变成|biàn chéng} is "to become, to turn into": {水|shuǐ}{变成|biàn chéng}{了|le}{冰|bīng}。 (The water turned to ice.) {他|tā}{从|cóng}{一|yí}{个|gè}{小|xiǎo}{孩子|hái zi}{变成|biàn chéng}{了|le}{一|yí}{个|gè}{大人|dà ren}。
(He changed from a child into an adult.) Compare {变|biàn} (to change, lesson 10): {天气|tiān qì}{变|biàn}{了|le} (the weather
has changed) has no result after it; {变成|biàn chéng} always names what something becomes.

## {长|zhǎng}: to grow; head of…

The character 长 has two readings. You know {长|cháng} (long) from HSK 2. Read zhǎng, it means "to
grow" and "head, chief":

- {长大|zhǎng dà}: to grow up. {我|wǒ}{在|zài}{上海|Shàng hǎi}{长大|zhǎng dà}。 (I grew up in Shanghai.)
- {长|zhǎng} + adjective: {孩子|hái zi}{长|zhǎng}{高|gāo}{了|le}。 (The child has got taller.)
- {长|zhǎng}{得|de} + description: how someone looks, as nature made them: {她|tā}{长|zhǎng}{得|de}{很|hěn}{像|xiàng}{她|tā}{妈妈|mā ma}。 (She looks like her
  mum.)
- At the end of a word, "head of": {校长|xiào zhǎng} (head teacher, lesson 29), {班长|bān zhǎng} (class monitor),
  {市长|shì zhǎng} (mayor).

Context decides the reading: 长 for growing ({长大|zhǎng dà}, {长|zhǎng}{高|gāo}, {长|zhǎng}{得|de}) or after a noun as a title is zhǎng;
describing length ({这|zhè}{条|tiáo}{路|lù}{很|hěn}{长|cháng}) it's cháng. Both are 長 in traditional script.

## {过去|guò qù}: the past

You know the verb {过去|guò qù} (to go over, HSK 2: {你|nǐ}{过去|guò qù}{看看|kàn kan}). As a noun, {过去|guò qù} is "the past", and it's
usually set against {现在|xiàn zài}:

{过去|guò qù}{我|wǒ}{不|bù}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{吃|chī}{辣|là}{的|de} ({辣|là}: spicy)，{现在|xiàn zài}{很|hěn}{喜欢|xǐ huan}。 — I used to dislike spicy food; now I love it.

{这个|zhè ge}{城市|chéng shì}{跟|gēn}{过去|guò qù}{不|bù}{一样|yí yàng}{了|le}。 — This city isn't what it used to be.

{过去|guò qù}{的|de}{事|shì}，{就|jiù}{别|bié}{想|xiǎng}{了|le}。 — What's past is past: don't dwell on it.

At the start of a sentence, or before {的|de}, it's the noun; after a verb of movement it's the verb ({走|zǒu}{过去|guò qù},
walk over).

## Arguing a point: {当然|dāng rán}, {其实|qí shí}, {比如|bǐ rú}, {关于|guān yú}, {主要|zhǔ yào}, {重要|zhòng yào}

- {当然|dāng rán}: of course, naturally. {你|nǐ}{想|xiǎng}{来|lái}{吗|ma}？——{当然|dāng rán}{想|xiǎng}！ (Do you want to come? Of course!)
- {其实|qí shí}: actually, in fact: it corrects what someone (or you) thought. {大家|dà jiā}{都|dōu}{说|shuō}{这个|zhè ge}{很|hěn}{难|nán}，{其实|qí shí}{很|hěn}{容易|róng yì}。 (Everyone
  says it's hard; actually it's easy.)
- {比如|bǐ rú}: for example. {我|wǒ}{喜欢|xǐ huan}{运动|yùn dòng}，{比如|bǐ rú}{游泳|yóu yǒng}、{爬|pá}{山|shān}。 (I like sport: swimming and hiking, for example.)
- {关于|guān yú}: about, on (a topic). At the start of a sentence: {关于|guān yú}{这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}，{我们|wǒ men}{明天|míng tiān}{再|zài}{说|shuō}。 (About this, let's
  talk tomorrow.) Before a noun, with {的|de}: {一|yì}{本|běn}{关于|guān yú}{中国|Zhōng guó}{历史|lì shǐ}{的|de}{书|shū} (a book about Chinese history).
- {主要|zhǔ yào}: main, mainly. {我|wǒ}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}，{主要|zhǔ yào}{是|shì}{因为|yīn wèi}{工作|gōng zuò}。 (I'm learning Chinese mainly for work.)
- {重要|zhòng yào}: important. {这|zhè}{件|jiàn}{事|shì}{很|hěn}{重要|zhòng yào}。 {健康|jiàn kāng}{最|zuì}{重要|zhòng yào}。 (Health matters most.)

A short opinion often uses several of them: {我|wǒ}{认为|rèn wéi}{学|xué}{汉语|Hàn yǔ}{最|zuì}{重要|zhòng yào}{的|de}{是|shì}{多|duō}{说|shuō}。{当然|dāng rán}，{汉字|hàn zì}{也|yě}{很|hěn}{重要|zhòng yào}，{其实|qí shí}{写|xiě}{汉字|hàn zì}{没有|méi yǒu}{大家|dà jiā}{想|xiǎng}{的|de}{那么|nà me}{难|nán}。

— I think the most important thing in learning Chinese is to speak a lot. Of course characters are
important too, and actually writing them isn't as hard as people think.

## {怎样|zěn yàng}, {怎么办|zěn me bàn}, {行|xíng}, {不行|bù xíng}, {常见|cháng jiàn}, {常用|cháng yòng}

- {怎样|zěn yàng} is a more written "how": {这个|zhè ge}{字|zì}{怎样|zěn yàng}{写|xiě}？ (= {怎么|zěn me}{写|xiě}). In speech you'll mostly hear {怎么|zěn me} and {怎么样|zěn me yàng}.
- {怎么办|zěn me bàn} is "what should I do?, what can be done?": {我|wǒ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{丢|diū}{了|le}，{怎么办|zěn me bàn}？
- {行|xíng} is "OK, fine, all right" ({行|xíng}，{我们|wǒ men}{走|zǒu}{吧|ba}) and "capable, good at it" ({你|nǐ}{真|zhēn}{行|xíng}！ You're great!). {不行|bù xíng} is "won't
  do, no good, not allowed": {这样|zhè yàng}{不行|bù xíng}。 (That won't do.) {明天|míng tiān}{不行|bù xíng}，{后天|hòu tiān}{行|xíng}{吗|ma}？ (Tomorrow's no good: how
  about the day after?)
- {常见|cháng jiàn} (common, often seen) and {常用|cháng yòng} (in common use): {感冒|gǎn mào}{是|shì}{很|hěn}{常见|cháng jiàn}{的|de}{病|bìng}。 {这些|zhè xiē}{是|shì}{最|zuì}{常用|cháng yòng}{的|de}{汉字|hàn zì}。

{行|xíng} is xíng here. The same character is read háng in {银行|yín háng} (bank, lesson 09).

## Rhetorical questions

A **[[rhetorical question]]** asks something whose answer is obvious, to make a point more strongly.
English does it too ("Didn't I tell you?"). Chinese has a few set frames:

| Frame | Example | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| {不|bú}{是|shì}…{吗|ma}？ | {你|nǐ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{去|qù}{过|guo}{北京|Běi jīng}{吗|ma}？ | You've been to Beijing, haven't you? (So you know.) |
| {这|zhè}{不|bú}{是|shì}…{吗|ma}？ | {这|zhè}{不|bú}{是|shì}{你|nǐ}{的|de}{手机|shǒu jī}{吗|ma}？ | Isn't this your phone? (Here it is!) |
| {怎么|zěn me}{会|huì}…{呢|ne}？ | {他|tā}{怎么|zěn me}{会|huì}{不|bù}{知道|zhī dào}{呢|ne}？ | How could he not know? (Of course he knows.) |
| {谁|shéi}{不|bù}…？ | {谁|shéi}{不|bù}{想|xiǎng}{去|qù}？ | Who doesn't want to go? (Everyone does.) |
| {哪儿|nǎr}…{啊|a}？ | {我|wǒ}{哪儿|nǎr}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān}{啊|a}？ | Where would I find the time? (I don't have any.) |

The trick is that a negative question makes a positive statement, and a positive one a negative:
{不|bú}{是|shì}{去|qù}{过|guo}{吗|ma} = you have been; {哪儿|nǎr}{有|yǒu}{时间|shí jiān} = no time at all. Listen for the tone of voice too: rhetorical
questions are often said with surprise or impatience, and sometimes end in {呢|ne} or {啊|a}. Don't answer
them as real questions.

## Characters
{=

| Character | Meaning | Pinyin | Radical | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 主 | master; main | zhǔ | 丶 | 5 | {主要|zhǔ yào} |
| 重 | heavy; important | zhòng (also chóng) | 里 | 9 | {重要|zhòng yào} |
| 遇 | meet | yù | 辶 | 12 | {遇到|yù dào}, {遇见|yù jiàn} |
| 束 | bundle; tie | shù | 木 | 7 | {结束|jié shù} |
| 当 (traditional 當) | act as; ought to | dāng | ⺌ | 6 | {当然|dāng rán} |
| 实 (traditional 實) | real, true | shí | 宀 | 8 | {其实|qí shí} |

- {主|zhǔ}: a dot over 王. The oldest forms are explained as a lamp with its flame on top. {主|zhǔ} is a strong
  sound component: it gives zhù in {住|zhù} (to live, HSK 1) and {注|zhù} ({注意|zhù yì}, lesson 05), close to its own zhǔ.
- {重|zhòng}: "heavy" and "important" ({重要|zhòng yào}). In other words it's read chóng, "again" (you'll meet {重新|chóng xīn},
  anew, in HSK 4). Make Me a Hanzi files it under {里|lǐ}, as dictionaries do. With the
  traditional script on, you'll see {重|zhòng} inside 動 (to move: {运动|yùn dòng} 運動).
- {遇|yù}: 辶 (walking) and 禺, which once gave the sound yú: close to yù, but only just.
- {束|shù}: 木 (wood) tied round the middle by a {口|kǒu}-shaped cord: a bundle. {结束|jié shù} is "tie up, end".
- {当|dāng}: three short strokes on top and 彐 below. Traditional 當 has 尚 over 田 (13 strokes).
- {实|shí}: 宀 (roof) over {头|tóu}. Traditional 實 is 宀 over 貫 (a string of coins): a house full of
  money, "solid, real". The simplified {头|tóu} is just a shorter shape, not a meaning.

### Stroke order

- **主**: the dot first, then 王: top horizontal, middle horizontal, the vertical, the bottom
  horizontal.
- **重**: the short left-falling stroke on top first, then the long horizontal, the box ({日|rì}), and
  only then the long vertical down the middle, then the last two horizontals.
- **束**: the horizontal, then {口|kǒu}, then the long vertical through it, then the left- and
  right-falling strokes.
- **当**: the middle vertical on top, then the left dot and the right left-falling stroke, then
  彐 (the horizontal-turn and two horizontals).
- **遇**: the inside first, 辶 last, as in {这|zhè} and {还|hái}.

```trace
主重遇束当实
```

{安娜|Ān nà} (安娜) can't find her phone. {大卫|Dà wèi} (大卫) helps.

- {你|nǐ}{不|bú}{是|shì}{把|bǎ}{它|tā}{放|fàng}{在|zài}{包|bāo}{里|lǐ}{了|le}{吗|ma}？: a rhetorical question with a {把|bǎ} sentence (lesson 03): "you put it in your
  bag, didn't you?"
- {哪儿|nǎr}{有|yǒu}{啊|a}？: "where is it, then?", said in frustration: it doesn't seem to be anywhere.
